## 26. BONUS: Dream 100 Claude Project Setup

Source: https://learn.clientascension.com/products/ai-assisted-agency/categories/2158957593/posts/2196059115

Prompt document: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1lTLfJA7Y6ZPkcZSnm-v3tIxwnwOqb6CJS1Br1nUGdBQ/edit?usp=sharing

Reviewed the full 17.6-minute audio using a locally generated automatic transcript and read the complete linked **Marquee Method AI Outreach — Prompting Guide** by Christian Bonnier. Original prompt document preserved in `sources/d100-26-prompt-document.md`.

- **0–1:** Create a Claude project for Dream 100 outreach. Put the guide in project **instructions**, not merely the files area. Start with “run step zero.” The project asks for business and offer information.
- **1–4:** Supply service, offer level, ideal client, lead magnet, proof and chosen niches. The demonstration asks for niche suggestions because it depicts a beginner; DRM already has its niches and should supply them. The output suggests qualification signals, disqualifiers, discovery channels and a scoring rubric.
- **4–7:** Find real prospects, choose one and research a specific relevant hook, current offer, audience, public pain points, tone and recent news. The coach tests against his business partner so he can recognize errors. His initial enthusiasm does not establish that all AI research is correct.
- **7–10:** Generate and edit email/DM/voice-note drafts. He says the initial copy needs judgment and corrections. He explicitly invents a low-YouTube-activity scenario only for illustration and calls it false; do not repeat it as a real fact about Daniel Fazio.
- **10–13:** Generate the actual sample deliverable, illustrated by a YouTube script and thumbnail concept, then review it. This is a sample for the demonstrated content service, not a requirement to add that service to DRM.
- **13–17:39:** Repeat with a new prospect. The demonstration confuses people, companies and biographical details. The coach explicitly asks for sources and ends by telling students to fact-check everything used in outreach. This directly supports retaining URLs and checking identity before using AI-generated research.

### Prompt guide details and difference from the earlier lessons

The guide has four prompts: **0 prospect criteria/discovery/scoring**, **1 research brief**, **2 three outreach versions**, and **3 a finished deliverable**. Research outputs should include a specific verifiable hook, offer, ICP, public problems, tone, news and outreach angle. It asks for a 1–10 prioritization rubric; hypothetical example types are allowed in initial ideation, so they must not be mistaken for verified leads.

The guide classifies offers by awareness: level 1 prospects know they need the service; level 2 know the category but need a reason to choose the provider; level 3 need more education and upfront work. Categories overlap in its examples (ads appear in both levels 2 and 3), so the prospect's situation matters more than a universal label.

**The resource teaches a different sequence from Daniel James's core Dream 100 lessons.** Christian's guide asks permission to share, then creates the deliverable after a positive reply. It proposes day 1, day 3 and day 7 follow-ups, with the same offer and brief wording. Daniel's earlier lessons recommend finished work and a direct viewing link upfront. Preserve these as two course-taught variants; do not silently combine contradictory first-message CTAs. The guide's universal claim that ten personalized messages always beat 500 generic messages is motivational copy, not a supplied test result.

**DRM status:** Source instructions saved and ready to adapt using the existing niches and actual verified proof. No Claude project was created and no new subscription started during video-first review.

<a id="coaching-section-73"></a>
## 27. Social Proof Deck Creation

Source: https://learn.clientascension.com/products/ai-assisted-agency/categories/2158957593/posts/2197446843

Reviewed the entire 19.8-minute audio through a locally generated automatic transcript. Recording filename identifies May 13, 2026. No published captions were exposed. Unclear automatic-transcript tool names are not treated as verified names.

- **0–3:15 — collect proof continuously:** Build one accessible collection of genuine client results, positive client comments, screenshots and other relevant evidence. Add new proof as it appears. The coach shows long proof collections and places his link in outreach, sales conversations and YouTube descriptions. A business with little proof should start with what it actually has and grow the collection.
- **3:15–5:15 — explain the offer:** Build process, guarantee and FAQ assets. Mine sales-call recordings/transcripts for repeated objections and questions. His examples include cost per large client, how meetings are booked, whether it fits an industry, scalability, turnaround, how it compares with alternatives and brand/compliance concerns. These describe his creative-outbound offer; DRM needs its own answers.
- **5:15–8:40 — pre-call education:** Put short answers and proof on the booking confirmation page. Explain the process and why its mechanism suits the buyer's situation. His example uses client lifetime value and large-client economics; the same reasoning structure can explain an industry-specific DRM offer. Claims comparing channels need to reflect actual fit and evidence, not automatic dismissal of every alternative.
- **8:40–9:55 — make the collection an ongoing habit:** Keeping proof in one place makes it easier to notice and save new evidence. The coach says he created assets for his new offer in two days; that is his own production account, not a DRM completion estimate.
- **9:55–14:55 — prepare for objections:** Use real calls, coach/peer feedback, your own delivery knowledge and AI brainstorming to enumerate questions before they arise. Write the response/value proposition beside each, then rehearse. He describes reviewing this material about 20 minutes daily. Separate concerns about price, competing providers, existing inbound demand, premium positioning, process and implementation. His own assurances about his method's compliance do not establish a factual answer for every DRM industry.
- **14:55–18:45 — expand into lead magnets:** Create useful guides around the ICP's problems, pair relevant videos with those guides, collect email addresses on a landing page and follow with an email sequence. The coach references another business's roughly 50-email sequence; he does not supply a complete sequence or require that exact length. His spoken guide invitation emphasizes the useful free guide rather than the marketing term “lead magnet.”
- **18:45–19:50 — order of work:** Build sales assets first, then expand the objection/reference guide, then add lead magnets. Keep improving the collection as the business learns.

**DRM exercise and dependencies:** Assemble verified proof from the existing paying client and any supportable current case studies, plus industry-specific process and FAQ explanations. The user has been asked what client results/testimonial may be used and whether the client can be publicly named. A question is not approval; no unverified result or permission has been assumed. Existing website case-study claims still need their supporting evidence before being repackaged as verified proof. No public proof deck or lead magnet was published during review.

<a id="coaching-section-79"></a>
# Dead River Management — Dream 100 operating workflow

Prepared from the Dream 100 lessons. This is a saved operating procedure, not an activated campaign. The full main-video review and filled business exercises are recorded in dream100-notes.md and dream100-task-workbook.md.

<a id="coaching-section-80"></a>
## Identity, capacity, and ownership

Prospect-facing sender: **Brandon**, **brandon@deadrivermanagement.com**. The exact connected sending mailbox must be selected from the existing accounts.

Existing capacity confirmed by the user: **12 warmed inboxes, 20 emails per day per inbox = 240 total emails per day**. Every follow-up counts toward that total. Existing Instantly campaigns consume capacity too. For each inbox, the available Dream 100 allowance is `max(0, 20 - other planned sends that day)`. Never allocate the full 240 twice across campaigns. The user has 10–20 hours weekly; production capacity and relevant prospect selection, rather than the mailbox ceiling, determine the new-package pace.

The coach's email lesson later recommends rotating 15–20+ inboxes, while the introductory setup lesson starts at six. These are different scale examples. DRM's existing 12 exceed the starter example but do not equal the later 20+ recommendation. No purchase has been made and delivery performance has not been inferred from the count alone.

<a id="coaching-section-81"></a>
## Stages and required next actions

| Stage | Entry evidence | Next action | Exit evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Research | Business fits an existing industry offer | Verify business need, relevant stakeholder, source links, and usable contact | Research and actual need documented |
| Package production | Research complete | Build useful finished work and explain its business benefit | Working deliverables, correct terms, proof and link checked |
| Ready | Package passes review | Select available inbox, relevant recipient, initial message | Actual sent event |
| Sent; no known package view | Message sent; no reliable package-view signal | Encourage viewing the package, with one main CTA | View signal or reply |
| Package view signal | Gamma/Loom or equivalent event | Notify Brandon promptly; prepare relevant response/call invitation | Reply, booking, or further review task |
| Replied | Actual incoming message | Answer the question and arrange a time when appropriate | Confirmed booking, later date, disqualification, or stop |
| Call booked | Calendar confirms appointment | Supply relevant pre-call materials and confirmation | Attendance or no-show |
| Call held | Attendance confirmed | Record needs, decision process and agreed next step | Proposal, won, lost, or follow-up date |
| Won | Actual agreement/payment record as applicable | Begin the existing fulfillment process | Handoff complete |
| Stop | Explicit stop request, invalid address, or disqualification | Remove from further Dream 100 follow-ups | Suppression recorded |

<a id="coaching-section-82"></a>
## View-signal handling

Keep package views separate from email opens and link clicks. A signal does not demonstrate full reading or purchase intent. Store the source, time, package ID, and viewer identity when actually available. If a package is shared among stakeholders and the viewer is anonymous, do not name a person as the viewer. Do not label absence of tracking as proof that somebody has never read it.

The coach calls for immediate follow-up upon viewing. Implementation needs a working notification destination and account capability; until verified, it remains an open setup item. No automatic messages are enabled by this file. Any future automation must stop obsolete pre-view follow-ups when a verified view or reply changes the stage, and stop all prospecting follow-ups after an explicit stop request or booking.

<a id="coaching-section-83"></a>
## Stakeholder handling

Start with the actual decision maker and relevant functional owner. For a larger company, the coach also suggests an assistant and a small number of relevant department employees. Do not select an arbitrary number of employees merely to increase volume. Associate stakeholders with one company and one package. A company-wide view signal must not be counted as several distinct prospects responding.

<a id="coaching-section-84"></a>
## Package production checklist

- Keep the existing industry-specific service and pricing; Growth Partner is obsolete.
- Record the actual public observation and source that led to selecting this prospect.
- Supply finished useful work, not a list of tasks for the prospect to do.
- Explain how the finished work addresses the observed issue and desired business outcome.
- Include an outcome headline, simple contents, clear sections, relevant proof, and a next step.
- Use actual DRM evidence when available. Clearly attribute any external example.
- Explain client effort, delivery, and common objections without inventing capabilities.
- Use large readable text and plain language; check mobile readability and link access.
- Test the actual package notification flow before depending on it.
- Keep the package link as the initial email's main CTA; the package itself can offer a call.

<a id="coaching-section-85"></a>
## Diagnostic review

Based on lesson 6, inspect each transition rather than changing everything at once: poor package-view activity suggests reviewing message, recipient and delivery; views without responses suggest package relevance and follow-up; responses without bookings suggest booking logistics; no-shows suggest pre-call materials and confirmation; held calls without sales suggest the sales process. The instructor assumes a sound list and offer in this model; those assumptions and reliable tracking must be checked before treating the diagnosis as certain.

<a id="coaching-section-86"></a>
## Setup still required

Gamma/Loom accounts are available. The approved Loom first-view/comment email alerts are enabled; a private Gamma folder and an eight-slide approved website proof deck are created. Still required: existing inbox allocation; researched prospects; finished individual packages and Brandon recordings; booking destination checks; actual event test and CRM mapping. This document does not establish that those remaining external actions are complete.

# Dead River Management — Dream 100 task workbook

Updated September 27, 2026. These are filled business exercises and prepared operating materials. A completed worksheet is not a sent campaign, recorded Loom or researched prospect package. External setup status is listed at the end.

<a id="coaching-section-89"></a>
## 1. Business and acquisition brief

**Business:** Dead River Management. **Sender:** Brandon, brandon@deadrivermanagement.com. **Current position:** one paying client. **Goal:** $20,000 monthly profit. **Available time:** 10–20 hours per week. **Sales experience:** comfortable with strategy calls and consultative selling.

**Existing niches:** home services, dental, med spas, ecommerce and real estate. Each uses its existing industry-specific offer. Demand Intelligence stays a separate product. Growth Partner is obsolete. No niche changes are proposed.

**Available tools:** GHL CRM and calendar, existing Instantly infrastructure, 12 warmed inboxes with a user-stated limit of 20 emails each per day, existing Loom and Gamma accounts. LinkedIn company page and YouTube channel exist. Whop remains deferred.

**Chosen initial Dream 100 format:** Gamma document containing finished useful work, supported by a personal Loom from Brandon. Use Daniel James's work-first method for this implementation. Christian's permission-first bonus is a separate later test, not mixed into the first sequence.

**Entry offer:** A prospect-specific acquisition improvement package prepared before outreach. It demonstrates work relevant to the existing paid service. The next step is a conversation about using the work and ongoing delivery. This does not add unlimited free implementation or alter published paid terms.

<a id="coaching-section-90"></a>
## 2. What would we actually do for a substantial paid engagement?

This answers lesson 17's exercise without creating a new $10,000 price.

| Existing industry | Business outcome to investigate | Useful Dream 100 deliverable | Proof to pair with it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Home services | Qualified estimates that turn into booked jobs | Rewrite one actual service landing page, create matching search-ad copy, and write estimate/no-show follow-up | Gonzalez & Sons Roofing or The Pipe Whisperers, choosing the closest trade |
| Dental | New attended patient appointments | Rewrite one actual treatment/new-patient booking page, create matching ad copy, and prepare inquiry-to-appointment reminders | Use existing acquisition/process proof with the actual client industry named; no dental case-study result invented |
| Med spas | New treatment bookings and revenue | Prepare one treatment-specific campaign angle, landing-page copy and consultation follow-up | Existing lead capture/follow-up examples, clearly identified by their actual industries |
| Ecommerce | Profit from customer acquisition | Prepare a specific product campaign, landing-page changes and a relevant welcome/cart flow when that solves the observed problem | PMG for acquisition testing/process and Only Fish for brand/website execution, without calling either ecommerce profit proof |
| Real estate | Qualified attended appointments | Prepare a specific buyer/seller campaign and booking page with qualification and appointment follow-up | Existing lead-generation examples with their actual industries retained |

**Best-results exercise:** Research the prospect's actual offer and conversion path, identify one consequential problem, deliver the corresponding finished asset, explain why the change fits, connect it to follow-up, and make the next action easy. Do not substitute a generic list of suggestions for the promised deliverable.

**Maximum-effort exercise:** Put the prospect's own services, audience, geography, proof, objections and destination links into the sample. Show finished copy/creative or a working page preview. Use a personal introduction and a relevant DRM result. Spend extra effort on specificity before increasing length or production volume.

<a id="coaching-section-91"></a>
## 3. Prospect criteria and scoring

These are DRM implementation choices derived from lessons 17–18 and the bonus guide, not numerical rules stated by the coach.

Score each dimension 0, 1 or 2, for a total of 10:

1. **Offer fit:** 0 outside current service/industry; 1 plausible; 2 clear match to an existing offer.
2. **Observable opportunity:** 0 no supported problem; 1 a hypothesis; 2 a documented issue/opportunity with a source and specific fix.
3. **Business readiness:** 0 clearly unable to take more business; 1 unknown; 2 visible capacity/growth signals. Do not invent revenue or budgets.
4. **Stakeholder access:** 0 no suitable route; 1 general business contact; 2 a confirmed relevant decision maker or functional owner.
5. **Useful sample:** 0 generic pitch; 1 partial sample; 2 finished work that this business can understand and use.

Research the strongest-fit slice of a relevant list first. Treat 8–10 as priority once essential facts are confirmed; do not fill a score merely to reach the threshold. Unknowns remain unknown. Exclude existing clients, active opportunities already handled elsewhere, explicit stop requests and businesses outside the agreed scope.

**Discovery routes:** company websites and public business directories for local industries; relevant LinkedIn company/employee profiles for stakeholder roles; actual product/store pages for ecommerce. Use current sources for contact details. An email being available does not establish fit.

**Stakeholder rule:** Start with the owner/decision maker and the person responsible for the issue. Add other stakeholders only when their role is relevant. Store them beneath one company record and one package so one company view is not counted repeatedly.

<a id="coaching-section-92"></a>
## 4. Package specification

The completed package will contain:

1. A headline tied to the prospect's actual service and opportunity.
2. Brandon's short personal Loom introducing the observation and showing the finished work.
3. The observed problem, source link and business consequence, clearly separating fact from hypothesis.
4. A finished landing-page/ad/follow-up or other appropriate asset.
5. A short explanation of why each important change fits that business.
6. One or two relevant case studies from the approved website proof library.
7. Clear scope: what is already included, what implementation would involve and what belongs in the paid engagement.
8. A single next step to discuss fit with Brandon, with contact details at the top and bottom.

**Review score:** No package receives a quality score before it exists. Review for prospect specificity, usefulness, plain language, correct links, accurate proof, clear scope and accessible formatting. Compare the result to the coach's strongest examples before production is scaled.

<a id="coaching-section-93"></a>
## 5. AI production instructions filled for DRM

Use this business context in the coach's project/research workflow:

> You are preparing Dream 100 materials for Dead River Management. Brandon is the sender and brandon@deadrivermanagement.com is the contact address. Our existing industries are home services, dental, med spas, ecommerce and real estate, each with its existing industry offer. Do not choose a new niche or use the retired Growth Partner offer. Demand Intelligence is separate. Start by identifying the prospect's actual industry, offer and public conversion path. Research a specific opportunity using current source URLs. Keep facts, hypotheses and unknowns separate. Check that statements refer to the correct business and person. Use the approved DRM case-study library, preserving each client's name, actual industry, time period and units. Do not turn revenue into profit, leads into customers, or an annual contract value into collected cash. Prepare finished useful work for this prospect before drafting Daniel James-style outreach. The initial message's one CTA is to view that finished package. Do not claim an asset is ready before it exists. Keep each prospect's research separate. Ask only for material information that cannot be established from available sources.

**Production sequence:** research; draft actual deliverable; check sources and links; assemble Gamma; record Loom; review consumption experience; then prepare the individual message. Validate responses before delegating or scaling. No VA hire or new paid AI tool is necessary to complete the first example.

<a id="coaching-section-94"></a>
## 6. Communication tasks

**Initial email brief:** fewer than roughly 100 words, a distinctive relevant opening, actual work described in one sentence, one viewing CTA and the prospect's correct package link last. Use natural language. It cannot be finalized until a real prospect and finished package exist.

**Initial DM brief:** same principle in roughly 60 words or less. Check Brandon's relevant personal profile before using DMs; the supplied LinkedIn page is a company page. Do not infer personal-profile access from that URL.

**Before-view follow-up:** Keep attention on the useful package. Do not pretend to know the prospect has not read it just because tracking is absent.

**After-view follow-up:** Discuss the specific sample and next step. Do not tell a named person they watched it when the viewer is anonymous. Stop obsolete automatic messages on reply, booking or an explicit stop request.

**Call confirmation:** Include the actual date, time and time zone; ask the prospect to accept/confirm the invitation; send the relevant proof and FAQ/process assets immediately. A personalized confirmation video uses Brandon's real recording.

**Free-work boundary:** Try to close the paid engagement on the first call. If additional free production is agreed, write its scope and schedule the presentation call during the first call. Do not silently promise implementation of every asset in the sample.

**Public Dream 100:** Only prepare a public post once there is finished work worth showing. Feature the strongest visual component and explain its relevance. No public post or prospect message has been sent by this workbook.

<a id="coaching-section-95"></a>
## 7. Proof selection and objection answers

Website case studies approved by the user for reuse on September 27, 2026. Named published testimonials may be used. The prior request for case-study naming approval is resolved.

**“Have you done this before?”** Yes. For example, Gonzalez & Sons Roofing grew from 2 to 8 roofs per month over 6 months. The work included Google Ads, storm-damage landing pages and estimate follow-up. Show that case when the relevant mechanism is local service acquisition.

**“What happens after a lead comes in?”** The PMG case shows Facebook lead forms connected to CRM capture and automatic follow-up. Discuss the prospect's own assignment and response process, then show the relevant proposed follow-up asset.

**“Will the same result happen for us?”** The case studies show specific business outcomes and periods. The strategy conversation establishes the prospect's starting point and the current industry-specific service terms. Do not replace those terms with another client's outcome.

**“We already have an agency.”** Review whether the prepared sample addresses a gap in the current process. Explain the particular improvement and ask how it is handled today. Do not assume the agency is performing badly.

**“We get enough leads.”** Determine whether the actual issue is qualification, response, booking, attendance or conversion. If there is no meaningful need or capacity, deprioritize the prospect rather than inventing one.

**“How much work will our team do?”** Explain what DRM prepares and manages, then identify the prospect's approvals, access and sales/appointment responsibilities. Set exact responsibilities in the agreed scope rather than promising zero involvement.

**“What is the price or guarantee?”** Use the current offer for that prospect's industry and the agreed scope. Do not reuse historical case-study investment figures as present prices. Resolve any website headline/detail discrepancy before quoting a guarantee.

**“How do we measure it?”** Track the agreed business outcome through its stages. PMG's 49 are lead-form completions; Wicked's $1.2M is annual contract value. Keep these definitions explicit in the conversation.

<a id="coaching-section-96"></a>
## 8. Capacity, schedule and measurement

**Sending ceiling:** 12 × 20 = 240 total messages/day, including all follow-ups and existing campaigns. For each mailbox, available Dream 100 capacity is the configured limit minus other planned sends. A maximum is not a production target.

**Initial weekly time allocation (DRM working plan):** For a 10-hour week, allocate 2 hours to research, 4 to useful package production, 1 to recording/review, 1 to follow-up and 2 to calls/learning. With 20 hours, add 4 hours of research/production, 2 of recording, 2 of follow-up and 2 of sales work. Measure actual production time before setting a package quota. This is a practical allocation of the user's time, not a coach-specified schedule.

**KPI definitions:** unique companies researched; packages completed; companies contacted; messages sent; known package views; unique replies; positive replies; calls booked; calls attended; cancellations; clients won; production hours. Keep company and contact counts separate.

**Rates:** view rate = known company views / companies contacted; reply rate = replying companies / companies contacted; booking rate = booked companies / companies contacted; show rate = calls attended / calls due; close rate = wins / attended qualified sales calls. State date range and denominator. Track cancellations and reschedules separately. Until events exist, rates are unmeasured rather than invented.

**Profit goal:** $20,000/month is a profit goal, not revenue. A client-count target requires actual service margins and operating costs; no arbitrary client count has been asserted.

# Dead River Management — Dream 100 email sequences

Use one coherent work-first sequence, separate from the permission-first bonus.

<a id="coaching-section-103"></a>
## Required fields before sending

`company`: prospect business; `first_name`: confirmed person; `service`: actual service/product; `specific_observation`: brief sourced public observation; `package_url`: completed individual package; `asset_detail`: concrete finished improvement; `calendar_url`: checked industry-appropriate booking destination; `meeting_date`, `meeting_time`, `time_zone`: confirmed appointment details.

<a id="coaching-section-104"></a>
## 1. Initial messages by industry

### Home services

Subject: built around your {{service}}

Your {{service}} page gave me a specific idea: {{specific_observation}}.

I built a page rewrite, matching ad copy and estimate follow-up for {{company}}. The package shows how they fit together, plus our roofing case study: 2 to 8 roofs a month over 6 months.

Brandon, Dead River Management

Here’s the finished work: {{package_url}}

### Dental

Subject: your patient booking flow

{{specific_observation}}

I put together a {{service}} booking-page rewrite and inquiry follow-up for {{company}}, with the reasoning beside each change. It’s built around getting the right inquiry to an attended appointment. I included an example of our lead-capture and follow-up work so you can see how we approach it.

Brandon, Dead River Management

The package: {{package_url}}

### Med spas

Subject: made for {{service}}

{{specific_observation}}

I built a campaign angle, treatment-page rewrite and consultation follow-up around {{company}}’s {{service}}. The package explains the changes and includes our published acquisition work. You can see the actual copy, not just recommendations.

Brandon, Dead River Management

Open it here: {{package_url}}

### Ecommerce

Subject: your {{service}} campaign

{{specific_observation}}

I built {{asset_detail}} for {{company}}, using your product and customer language. The package shows the finished work and why each change fits. It also includes examples of our campaign testing and website delivery, with the client and result clearly identified.

Brandon, Dead River Management

Your package: {{package_url}}

### Real estate

Subject: built for your appointments

{{specific_observation}}

I put together a campaign, qualification page and appointment follow-up for {{company}}’s {{service}}. The goal is a clear path from the initial inquiry to a useful conversation. The package includes the finished copy and examples of our lead-generation work.

Brandon, Dead River Management

Here’s the work: {{package_url}}

<a id="coaching-section-105"></a>
## 2. Before-view follow-ups

Keep the focus on viewing the finished work. A missing view signal is not proof the person has never opened it. Timing is a campaign configuration choice, not a claimed universal coach requirement. Check actual replies and suppression before every send.

### Follow-up A

Subject: same thread

The most useful part for {{company}} is {{asset_detail}}. I wrote it around your actual {{service}}, so you can see exactly what I’d change and why.

Brandon

It’s here: {{package_url}}

### Follow-up B

Subject: same thread

One quick note on the package: the finished work is included. You don’t need to book a call just to see the idea.

Brandon

{{package_url}}

<a id="coaching-section-106"></a>
## 3. After-view follow-ups

Use the package view as an internal trigger. The message does not claim that a named individual watched when only an anonymous view is known. Stop the pre-view sequence before switching stages.

### Implementation conversation

Subject: same thread

The next step would be to walk through {{asset_detail}} and see how it fits your current process. What does your team do today after someone enquires about {{service}}?

Brandon

### Offer conversation after an engaged reply

Subject: same thread

Happy to walk you through it. We can cover the sample, what your team already handles and where our existing service would fit. What time works for you this week?

Brandon

### Calendar handoff once they want a call

Subject: same thread

You can choose a time here: {{calendar_url}}

We’ll use the call to review the work for {{company}} and the next steps that make sense for your business.

Brandon

<a id="coaching-section-107"></a>
## 4. Booking confirmation

Subject: confirmed for {{meeting_date}}

You’re booked for {{meeting_date}} at {{meeting_time}} {{time_zone}}. Please accept the calendar invitation so it’s easy to find.

Here’s the work we’ll discuss: {{package_url}}

You can also review our client results before we meet: https://gamma.app/docs/r6t43ymjbvjt782

If there’s a particular question you want covered, reply here and I’ll make sure we address it.

Brandon

**Access check:** Confirm the proof deck is viewable by the intended recipient before inserting that link into a live message. Creation in a private folder alone does not confirm external access.

<a id="coaching-section-108"></a>
## 5. Short DM version

{{specific_observation}}

I built {{asset_detail}} for {{company}} and put the reasoning beside it. You can open the finished work here:

{{package_url}}

<a id="coaching-section-109"></a>
## 6. Loom recording outline for Brandon

- Introduce yourself and name the specific business observation.
- Show the finished asset and explain the two most consequential choices.
- Show the closest relevant approved case study and state its actual time period.
- Explain what the prospect can use now and what ongoing implementation would involve.
- Invite a conversation about fit. Keep it concise; follow the coach's roughly 4–6-minute guidance where the material supports it.

Record after the actual package is ready. Do not present this reusable outline as a recorded video.

<a id="coaching-section-110"></a>
## 7. Sequence controls

Map every prospect to the correct package link. Preview every variable. Stop on reply, booking, invalid address or explicit stop. Count initial and follow-up messages against the 20-per-inbox daily limit alongside existing campaigns. Use the correct time zone. Keep company-level reporting distinct from multiple contacts. No sequence in this document has been activated in Instantly or GHL.

## Additional lessons transcribed from audio

### LinkedIn Mastery 2026 (2200745906)

- 00:00-03:20: The stack centers on HeyReach for sequences and list imports, optional Sales Navigator, Apify/Harvest API for activity checking, a small AI classifier for ICP fit and an existing CRM or sheet. A booking link supports conversion. A comment-to-DM tool is suggested for lead magnets; Slack alerts are optional. Tool names are imperfect in the automatic transcript. Sales Navigator is not presented as a necessary first purchase before validating the channel.
- 03:20-10:20: Optimize the profile so visitors quickly understand who you help, the result and the next action. The HeyReach walkthrough connects an account, configures authentication and inbox syncing, then sets limits. He starts connection requests around 20 daily on a new profile, calls 30 a middle ground and 40 aggressive. These are his examples, not verified current platform allowances. Multiple automation tools do not multiply an account's allowance. His initial claim that accounts do not get banned is qualified later by examples of restrictions and suspensions.
- The walkthrough includes authentication setup and an MCP connection. No credentials, authentication secrets, account connections or outreach settings were changed for DRM in this review. The speaker's preference about credential login versus cookies is preserved as a lesson detail, not an instruction to expose secrets in chat.
- 10:20-16:50: Define buyer, company size, geography, problem and exclusions, then check whether the audience is active on LinkedIn. Randomly sample about 1,000 prospects and examine recent reactions, such as the last 30 days. His example of 30% active in a 20,000-person market gives 6,000 active prospects. He uses roughly 2,000 viable prospects as a channel-selection heuristic and suggests resampling borderline cases.
- He favors title, keyword, recent-post and job-change filters over function, seniority and industry filters for this workflow. Quoted phrases differ from broad matching. Split searches by geography to stay within the demonstrated 2,500-result extraction limit. These interface limits are recording-time details.
- 16:50-25:30: Import search URLs or external CSVs, combine lists and maintain a master table keyed by LinkedIn profile URL. Track previously contacted and excluded records. A single most-recent reaction can establish activity. Manually inspect at least about 50 AI-scored profiles before trusting broader classification.
- Warm audiences include relevant post reactors, commenters and profile visitors. Keep lead-magnet respondents distinct from general engagement lists. Inspect whether people are qualified, not merely whether a post has many reactions. Referencing a relevant comment creates a natural conversation. The biohacking campaign is the coach's example, not a DRM campaign or result.
- 25:30-35:00: Messages should resemble a short business conversation, often 30-45 words. Default to a blank connection request unless there is a specific reason for a note. Message promptly after acceptance; the demonstration reduces the tool delay to three hours. Personalization should connect to the business problem, not an unrelated compliment followed by a pitch.
- Offer a useful resource, relevant case study or playbook before a call when appropriate. A strong direct offer can justify a direct call ask. Templates are examples to adapt, not wording to copy blindly. Open with a relevant problem, desired outcome, qualifying either/or question or decision-maker question. Follow-ups should add value rather than merely bumping. Later messages can be spaced by weeks. Test variants as separate campaigns and prevent duplicates across campaigns/senders.
- 35:00-43:10: Check recipient time zone, schedule, merge fields, list quality, limits and the accepted-connection branch. Maintain reporting. Start inbox management manually, using AI for drafts and learning from actual response quality. Add product facts and FAQs to the drafting context. Tags and campaign filters keep the unified inbox manageable. Voice notes can support warm conversations. Slack routing and more complex automation are optional after the channel works, not required beginner setup.
- 43:10-47:30: Coach's directional targets: about 20% minimum connection acceptance, above 20% response on a three-message sequence, at least 10% of replies positive with roughly 25% a stronger goal and 50% excellent, and more than half of interested leads booking calls. Diagnose acceptance through profile/targeting/activity, response through relevance, and booking through timely follow-up. Positive-reply percentage here uses replies as denominator, not all prospects.
- He describes around 500 connection requests as a useful evaluation sample while allowing obvious failures to be corrected earlier. The inbound opt-in benchmarks vary by audience breadth; the transcript does not establish every displayed metric's denominator, so the incomplete on-screen table should not be reconstructed as exact. His 10% opt-in-to-call figure is a stretch example rather than a guarantee.
- 47:30-end: A lead magnet should promise one useful outcome or solve one relevant pain, connect to the service, contain substantive resources and include a next action. Match the opt-in page headline to the post. Use real result screenshots or resource previews and consistent branding. The speaker recommends putting the comment keyword CTA in the image, avoiding a link in the post and replying so people check DMs. Those distribution claims are his recording-time guidance.
- His preference is five to seven quality posts weekly, but three good posts beat five weak ones. Formats include sales objections, client breakdowns, process walkthroughs, lead magnets and case-study teardowns. Sales calls, outreach questions and actual work supply topics. About two lead magnets weekly is his suggested cadence.
- Configure the comment-to-DM tool with the post, keyword, message and public reply. He discusses moderation of high DM volume and sharing a pinned resource link when volume is high. Engage personally during the first 90 minutes. After an opt-in, ask a specific qualifying question, have a relevant conversation and then offer a call.
- Exercise sequence: optimize profile, validate active ICP size, clean/deduplicate and sample-score the list, draft relevant sequences, configure tracking, handle early replies personally and test a relevant lead magnet. No messages, posts, tool purchases or launches were executed in this archival pass. The spoken lesson is fully preserved; the companion guide's unspoken prompts, screenshots and tables are a separate resource gap.

The following lessons lacked published captions. Their full timestamped automatic transcripts are archived by lesson ID. Wording, names and numbers can contain speech recognition errors; the notes distinguish examples from DRM settings.

### How to Do Cold Email in 2026 (2197048984)

- 00:00-17:00: Cold email is a delivery channel. Start with expertise in the offer, customer and product. Relevance matters more than elaborate personalization. Revisit offer training and keep testing rather than leaving one campaign unchanged. The coach's scale example is 1,000 daily emails, a new campaign or meaningful variation daily and 90 days of iteration. These are his operating examples, not a change to DRM's 240-email daily capacity.
- 17:00-25:00: Diversify channels, learn from actual replies and build lookalikes from responding customers. Dream 100 describes a highly relevant, personalized offer, deliverable by email, LinkedIn, mail or another channel, rather than a separate sending technology.
- 25:00-45:00: Four infrastructure pieces are domains, inboxes, leads and a sender. Claude skills support strategy. Use separate outreach domains, warm inboxes for at least two weeks, preferably three, and keep backups. He discusses Porkbun, ScaledMail, Peaker, InboxKit and CheapInboxes. Prices and provider capacities are recording-time examples. This overview favors inexpensive .info domains based on his tests; the dedicated infrastructure lesson recommends .com for beginners. Both teachings are retained.
- ListKit is presented as verified, ready-to-send data; the speaker discloses his ownership. DIY scraping and an email-finding waterfall can cost less money but require more work. Smartlead is his preferred sender; Instantly, EmailBison and PlusVibe are alternatives. Use plain text, disable open tracking, send during business hours and use a short follow-up sequence.
- 45:00-58:00: Feed the writing system actual sales calls, feedback, voice notes, prior campaigns and customer language. Review the output before uploading a list and launching. Revisit nonresponders with new angles after a cooling period, typically discussed as one to three months. Nonresponse is not proof that an email was unseen; suppression and opt-out records remain separate.
- Review angles, reply sentiment and infrastructure weekly; review sends, campaigns, replies, positive replies, calls and cash monthly. His daily maintenance estimate is 10-20 minutes plus response handling, not a verified DRM workload.
- 58:00-end: A separate client project should contain sales calls, onboarding information, campaign history and communication. AI supports the operator rather than replacing review. Staffing capacity examples belong to the coach; hiring remains deferred for DRM.
- Exercise sequence: clarify offer and ICP, calculate infrastructure, warm inboxes, prepare verified lists, generate and review campaigns, measure outcomes and iterate. This transcript review did not launch campaigns or purchase capacity.

### Domains and Inboxes (2198240433)

- 00:00-08:00: Protect the main business domain with separate outreach domains. Work backward from desired sending volume and provider capacity. Begin warming while preparing copy and lists. The Peaker demonstration uses a developing interface; alternatives include ScaledMail, InboxKit and Maildoso.
- 08:00-21:00: Beginner default is .com. The suggested Google/Microsoft mix is approximately equal sending volume, not equal numbers of domains. Connect the sender workspace using its API key, then verify the connection. A failed first demonstration attempt is corrected; it is not a necessary workflow step.
- The recorded example uses 13 Google domains with two inboxes each and three Microsoft domains with 50 inboxes each. At 20 and four sends respectively, the arithmetic is 520 plus 600 daily sends, not precisely 1,000. Provider-specific safe/large settings also appear. Do not transplant those limits into existing DRM inboxes without checking their actual provider.
- 21:00-end: Search for or import domains, forward them to the business website and use one or two real sender identities. He explicitly discourages invented sender names. Use the person's photo or business logo. Recorded costs and provisioning times are examples. His practice of disabling domain renewals is not an action taken for DRM.
- Confirm inboxes appear in the sender and warmup is active before sending. This lesson suggests little extra benefit beyond three weeks, whereas the overview discusses longer-warmed backups; the distinction is preserved.

### Leads List Building: Before You Start (2198206510)

- Define the offer, geography, customer value, sector terminology, buyer titles and total addressable market before exporting records. A roughly 10,000-company market is a guideline, with local and high-value exceptions.
- Example: 10,000 companies x three contacts x 65% reachable equals 19,500 contacts. Three emails each yields 58,500 sends, about 58.5 days at 1,000 daily sends. The automatic transcript misrecognizes one number; the arithmetic is stated explicitly here.
- He discusses recycling after 30-90 days, using 60 as an example. A tiny market can exhaust too quickly for the proposed volume.
- The /TAM skill estimates market size with assumptions. Challenge and refine those assumptions rather than treating an AI estimate as a verified count.
- His crypto-recruiting example failed to support the promised outcome because the market was too small despite multiple channels. Exercise: estimate reachable market before promising campaign output. The linked skill file has not been acquired in this pass.

### Leads List Building: ICP (2198921798)

- Persist an ICP.md and the client's onboarding form/call in the client project. Use them to assess proposed lists and explain exclusions.
- Search companies then people, or test direct people search. Database industry labels may be self-reported; combine relevant adjacent categories and inspect results. Verify AI-suggested filter labels against the actual interface.
- Headcount ranges generally have better coverage than revenue estimates or exact headcounts. Add relevant geography, company type, keywords, exclusions and, when useful, technology usage. Do not exclude organizations merely because the coach excludes them for his own offer.
- Buyer titles vary by business size. Understand exact versus contains matching and include genuine title variants. New hires can be a timing signal. Person location and company location are different filters.
- His stated customer-value and headcount preferences are his ICP, not DRM's niche. Exercise: inspect actual matched companies and decision-makers before scaling.

### Leads List Building: Two Types of Lists (2198206523)

- Large databases such as ListKit, Clay-connected sources, Sales Navigator, Apollo and AI Ark are convenient and often more heavily contacted.
- Custom or niche sources include Maps, Outscraper, Apify, directories, Discolike and Storeleads. They can expose less-used segments but require more cleaning and work.
- Budget for data experimentation as well as sending infrastructure. Avoid accumulating subscriptions without a use case. Vendor prices and reseller examples are historical, not purchases approved or made for DRM.

### Leads List Building: AI Ark (2198206527)

- Compare company-first account targeting with direct people search. The demonstration targets US AI-related companies with 11-200 employees and funding in the last five years. Funding date is not founding date.
- Use AI to suggest keywords, then test actual search counts and inspect websites. Excess keywords can eliminate useful matches. The recorded counts are demonstrations, not current database availability.
- Roles should fit the offer. Broader people searches and alternate terms such as machine learning produce different coverage; a term returning zero does not establish that the market is absent.
- Export charges can precede discovering email coverage. Verify addresses afterward. Ask an AI cleaning pass to return excluded records and reasons, then inspect the decisions.
- Preserve previous exports to avoid duplicate charges. The demonstrated bulk include/exclude function accepts LinkedIn URLs. Exercise: compare coverage, cost and relevance on a small sample before scaling.

### Leads List Building: Clay (2198206531)

- Clay coordinates multiple data providers. Start with suitable company industries, keywords, size, type and location. Adjacent labels may be needed when a niche is not a selectable industry.
- The recorded search cap is 25,000; larger searches can be split and prior results excluded. Limits and pricing depend on the account and recording date.
- Link people searches to the company table, preferably using LinkedIn company identifiers where domain matching introduces noise. Test title matching and inspect unexpectedly small results rather than accepting them.
- Basic profile results do not necessarily include email. Enrich using a suitable provider or waterfall, then verify. The lesson demonstrates providers including Prospeo, LeadMagic and AI Ark, followed by verification and a possible sender integration.
- Optional AI qualification can score ICP fit. Account for enrichment and AI costs separately. No DRM enrichment purchase or export was performed in this review.

### Leads List Building: Google Maps (2198922608)

- A linked free business directory is organized by niche. Copy the working sheet, choose the category and export the relevant records. This pass preserves the lesson transcript, not the linked multi-million-record dataset.
- Inspect name, description, category, website, phone, email, ratings and review counts. The med-spa demonstration contains substantial irrelevant matches; category membership alone is insufficient.
- The coach uses substantial review volume and a rating threshold for some blue-collar searches. These are examples rather than universal rules or new DRM filters.
- Enrich missing descriptions from websites when needed. Use a generic greeting for a role inbox instead of inventing a person's name. Clean legal suffixes and overly long company strings while preserving identity. Verify emails before upload.

### Leads List Building: Custom Scraping (2198206536)

- Compare Outscraper convenience with Apify actors, reviews, usage and pricing. Test a small city/category before a broader run. Tool and plan prices are recording-time examples.
- Maps records can be misclassified. Filter for the intended business, inspect reviews/ratings and verify public email data. Use appropriate company greetings where personal names are unknown.
- Other sources include Storeleads, public government lists, associations, member directories and trade-show exhibitors. These can reveal companies missing from mainstream databases.
- A large free US business dataset is mentioned, with a GitHub resource and ZIP-code filtering. The automatic transcript is not sufficient to establish its exact URL; the dataset is not represented as downloaded.
- The energy-broker and security-company examples illustrate niche sources. A high total reply rate can still contain unqualified responses. Exercise: inspect qualification and positive replies, not just response volume.

### Leads List Building: Cleaning (2198206539)

- Reverify data, including provider-labeled verified records. This is stricter than the overview's ready-to-send ListKit description, and both are retained. He prefers MillionVerifier in this lesson.
- Keep valid addresses; catchalls are a separate decision and may be checked with a specialized verifier. His bounce target is around 1% or lower, with 2-3% prompting investigation rather than an automatic conclusion that infrastructure is ruined.
- Segment by company size, buyer role and buyer priorities. Technical and financial buyers may need different messages even in the same business. Separate campaigns make comparison clearer.
- Identify security email gateways through MX data or an enrichment tool. He discusses excluding or separating them based on his experience. His deliverability claims are attributed to him, not asserted as universal facts.
- Ask about buying priorities during onboarding and maintain the agency's own acquisition while delivering client work. Exercise: clean and segment before upload, preserving exclusion reasons.

### Leads List Building: KPIs (2198922535)

- 00:00-02:00: Allow meaningful sample size and time before judging a list. His example is at least 48 hours and a few thousand sends. Target roughly 1% or lower recipient bounces; investigate data source/verifier if persistently higher. Sender bounces are a different diagnostic and require checking inboxes/provider/sender support.

Positive reply rate here means positive replies divided by all replies. This denominator differs from lessons measuring positive replies per prospect; do not compare them as the same metric.
- 04:00-end: Read reply content for wrong-person, irrelevant-industry or nonprofit/education mismatches. Hold offer/copy reasonably constant while testing audience, or isolate another variable. Provide the actual list, titles, replies and earlier campaign context to AI for diagnosis. Check its conclusions against the data. Low positive response may come from offer, copy or targeting; iterative testing distinguishes them.

Lesson IDs below identify the corresponding text and media metadata. Published captions may contain transcription errors. Locally generated transcripts are explicitly labeled automatic. These are the coaches' teachings and examples, not new DRM promises or instructions already implemented.

<a id="coaching-section-114"></a>
## Cold Email

### Intro to Cold Email (2190721877)

Christian introduces proactive outbound through email, DMs and calls rather than depending on referrals or inbound. Learn offer, audience/list quality, copy, sending infrastructure and response handling before using AI to accelerate them. Getting a reply is only the first stage; the business outcome requires booking and closing. His ListKit relationship is disclosed in the teaching. Examples describe his campaigns, not DRM's results.

### Cold Email KPIs and What to Look For (2190726593)

- Measure unique prospects, total replies, positive replies, booked calls, attendance and sales separately. Total replies include negative responses.
- Coach's directional benchmarks: 2-4% total replies; 0.25-0.5% positive replies, approximately 3-5 per 1,000 prospects; 2-4 calls per 1,000; 2-3 attendees; one deal per 1,000 as his ideal benchmark. These are teaching targets, not guaranteed outputs.
- Offer affects the baseline: podcast invitations can produce 3-10% positive replies, whereas cybersecurity, web design or branding may be around 0.1-0.2%.
- Diagnose each stage: low total replies suggests deliverability; low positive replies suggests copy, offer or audience fit; poor meeting conversion suggests response management; poor closing requires attendance/sales review.
- He recommends disabling open tracking. He explicitly acknowledges uncertainty about the deliverability effect of tracking pixels, while arguing that response and sales measures suffice.
- Initial outreach: plain text, no HTML, links, pictures or headshot signature. Maximum 20 daily emails per inbox in this lesson; scale through additional warmed inboxes rather than exceeding that cap.
- Move interested prospects into a CRM and follow up. He includes LinkedIn and phone follow-up as possible channels.
- Illustrative economics: $120 to reach 1,000 prospects and one sale per 4,000 produces $480 acquisition cost. This is an example, not current vendor pricing.
- Exercise: build a funnel scoreboard with the correct denominators, identify the weakest stage, and compare acquisition cost with client economics. DRM has 12 warmed inboxes and a user-stated 240-email total daily capacity including follow-ups. No additional inbox purchase or campaign launch was performed in this review.

### How to Write a High-Converting Cold Email Script (2190721595)

- The first message sells a reply, not the entire service. Keep it about 2-3 sentences and end with an easy yes/no permission question.
- Two main approaches: offer useful custom work/sample/audit, or state an outcome with timeframe and guarantee, briefly explain delivery, then offer a short video/resource.
- Ads/funnels examples: 3-5 ad scripts, custom creatives, a funnel using the prospect's existing proof, or a website audit. Specific work for the recipient is stronger than a generic template.
- Email marketing examples: welcome flows, re-engagement, email designs, customer reviews/bestsellers, and auditing the opt-in journey. Content examples: LinkedIn posts, blogs, short-form scripts or a profile audit grounded in the recipient's website, social posts or press.
- AI automation examples: repurposing long-form material into clips/posts, multichannel publishing, transcription and sales-call scoring. Demonstrate a concrete functioning workflow rather than selling the phrase AI automation.
- The coach sometimes pitches work as created and fulfills it after interest; that is recorded as his method, not a statement that DRM has created any prospect deliverable.
- Vary the building blocks: opening, outcome, proof, timeframe, guarantee and CTA. He explicitly asks students to think and adapt, rather than copy blindly.
- Examples such as 15 clients in 60 days or $50,000 from email are sample offers in the lesson, not changes to DRM's offer.
- Exercise: prepare short variants suited to the actual service and audience, with a resource that can be delivered when requested.

### Writing Cold Email Scripts Using AI (2190722060)

- Supply the dashboard bot with service, target audience, background, evidence and campaign preferences. Ask for a three-step sequence with A/B first-email angles.
- Export to a document, clean formatting, replace detached audience language with direct you/your wording, add appropriate first-name/company fields, and ask for a shorter version when necessary.
- Knowing copy fundamentals is necessary to judge the output. AI drafts require review and are particularly useful when managing multiple client campaigns.
- The Andre LinkedIn case and unusual demonstration business are invented in the lesson. They are not usable client proof.
- Exercise: generate, inspect and edit variants, then compare them with the principles of the preceding lesson.

### Personalize Cold Emails with Claude (2200299127)

- Install the three supplied ListKit skill files in Claude, provide the lead CSV, required API connection and the actual campaign context. Replace the instructor's default campaign with your own.
- Demonstration: US home-service/construction owners, founders and CEOs. Start with 10 rows and inspect results before expanding to 50 or the full list.
- Good personalization describes actual work: industrial coating/facility managers, local dumpster delivery, dental recalls, driver recruiting, or other recipient-specific tasks. Merely repeating appointments or generic leads is inadequate.
- Use website, location and industry context. Generate use-case fields and/or complete personalized email columns. Check column mapping, grammar, and whether and/or changes the meaning.
- Give a good output as a style example, but check that subsequent outputs remain specific to each recipient rather than recycling that example.
- Preview expanded fields in the sending platform. Use a plain fallback when there is insufficient website evidence.
- Sequence: install skills, establish context, load CSV, test a small sample, revise, process the full list, map fields, preview messages.
- API secrets from demonstrations are not copied into notes. The speaker's claims of much better performance are not established benchmark data.

### EXAMPLES of Winning Cold Email Scripts (2190721934)

- Email marketing example: 33 positive replies from 8,100 prospects, approximately one per 247. Instructor considers better than one per 500 good in this context.
- Structure combines direct revenue outcome and guarantee with an offer to share a redesigned welcome email. Variants change framing while preserving the same useful deliverable.
- Three-message sequence: initial email, a four-day follow-up in the demonstrated campaign, and a final reminder emphasizing the redesigned flow. The instructor then stops that automated sequence and moves on. This is distinct from managing someone who has already replied positively.
- Content/ghostwriting example uses an outcome, client evidence and permission to send a strategy video. Later messages reframe the content bottleneck or ask who handles business development.
- Real-estate lead generation example emphasizes motivated seller leads and offers local inventory/pricing. It sells the outcome, not the technical ad service.
- AI automation example combines a client outcome with a short demo showing nurturing, qualification, follow-up and scheduling with n8n, ChatGPT and Make.
- Subject examples: question for first name, relevant outcome, company-to-company introduction, or new pipeline. Simple sender/company signature.
- Prospect replies include requests for the design, pricing, a call, or more review time. Initial interest still requires fulfillment and booking work.
- Exercise: model the underlying structure and adapt it to the actual service. Do not copy the displayed third-party proof into DRM's claims.

### Setting Up A Campaign From Scratch (Scripts + Leads) (2194599608)

- Create and name the campaign, then build a relevant list. Demonstrated ListKit filters: marketing/advertising, social-media keywords, US/UK/Canada, and decision-maker titles. He exports 1,000 from about 7,600 matches while writing copy.
- Create four first-email variants, two second-email variants four days later, and a third step three days after that. The example offer and 63-lead case belong to the instructor's campaign.
- Apply light spintax using an LLM, then preview the rendered text and variables. His stated purpose is variation; the lesson's deliverability explanation is his claim.
- Download verified CSV, map company, business email, first and last name correctly, then select only the intended sending accounts. He explicitly avoids accidentally using client inboxes.
- Set schedule/timezone, inspect the platform's campaign-level new-lead limit, disable open/link tracking, and use the demonstrated 70% new/30% follow-up allocation.
- His very high campaign-level cap removes an unintended bottleneck; it is not permission to exceed individual inbox daily caps.
- Preview all substitutions before launch. Once a campaign works, replenish relevant leads rather than rebuilding it each time, while recognizing that the reachable market is finite.
- Exercise: assemble and preview a campaign. This review did not launch a new campaign or change the existing DRM pilots.

### Inbox Management & Booking Sales Calls from Cold Email (2190726403)

- Coach checks the unified reply inbox at least twice daily. Positive replies require timely, concise human response.
- Fulfill the request or answer the question, then propose a call. Offer two concrete times with timezone and optionally a calendar link. Do not write a long explanation when a short answer works.
- If an interested prospect goes quiet, follow up. The lesson criticizes a July 16 to August 7 gap and shows a next-day follow-up securing a booking.
- Respond directly to pricing/model questions using the actual business's terms. His ListKit pricing explanation is not DRM pricing.
- If the prospect supplies their calendar, scheduling there can reduce friction.
- Verify name, date, timezone and which team member will attend. A demonstration contains a wrong name and apparent timezone mismatch; the coach identifies these as mistakes.
- After booking, confirm the invite and share a short service overview so the person arrives informed and can identify a mismatch beforehand. He suggests about five minutes, although the displayed example is 13 minutes.
- The lesson references a vault of 100 reply conversations and an overview video. Referenced resources need separate retrieval; the transcript itself does not contain all 100 examples.
- Exercise: create a reply-handling process for questions, resource delivery, follow-up, booking and confirmation. No prospect messages were sent by this transcript review.

### Testing New Cold Email Strategies (2190726305)

- If a message underperforms, simplify the outcome and permission CTA. Test question versus statement openings, resource/video/free-work CTAs, subject lines and the language used for outcomes.
- Demonstrated winning angle generated 20 positives from about 7,600 prospects, around one per 384. Smaller variants performed differently and some replies arrived later.
- The instructor does not claim to know exactly why every winner wins. Market response decides; stop losing variants, expand winners and keep iterating.
- Exercise: retain variant-level results and change deliberate elements rather than treating personal preference as evidence.

### Financial Modeling for Lead Gen Systems (2190576435)

- Make a copy of the spreadsheet and edit its green inputs. Model daily volume, days sent, costs, total and positive reply rates, booking and closing rates, retention, monthly fee and margin.
- Example automated channel assumptions include 500/day, 3% replies, 20% of replies positive, 30% booking, 20% closing, $2,000/month, 70% margin and five-month retention. Illustrative lifetime gross profit is $7,000 and CAC approximately $296. Do not confuse different denominator percentages.
- The model excludes the owner's time and the demonstrated cash-flow view excludes churn. Treat those limitations explicitly.
- Include warm-up and sales-cycle delay. The example first closes around week six, not day one; the speaker corrects a verbal month/week slip. Later cash recovery can require months.
- Free-work outreach trades channel cash costs for labor and fulfillment cost. Example: 15 items at $100 costs $1,500 before results; high-volume expensive samples can consume significant cash.
- Stress-test weaker conversion and calculate runway. Target prospects able to buy, rather than assuming every recipient can afford the service.
- Automated outreach can be combined with custom work for qualified interest.
- Exercise: model the actual channel and client economics before scaling. Example forecasts are not promises of DRM results.

<a id="coaching-section-115"></a>
## Cold Call

### 1 - Cold Call Roadmap (2191624539)

Jake's core principles apply whether a company supplies a fixed script or the caller can write their own: human introduction, useful hook, real questions/conversation and a meeting request. Work chronologically and practice each stage. His improvement percentages are coaching claims, not measured DRM outcomes. Exercise: practice the actual wording you will use rather than merely watching.

### 2 - Cold Calling Overview (2191624540)

The cold call sells a meeting, not the complete service. Conversation is nonlinear, but still cover the framework's necessary areas even if someone agrees to meet early. Make a copy of the linked roadmap and write relevant wording/questions. Reach roughly B+ proficiency in each stage before progressing. Polishing the meeting ask has little value if the opening never earns a conversation. It is a framework with some scripted passages, not a robotic full-dialogue script.

### 3 - Cold Calling - Intro (Pattern Interrupt) (2191624542)

- Sound like a comfortable, confident human rather than an excessively enthusiastic telemarketer. Confirm the person's identity first to establish an actual exchange and catch wrong numbers.
- Identify yourself/company, acknowledge that the call is unexpected, ask for about 30 seconds to explain why, and allow the person to decide whether to continue.
- Variants include odd-number timing, acknowledging a cold call, or light humor. Choose language fitting the caller and audience; the principle is clarity and permission.
- Exercise: spend five minutes writing your introduction, then deliver it smoothly ten consecutive times aloud. Restart the count after an error before moving to the next lesson.

### 4 - Cold Calling - The Hook (2191624544)

The 30-second commercial should make the prospect recognize their situation. Thank them, identify the company, describe their relevant role/business stage, and use real relevant proof if available. Explain two or at most three common frustrations at the level of time, revenue or workload, rather than overly specific software features. Put the most common problem first and a contrasting problem second. Remove a third problem if it rarely resonates. Match the prospect's pace while remaining concise and confident. Aim near 30 seconds, around 45-50 seconds at most. Exercise: write the persona, appropriate proof and problems, read aloud, time it, and practice intro/hook to B+ before proceeding.

### 5 - Cold Call Script Writing - Intro (2191624548)

For cold calls, confirm identity, introduce yourself, acknowledge the unexpected call and ask permission for a brief reason. For a warm lead, use the genuine form/application they submitted as the reason and ask for a couple of minutes to clarify it. Old pipeline leads may need a blended reminder. Keep it simple and deliver it naturally.

### 6 - Cold Call Script Writing - Hook (2191624665)

Write a solution-oriented hook: whom you help, why they invite you in and what distinguishes your approach. Use relevant real proof. Spend time refining two or three reasons; do not accept generic AI pain points without examining them. If appropriate, address the one or two most common objections inside the hook. End by recapping the actual alternatives in the question, rather than asking vaguely which one resonated, because the listener may have missed part of it. Review recordings and end-of-day notes; prune reasons that fail to resonate. Warm leads generally need a relevant opening question rather than a full cold pitch.

### 7 - Cold Call Script Writing - Objections (2191624710)

Use acknowledge/agree, answer, ask. Give a short answer, then a question connected to what the prospect requested. For send me an email: agree, confirm the address, and ask which problem the email should address. For an existing provider: acknowledge it and explore whether the relevant need is already met. The goal is a useful conversation about actual pain, not reciting rebuttals. Write examples suited to the offer and practice responding. The coach targets calls generally under seven minutes.

### 8 - Unscripted Sections - Impact & Commitment (2191624712)

Understand the present situation, desired situation and gap. Impact asks how the problem affects them; commitment asks how important changing it is and whether it is a priority. These answers help make the meeting meaningful and improve attendance. They may emerge naturally, so avoid repeating questions already answered. Even an early request to book a meeting should be followed by a relevant question about what they want covered. The coach suggests enough genuine conversation to establish significance, often about five minutes, while generally avoiding calls over seven minutes.

### 9 - Unscripted Sections - Qualifying (2191624715)

Keep cold-call qualification to one or two simple, tactful requirements. Avoid excluding useful internal champions solely because they are not the CEO. Warm/paid leads may warrant more specific qualification. The coach favors beginning with a broad enough opportunity flow and refining criteria based on results, rather than making callers hesitant to book any meeting.

### 11 - Practice Intro & Hook (2191624722)

Record yourself. Practice tiny sections independently, correcting tone, pauses and recurring stumbling points. Get ten smooth repetitions in a row, ideally across three days. Restart after mistakes. Practice the hook separately before joining it to the introduction, then practice the transitions. Keep one excellent recording to replay while walking or commuting. After the final question, stop speaking and let the prospect answer. Do not keep rehearsing the entire call to fix one troublesome phrase.

### 12 - Practice Everything After Intro & Hook (2191624725)

Identify a precise weak moment from metrics and recordings. Tell the role-play partner the objection, personality and context to simulate. Write candidate responses beforehand. Start one sentence before that moment, repeat it, and go only one or two questions beyond it to practice the transition. After mastering one response, introduce two or three alternatives to train active listening and responsiveness. Do not substitute full-call rehearsals for targeted repetition.

### 13 - Tracking Cold Call Metrics (2191624728)

Copy/rename the monthly spreadsheet tab, update the first date and fill down. Enter activity counts while preserving percentage formulas and green summary cells. Leave non-working days blank instead of entering zero; optional shading identifies weekends/absence. Link the year-to-date view to each monthly summary and retain percentage formatting. Duplicate a month for the next month, clear only entered counts, and update dates. Exercise requires the actual linked tracker; this transcript describes its operation but does not recreate all cell formulas.

### 14 - Make Improvements Cold Calling (2191624731)

- Combine metrics with recordings, comparisons with strong calls, and outside feedback. The displayed spreadsheet contains dummy numbers, not performance evidence.
- Connect rate: coach's range 6-10% for high-volume outbound. If low, examine data quality, repeat attempts, timezones/time of day, caller-number reputation and spam marking. He suggests diminishing returns after six or seven attempts and usually no more than eight or nine, spread across times/days.
- Connect to conversation: about 40-65% in his framework. Conversation means accepting the introduction. Diagnose tone, sharpness, practice and whether the call arrives at an inconvenient time.
- Conversation to booking: he has seen roughly 20-40%+. Falling conversion often means too much talking, weak questions, insufficient pain/impact/commitment or poor objection handling.
- Attendance: at least 75%, with 85%+ preferred by the coach. Improve impact, commitment, post-booking preparation, reminders and scheduling proximity. Prefer the same week or early next week when possible.
- Compare four-day, seven-day and month trends, but inspect sample sizes and cohorts. One booked meeting and one attendee may be different people, so a displayed 100% is not necessarily meaningful.
- Poor qualification means checking the agreed qualification questions, not assuming the prospect is already sold.
- Exercise: identify one highest-impact skill, review relevant calls, write better questions, practice around 30 minutes daily for that focus, and maintain a short intro warm-up. Strategy problems such as phone reputation need operational fixes alongside skill practice.
