## UpWork Mastery

The following lesson sources are automatic local speech transcripts because the videos have no published captions. Names and unclear wording require verification against audio. Prices, platform behavior and policy descriptions below are what the instructor says in the recording, not a fresh verification of current Upwork terms.

### UpWork Mastery Introduction (2199623435)

- 00:00-01:35: Course covers mindset, profile/keywords/portfolio, proposals, response handling, first contract and retention.
- 01:43-06:33: Instructor challenges the idea that Upwork only contains low-priced work. His own $18,000 supplement-brand contract is an example. Clients seek speed, execution quality and certainty, supported by relevant reviews, earnings and badges.
- 06:37-11:24: Position Upwork alongside Dream 100 and cold email when resources allow. Instructor's illustrative comparisons: Dream 100 can start free, first client 2-4 weeks; Upwork roughly $20-$250+ monthly, 1-2 weeks; cold email $500+ monthly, 3-6 weeks. He qualifies these times as variable. Upwork is constrained by available suitable jobs. Use completed work/proof across acquisition channels.
- 11:26-14:29: Discusses free versus Freelancer Plus, connects and instant job alerts. Recording cites a roughly $20 membership and 100 monthly connects, plus additional spend. He prefers applying within the first 15 minutes. His $245 spend/$8,000 contracts example is his result and excludes the distinction between contract revenue and profit.
- 14:31-20:59: Coach says review platform terms regularly, communicate professionally and promptly, avoid contact sharing before a contract, avoid moving job prospects to LinkedIn to bypass the platform, and do not trade fabricated reviews. Ask the coaching call when unsure.
- 21:03-23:47: Treat platform fees as acquisition/referral costs and include them in economics. Recording discusses fees around 10% and up to 15%, payment protection and disputes. He also mentions later off-platform relationships; this is his description, not verification that any particular move meets current terms.
- Exercise: establish a realistic acquisition budget, understand the platform and complete a profile before consistent applications. No account, membership or proposal was created in this review.

### The 3 Keys to UpWork (2199624194)

- 00:26: After the initial profile setup sprint, spend approximately 80% of effort on proposals and 20% on profile optimization. Do not use endless profile perfection as procrastination.
- 01:04: Treat the profile as searchable. Use relevant service keywords while keeping it readable; the instructor says discoverability matters more than ornate copy.
- 01:48: Use the platform consistently and apply daily. The instructor links activity and earnings to visibility; this is a teaching claim about platform behavior.
- Exercise: finish the initial profile, then establish a recurring application habit and targeted profile maintenance.

### UpWork Profile Optimisation (2199630738)

- 00:36-04:06: Reach 100% profile completion. Start with buyer search terms before writing. Instructor's examples are Klaviyo and email marketing, repeated across relevant sections. The supplied keyword document is a starting point, not a substitute for researching your service.
- 04:06-06:46: Put service/tool keywords in the title. Write the overview like a landing page: client problem/result hook, three to six real authority points, relevant services, differentiation and a clear hire/invite CTA. Optional FAQ addresses project type, examples and timing.
- 06:47-08:54: Fill available relevant skill slots; recording says 20. Include at least three to five portfolio items. Actual client work and demo/spec work can demonstrate competence, but they are different kinds of proof.
- 08:55-12:17: Complete project catalog and thumbnails. Instructor uses a $5 audit as a real low-friction first contract and review opportunity, followed by larger custom work. Use relevant keywords in project titles/descriptions and clear service images.
- 12:18-14:32: Add genuine relevant certifications. Describe actual client consulting work in employment/experience sections with dates and keyword-rich descriptions. The instructor groups consulting experience rather than requiring traditional salaried employment.
- 14:33-16:43: Add an introduction video. His example is 10-15 seconds; a VSL is another option if external contact details are removed. External-client testimonials can be requested through Upwork's testimonial feature. Not every irrelevant connected-account field needs filling.
- 16:44-18:54: Build around one buyer/service. Use keywords naturally and integrate genuine proof throughout. Edit AI-generated profile copy rather than pasting the first output. Search/title leads to hook, authority, service match and CTA.
- 18:59-end: His $50/hour displayed rate is a starting profile rate while his work is project-priced. Review relevant comparable profiles; do not let the displayed hourly field block setup. This is not a change to DRM pricing.
- Exercise: complete the profile checklist, assemble portfolio proof, choose search terms, write/edit the overview and record the intro. Supplied profile/keyword/prompt documents are referenced resources and require separate retrieval for their exact contents.

### UpWork Keyword Maxxing (2199634273)

Search as a buyer would, then inspect relevant successful freelancers' titles and profile language. Instructor demonstrates YouTube specialists and Klaviyo/email marketing. Earnings help identify established profiles, but he does not assume every successful profile follows his strategy. He suggests frequent keyword repetition, including 75-100+ mentions in his example. These are his optimization targets, not verified ranking rules. Exercise: derive service-specific terms rather than blindly using the email-marketing-heavy reference list.

### UpWorks Talent Badges (2199634320)

- 00:27-03:15: Rising Talent requires an eligible complete, active, verified profile and good outcomes. The recording discusses 4.8+ ratings, $250 earnings and 90% job success if a score exists. The spoken eligibility wording is not a substitute for the current platform criteria. It describes a connects bonus and consultation access.
- 03:16-05:24: Top Rated example criteria include 90%+ job success, first project over 90 days ago, qualifying status for 13 of 16 weeks, complete profile, $1,000 in 12 months, current availability, activity and good standing.
- 05:25-07:27: Top Rated Plus adds larger-contract history and earnings; exact qualifying contract size varies by category. Instructor explicitly labels his idea that ordinary Top Rated might feel more approachable as hearsay, not fact.
- 07:28-end: Expert Vetted involves screening and demonstrated expertise/communication. He tells beginners to focus first on Rising Talent and Top Rated.
- Exercise: complete setup, deliver good work and track progress against the platform's actual badge page. Do not buy or invent reviews.

### Maximising Visibility on UpWork (2199635483)

Complete the profile first. Instructor recommends an availability badge, optionally boosted profile visibility using connects, and experiments with a newer boosted-message feature. He explicitly has no performance data for that new feature. Immediate consultations, where eligible, require availability to be switched on, notifications and fast response; the demonstration allows about one minute to respond. Keep availability accurate and remember features consume connects. No paid visibility feature was activated during this review.

### Intro to Proposal Mastery (2199624225)

Casey's sequence is finding suitable jobs, speed to lead, a distinctive custom-video proposal, and repetition. He favors the first hour, ideally first 15 minutes after posting, while the client is actively looking. The following lessons expand each step.

### Finding Jobs on UpWork (2199624358)

Search both service terms and tools. Examples: Klaviyo/email, cold email/lead gen/Smartlead/Clay, AI automation/Claude Code, media buying/Meta/Facebook ads, video editing/YouTube/short form. Inspect posting frequency and stated budgets to learn market demand. Budget and hourly framing can be discussed on the sales call; the coach says not to reject solely from the posted figure. Check morning and afternoon and periodically revisit the broader keyword list. A linked PDF contains the complete brainstormed terms, beyond those spoken in this transcript.

### Speed to Lead on UpWork (2199624379)

Apply when you find a suitable job instead of saving ten tabs for later. A good personalized submission while the buyer is still active has an advantage. Install/use phone notifications for timely responses. Speed must be paired with relevant, competent work. Initial proposals take longer while templates and habits develop.

### Winning Proposals on UpWork (2199624446)

- 00:11-01:18: Structure: preview-line hook, custom video, concise cover letter. The opening calls attention to a video specifically made for that job.
- 01:21-04:48: Video covers a confident job-specific introduction, relevant experience/proof, work samples, process and a reply-to-book CTA. Use the job description to guide AI prompts. If no client results exist, show spec work or an actual plan/flowchart demonstrating how the requested system would be built.
- The coach discusses prominent former employers as credibility, even for unrelated roles. Preserve the distinction between the real role and the service being proposed; this review does not invent affiliations.
- 04:52-06:43: A visual overview can organize strengths, proof and process. For automation, map the client's requested workflow and explain it quickly, inviting clarification of missing requirements. It should demonstrate that you have already thought through the project.
- 06:44-07:30: Optional variation: record with Loom/OBS/Meld and host on YouTube, then mention the custom YouTube video in the hook. This is a presentation tactic, not a requirement to produce a heavily edited video.
- 07:33-end: Cover letter summarizes the video with readable spacing/bullets, tangible evidence and the same CTA. Bring proposals to coaching calls for feedback.
- Exercise: assemble one job-specific visual, short recording and scannable letter. No proposal was submitted in this review.

### UpWork Proposal Prompts (2199624680)

Fill all bracketed inputs, supply the job and actual proof, and refine the template to the service. Convert a draft to bullet talking points for a natural recording. Distinguish the experienced-client version from the spec-project version; combine overlapping process/spec sections rather than repeating them. Reuse the stable service process and customize the job-specific material. A separate image prompt can turn the final outline into a flowchart; a separate cover-letter prompt should retain core points with bullets. The instructor repeatedly says the prompt is a starting point requiring thought and revision. Exact linked PDF prompts are not fully spoken in the transcript.

### Upwork Proposals - Graphics (2199624832)

Use a useful near-finished graphic without spending an hour polishing it. The example contains generic headings/imagery the coach dislikes, but he checks spelling and proceeds because speed matters. His target is roughly 90-95% ready. Exercise: make a clear visual that supports the recording, check errors and record promptly.

### UpWork - Volume & Reps (2199624873)

Early proposals take longer; use a 40-45 minute timer to avoid overthinking. Build toward 20-30 weekly proposals, initially perhaps with morning/afternoon work blocks. Track submissions and time so output per hour improves. Experienced users may reduce the routine to 30-60 minutes daily. Allocate about 80% of effort to proposals and 20% to portfolio/spec work. Instructor gives approximate reply/close examples and a 100-200-video repetition goal; these are not guaranteed conversions. Another lesson gives a more conservative first-job expectation, so retain both rather than merge them into one promised rate.

### UpWork - What are Connects & How do they work? (2199635552)

Recording prices connects at $0.15 each and gives examples around 6-20+ connects per proposal, with a live 22-connect example. Costs vary and membership connects can be used quickly. Greg favors applying about 15-20 minutes after posting rather than a suspiciously immediate generic application. He generally avoids boosting individual proposals initially, preferring volume and speed; selected dream-client bids are an advanced exception. This is distinct from his recommendation to boost the profile itself. Inspect client feedback and keep sufficient connects for enabled visibility features. No connects were purchased.

### UpWork - Communicating with Clients (2199635676)

Respond promptly to inbound messages because the client may be contacting others. Use Upwork's own booking link and send a short prepared proof summary. On the call, ask about the situation, listen and explain relevant help. Greg's email-marketing process often uses a call, audit and second call, but he says this varies by service and refers students to the sales training. Immediately summarize the call and next steps in Upwork chat. He emphasizes staying within platform communication rules, including when a client suggests moving elsewhere.

### Your UpWork Action Plan (2199635696)

Watch the preceding lessons. This week's prescribed work: create account, consider the recommended Freelancer Plus plan, complete every relevant profile section, optimize keywords, build three to five real/spec portfolio items, record a roughly 60-second intro, find suitable jobs and send custom-video proposals. Have notifications on and aim to respond in under five minutes. Note the intro length varies from his own 10-15-second example; both are retained as spoken. These are recorded tasks, not a claim they have been executed for DRM.

### UpWork - Landing your First Job (2199635755)

Target two or more relevant applications daily, including weekends, with at least one as a minimum. Set an actual daily target and seek feedback. Greg estimates roughly 30 proposals for a first job, subject to profile/proposal quality and other variables. Use the honest new-to-Upwork-but-experienced angle; if entirely new, demonstrate competence through portfolio/spec work. Submit proposal video/letter to Greg and Casey for coaching feedback.

### How to have Long Term Success with UpWork (2199635833)

Treat fees as part of acquisition economics, build earnings/history, and overdeliver especially on the first three jobs. Communicate proactively, deliver before the deadline where possible, and request genuine feedback. Continue proposals and good delivery rather than stopping after a win. The instructor describes his first $250 project leading to substantial later retainer value; the automatic transcript mangles the later dollar figure, so it is not adopted as an exact statistic.

## Linked resource lessons

### Filming Loom Videos for Cold Outreach (2192120621)

This lesson is a written Gamma guide rather than a missing video. The guide opened successfully despite old comments reporting a broken link. Source: https://gamma.app/docs/Loom-Video-Cold-Email-Strategy-Guide-jd52isf0c68b1s4

- Ask permission to send the video in the initial plain-text email; do not put the video link in the initial blast. Create personalized videos for qualified respondents rather than every cold lead.
- Check fit and apparent budget before investing in the custom video. Deliver within a few hours after a positive reply in the coach's workflow.
- Aim around 3-5 minutes: relevant introduction, clear agenda, useful recommendations and a call CTA. The guide explicitly calls the length a rule of thumb and allows longer useful videos.
- Start on the prospect's website so the thumbnail is recognizable. Show your face, explain about three practical improvements, and avoid making the whole recording a service pitch.
- End with specific proposed dates/times and a calendar alternative. A vague let me know is insufficient in the guide's method.
- For the requested-video reply, use Loom Share > Embed > GIF thumbnail. Tell the recipient to click it, highlight two useful timestamps and include a written meeting CTA. This comes after permission, unlike the plain-text first email.
- Follow up differently depending on whether it was watched. Reference a specific tip/timestamp, ask about applying it, and propose a concrete call time. Loom view alerts support this. Stop when asked to stop. The guide also mentions phone/LinkedIn follow-up and a playful detective-emoji reminder.
- The guide includes example embeds/templates and a ListKit sales pitch, including historical $597/month/1,000-email-per-day copy. That promotion is not a DRM purchase requirement. Nested example videos were not separately transcribed in this review.
- The guide repeats the instructor's claim of having recorded the video before actually recording it; retained as source teaching, not as a statement about completed DRM work.

### YouTuber Equipment & Setup Guide (2191624884)

This is a linked Google document, exported in full to `sources/acquisition-2026-09-30/2191624884-equipment-guide.md`. Source: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yuGRTe9GLF39hmHZa41buztZ53b_EVOnELm0Csv_tds/edit

It covers camera/lens and shallow depth of field, capture card/dummy battery/supports, microphone/interface, lighting and OBS. The author favors a dynamic microphone for isolation, discusses USB versus XLR and interfaces, and contrasts this with condenser room pickup. Key light illuminates the face, a softer fill reduces shadows, and colored background light adds separation. It recommends OBS for configurable long-form recording and Loom for quick client videos. Budget-tier product links and embedded tutorial references are preserved in the exported document. Equipment preferences and compatibility statements are the guide author's advice, not new purchases or current buying recommendations. External linked tutorials require separate review.

<a id="coaching-section-118"></a>
## LinkedIn: published-caption lessons reviewed

### Who Should Focus on LinkedIn (2191624787)

- Check whether the actual buyer is active, using recent posts, job changes and profile activity. The instructor favors corporate executives, HR/recruiters, sales, investors and midmarket B2B. His cautions about small ecommerce/local businesses are channel-fit generalizations, not changes to DRM's targeting.
- Expand an already working channel before adding a new one just because it is available. Compare likely return with time spent.
- Outbound tier one is about two hours monthly: basic connections and occasional inbox management. Tier two, about 6-10 hours, adds ICP refinement, note/follow-up/asset/timing tests and manual work on promising conversations. Tier three, about 10-30 hours, is for a proven channel: more profiles, open InMail, profile tests and personalized media.
- Inbound tier one repurposes existing content. Tier two, about 10-20 hours monthly, studies working examples, publishes on weekdays and replies to comments. Advanced inbound can consume half to a full workweek monthly with more formats, collaborations and follow-up. He describes diminishing returns above two posts daily.
- Exercise: assess buyer activity and current channel economics, choose an effort tier, then increase only with evidence.

### Basic Profile Optimization (2191624851)

Clear shoulder-up photo; headline saying who you help, what you do and relevant proof; branded offer banner; actionable website link; the then-current creator-mode settings; and a featured case study, useful resource or video. He treats the headline as the largest quick improvement and suggests completing the basic pass in about 15 minutes. Creator-mode references describe the recorded interface.

### Sales Navigator Targeting (2191624853)

- Core is the demonstrated subscription. Recorded prices are historical. Begin with geography, company size and actual decision-maker titles, then refine to the real business type.
- Owner/founder/CEO/president and seniority filters help, but generic keywords can be misleading. Ecommerce may need Shopify, DTC or retail terms. Boolean AND/OR and exclusions refine the list.
- Job-function and company-headcount fields can misclassify people with several roles. Inspect actual profiles, including later pages such as page 10 or 20, before trusting the search.
- Recent activity improves the likelihood that outreach is seen. Avoid overfiltering a small market. Copy the completed search URL for the outreach tool.

### LinkedIn Automation Setup (2191624854)

Demonstrates creating/verifying an Expandi account, connecting LinkedIn, choosing country/timezone and warming new automation gradually over about two weeks. Existing conflicting automation can interfere. Create a search from the Sales Navigator URL, create the connector campaign, add note/follow-ups, assign contacts and enable it. A mobile-connector variant omits the connection note. Several limits are pointed to visually without unambiguous spoken labels, so the transcript alone does not establish every exact setting. This is a recorded setup lesson, not evidence a DRM campaign was launched.

### Writing LinkedIn Campaigns (2191624857)

- Connection notes can use genuine commonality and a simple invitation; also test no note. The coach's 40-56% acceptance examples are examples, not a promise.
- Follow-up angles include referral/need questions, relevant expertise, a novel mechanism, permission to send a case study, relevant community membership, finding the responsible person, a qualification question, an outcome offer or a pain question.
- Direct pitches can generate fewer but clearer replies. Avoid empty bump messages; use relevant value or a natural check-in. Test different angles and review results over time rather than treating one script as universally best.

### Sign 3-5 High Ticket Clients with Ty Frankel (2191624860)

- Three pillars: profile as landing page, content that nurtures, and manual DM conversations that lead to calls. A large following, company page or expensive website is not a prerequisite in this method.
- Suggested initial allocation: 2-3 hours improving the profile, about 30 minutes weekly for 2-3 posts, and roughly an hour daily on DMs. He may automate connections but keeps conversations manual.
- His recorded benchmarks include 200 connection requests weekly, 40-60% acceptance, 20-35% replies and one call per 10-15 conversations. These are his reported examples and historical operating numbers, not platform guarantees or current limits.
- Build accurate target lists and contact active profiles. His preferred connection is blank; send around the prospect's morning. Review recent posts/comments and signs of investment in the profile.
- Before messaging he demonstrates endorsing relevant skills, liking posts, following the company and optionally commenting. These are warm-up actions, not a substitute for a relevant conversation.
- Multi-thread conversations mix genuine personal and business topics in short separate messages. Reflect what they said instead of interrogating them with question after question. Match language to the person and level of business.
- Use restrained compliments. Be warm, grounded and independent of the outcome. Demonstrate relevant understanding, then explore a real pain point or desired improvement.
- Build useful assets, such as a detailed case study written as a practical guide, with actual process, evidence, related training and a call CTA. Reuse appropriate assets in public content, DMs and pre-call preparation.
- Drop an asset because it fits the conversation. Foreshadow a genuinely useful introduction where relevant. Give reasons to continue the conversation before asking for a call.
- His authority-building observation technique connects a business observation to the prospect's problem. A distinctive phrase can invite a what-do-you-mean question; explain the idea, support it with relevant experience and offer a value-centered call.
- He often reaches the call invitation within roughly 5-15 exchanges, but emphasizes substance over a rigid count. Avoid 30 messages with no progress. Voice notes can convey warmth and move a stalled conversation forward.
- For no reply to an initial DM, he suggests 2-3 follow-ups and possibly revisiting months later. For previous interest, he may try 4-5 before spending effort elsewhere. Decide based on opportunity cost rather than frustration. His claim that even negative replies can become calls is retained as teaching, not authorization for DRM outreach.
- Higher-value enterprise accounts may need 3-4 relevant people per company, more proof, stronger content and a longer relationship. Combine channels when useful rather than assuming small-business benchmarks transfer unchanged.
- Sales Navigator is optional at the beginning: use several genuine ICP profiles and LinkedIn's related-profile suggestions, checking fit/activity manually. Track acceptance manually or through the connector tool's reporting.
- Personal profiles are the center of this method. For other platforms, adapt the conversational principles; Twitter/Facebook may depend more on brand building and people first expressing interest.
- Exercises: optimize the personal profile, build a relevant active list, create two useful assets, practice short contextual conversations, and track connections, replies and calls. No DRM messages were sent as part of this transcript review.

### Advanced Profile Optimization Checklist (2191624862)

- Use a friendly, competent, high-resolution close-up headshot. The coach distinguishes an approachable business portrait from a fashion pose.
- Use headline space deliberately, up to the recorded 220-character allowance. Avoid repeating company name or equivalent founder/CEO titles. Explain the audience, specific service/outcome, relevant proof and why someone should connect.
- Put strong evidence near the top rather than burying it in experience. Examples include actual revenue/ad-spend results, relevant publications or substantial operating history.
- Banner should communicate offer, proof or a useful CTA and complement the headline. Check the mobile layout and photo overlap. A beautiful unrelated landscape wastes valuable space in his checklist.
- Website-link wording should say why to click. Featured items need clear descriptive titles and readable previews: case study, lead magnet, product sample, video or booking page.
- About section: opening hook/incomplete thought that earns the see-more click, a real story or clear offer, credibility throughout and a specific CTA. Use short paragraphs and remove redundant words. Do not duplicate every section verbatim.
- Experience should explain relevant company credibility, services/results and distinctiveness, not just a resume of daily duties. Add appropriate skills, recommendations, education and certifications.
- The instructor also suggests trading or buying endorsements through LinkJetpack. That suggestion is preserved as source content; no endorsements were bought or represented as DRM customer proof.
- Review examples repeatedly stress plain language over insider slang, precise service descriptions over vague systems, properly clickable links and mobile banner checks.

### Top 8 LinkedIn Mistakes with Jeremy (2191624863)

- Grow the relevant network consistently. His older demonstration uses 750-request file uploads every two weeks and deleting pending invitations; these are historical techniques, not verified current LinkedIn capabilities or limits.
- Headline should give a concrete outcome, audience and proof. Generic lead-generation language and sales-job titles can make prospects expect an immediate pitch. Irrelevant personal descriptors do not explain business value.
- Follow up, but leave days rather than minutes. Message previews should create a relevant reason to open, not announce another bump. He describes a large lifetime-value deal after a simple courteous reply; this is his case, not DRM proof.
- Automate reporting: Expandi event webhooks to Zapier/Sheets or CRM; retain title, company, message and profile URL. Grade reply quality and notify the responsible person for good/medium replies. Alert when campaign tasks run out.
- Track requests, acceptances, messages and replies; segment by audience and test one change at a time.
- Fix cropped banners using mobile inspection. Use proof and CTA without unnecessary duplication of the headline.
- Occasionally test larger suitable accounts or distribution partners instead of assuming they will not respond. Small total markets warrant deeper relationships and coordinated channels rather than exhausting the list.
- Test content formats against both results and production time. Repurpose strong tweets, teach something concrete or tell a useful story. Shield is demonstrated for content analytics; he notes it does not by itself measure inbound leads.
- His suggested organic trial follows some outbound validation, with about three months of consistent testing. His skepticism toward weak content is his own channel advice.
- Sales Navigator exports can include stale roles or mismatches. He demonstrates filtering actual titles and mentions Evaboot cleanup. Default to blank connection requests unless a genuinely good note tests better.
- Existing connections can be a useful audience if they are relevant and not excluded. He usually limits a broad campaign to about two follow-ups and shows that excessive follow-ups caused many disconnections.
- Enterprise/very small markets can need events, targeted content and timely personal follow-up. He cautions that intrusive SMS can backfire and discusses opted-in reminders. Scale the channel already working when the market is large.

### B2B Meetings on LinkedIn, 2026 Update (2192924897)

- Recorded in late November 2025. Tool prices, model preferences, limits and feature availability are time-specific. The coach explicitly says to recheck limits later.
- He prioritizes active corporate/executive, technology, HR/sales and investment audiences. Distinguish inbound content, connection-based outreach, open/closed InMail and a hybrid of content plus outreach to engaged ICP prospects.
- LinkedIn outbound has lower scalable volume than cold email, but offers profile proof, network building and access to some people whose email is heavily filtered. Content compounds but old LinkedIn posts have less lasting discovery than YouTube in his comparison.
- Profile checklist: friendly headshot; title/value proposition/proof headline; actionable link; featured assets; useful banner; relevant experience; and a genuine story or offer in About. Optional recommendations should be made easy for actual recommenders. His endorsement-purchase suggestion is source teaching only.
- Historical daily baseline he names: 25 connection requests, 40 InMails and 50 messages to existing connections. He describes using higher volumes on established profiles, but these are not safe-limit guarantees. Gradual ramp-up and relevance are emphasized.
- He now favors Valley over his earlier Expandi/HeyReach workflow, discloses the affiliate link and reports better results. HeyReach remains his simpler volume option. He discusses employee, rented and synthetic profiles but does not establish them as necessary for DRM.
- Setup sequence: create Valley account; enter site/company/product/ICP/competitors; use its default writing template; connect the browser extension while logged into LinkedIn; add meeting link; subscribe; connect Sales Navigator Core; fill Studio value propositions, pains and proof.
- Create Valley AI connection campaign, select product/writing style/language and import Sales Navigator URL or CSV. Inspect generated messages and low-ICP fits before launch. The transcript points at six research selections without naming all of them; exact selections need the visual/Gamma source. Hiring trends are specifically mentioned for relevant offers.
- Target using titles, business type, headcount and recent activity. Second-degree connections may help established networks; leave that filter off for small/new networks or very narrow audiences. External databases can be used when Sales Navigator cannot identify the ICP.
- For external lists he demonstrates Clay profile enrichment and filtering for over 500 connections to reduce inactive profiles. A Valley last-90-days activity filter is described as an unverified vendor suggestion, not something he tested.
- Build a separate open-InMail campaign, initially leaving closed profiles off. Separate lists reduce unnecessary use of credits. Closed profiles may be included later if open-profile volume is insufficient.
- Unlike generic templated outreach, he prefers Valley's personalized notes rather than blank requests. Remove low-ICP fits, review messages and monitor remaining campaign days so lists can be replenished.
- Content: supply actual sales-call transcripts, case studies, testimonials and prior posts to the writing model. If using others' posts, identify them as structural/style references. Retain a standalone written post even when attaching a clip or tweet screenshot.
- Post categories: useful thought leadership for the buyer's role, real case studies, genuine personal stories and occasionally relevant trend content. CEOs need commercial implications, not necessarily operator-level tool settings.
- Collect post engagers into a warm list, select high-fit prospects and create a relevant outreach campaign. Optimize against ICP engagement and meetings, not total likes. Feed proven examples back into the writing model.
- Differences are deliberate: this newer lesson favors AI personalization and discourages time-heavy commenting; Ty's lesson favors manual conversations, and the earlier content lesson prescribes comments. These remain separate teachings.

<a id="coaching-section-119"></a>
## Content

### Exert Content into the World (2190824403)

The lesson frames organic content as associating your name with a useful capability through repetition. Documenting real learning is valuable even before becoming an expert. It contrasts paid ads as fast but costly, outbound as active prospecting, and organic as slower but cumulative. The instructor describes little early traction followed by growth and urges roughly 120 days of consistency. His daily exercise is three tweets, ten outward comments and replying to every comment/DM, with about 30 minutes writing and 45 minutes engaging. Repurpose across Twitter, LinkedIn and YouTube while developing your own voice. Conversion may occur long after a reader first encounters you. Statements of inevitable or unlimited results are motivational claims, not DRM guarantees.

### Generate 100 Content Ideas in 15 Minutes (2190826173)

- Goal: earn trust through useful free material. The speaker argues that customers pay for implementation, accountability, packaging, speed and outcomes, so useful teaching need not destroy demand for paid help.
- Two-year test: list skills gained, problems overcome, transitions, struggles, hobbies and experiences from the past two years. Ask what you now know that would have helped your earlier self.
- Pick 3-5 broad topics and add specificity through seven levers: price, problem, industry, location, situation, experience and demographics. Different combinations produce different readers and useful lessons.
- Build a reusable credibility sentence: Over the last [period], I achieved [outcome] without [common obstacle]. Use an actual experience; the speaker's Daniel examples belong to Daniel.
- Apply four A categories: actionable (how-to, tools, tips, guides), analytical (breakdowns, numbers, trends, swipe files), aspirational (journey, lessons, advice to past self) and anthropological (beliefs, mistakes, fears and why people behave as they do).
- Combine each specific topic and credibility statement with many angles in all four categories. One result can support a tools post, a teardown, a story and an explanation of mistaken beliefs without inventing new results.
- Exercise: complete the two-year inventory, narrow topics, write the credibility statements and build the idea matrix. The speaker offers a writing guide and historical TypeShare code; availability was not verified and no subscription was created.

### AI Content Creation with the Poppy Founders (2191194152)

- Poppy is demonstrated as a visual workspace for reference material, voice samples, frameworks and AI conversations. They explicitly say their example video was edited by a human, not by Poppy. Poppy helped produce the storyline, spoken script and voiceover plan.
- SIMPLE framework: Simple language; Instructions one at a time; Market/audience; Patterns showing good examples; Language/tone; External knowledge. Avoid relying on a generic claim that the AI has ten years of experience.
- Specify audience, topic, purpose and useful source material. Start with structure, then develop the script. One presenter demonstrates a combined request, while the other prefers choosing titles before proceeding to outline and body.
- Build framework references for titles, thumbnails, intros and full scripts from useful expert lessons. Ask for concrete examples, then consolidate a detailed framework. This is modeling useful structure, not importing someone else's identity or results.
- Provide your own scripts, emails, newsletters or spoken video transcripts. Ask the model to describe your voice and use your vocabulary, rhythm and tone. Two representative videos are used in the demonstration.
- Claude Projects demonstration: add framework documents, a voice transcript and relevant topic research as separately named knowledge sources. Ask for a structure using those materials, then iterate.
- Poppy demonstration: paste video links, let them process, group related sources and connect them to the chat. Begin by asking what it can see to confirm context. Separate frameworks, your voice, and topic/reference material. Correct misheard names or coined phrases before using the draft.
- The presenters favor Claude for writing at the time of recording. This is their historical model preference, not a current benchmark.
- For more authentic factual material, record a voice memo with your real thoughts and experience. Suggested interview questions: What do you do? Why do you do it? What do you dislike about the industry? What do you wish people understood? Let AI structure that material rather than invent a personal story.
- A participant specifically challenges invented revenue and productivity numbers in a generated hook. The presenters answer by supplying real personal/business context. Their earlier generated examples are not facts about DRM.
- Newsletter examples combine prior emails, the product website, a voice memo, a case-study interview and relevant book/source material. One board includes ratings explaining why past emails were strong or weak. Give specific feedback about what to keep/change and repeat until the draft matches.
- Their actual demonstration transitions from a proposed cold-email exercise to existing newsletter examples. Do not label that part as a demonstrated complete cold-email campaign.
- They demonstrate analysis of Instagram carousel visuals, video on-screen material, TikTok and Facebook ad references in addition to audio transcripts. These are source-analysis capabilities in the recording, not evidence of completed video editing.
- With too much context, process roughly ten videos at a time into detailed anecdotes, quotes and topic notes, then combine those outputs. They discuss then-current Claude/GPT context limits and warn that connecting dozens of long videos can exceed them. Preserve original sources separately so summaries do not erase details.
- The Q&A says local/private enterprise model deployment is not Poppy's core demonstrated use. The founders describe convenience, visual organization and faster ingestion as key differences from manually preparing a Claude project.
- Historical offers include a discount, scripting data pack and a coaching call. Those offers were made during the recording; current availability was not verified. The private shared data-pack links were not captured from this transcript.

<a id="coaching-section-120"></a>
## Additional Cold Calling Demonstrations

### Interview with Dylan, the SDR Whisperer (2191624732)

- Dylan distinguishes one-to-many email from one-to-one calling. He reports 40-60 monthly meetings from his call team and 15-20 from email, with stronger show/close rates for calls. These are his business results, not a forecast for DRM.
- Calling lets the rep clarify meaning, hear objections, control tone and learn how buyers understand the offer. Use the time after launching email campaigns for productive activity rather than repeatedly checking campaign statistics.
- Prioritize high-value members of an email list for manual calling. His example is the best 1,000 of 10,000. He describes email and first call on the same day, with 7-10 attempts over two weeks, while also noting diminishing returns around attempts 5-7. Cool the lead into nurture instead of calling endlessly.
- Good direct contact data matters. Gatekeepers and switchboards are not equivalent to reaching the intended person. ListKit recommendations are part of the hosted promotional interview and not an independent vendor comparison.
- A dedicated dialer provides pacing, recordings, dispositions and reporting. Aloware is his preference; JustCall and Kixie are also named. He discusses number reputation and local presence. Recorded pricing and capability claims are historical.
- Warm-reply method: when someone expresses interest by email, call promptly, refer to that reply, explain that you want to save the back-and-forth and request a brief conversation. If inconvenient, suggest a concrete later time.
- Demonstrated system: prospect data and email platform, automation into GHL/Slack with the lead link, then Aloware to call, calendar to book and payment tool later. This describes his stack, not verification of an equivalent DRM implementation.
- Work in focused blocks, often early or late in the recipient's business day. Midday can be less effective for the office-based decision makers in his examples.
- Metrics: dials; intended-person connects, even if they hang up; real conversations; bookings. His baseline targets are 7-15% dial-to-connect, 40-65% connect-to-conversation and 10-30% conversation-to-booking. Diagnose data/dialer first for poor connects, opener/tone for poor conversations, and the offer/conversation for weak bookings.
- Practice, record and review repeatedly. A bad prior call does not determine the next call. Hiring recommendations appear in the source but remain outside DRM's current requested implementation scope.

### Live Cold Calling Demonstration 1 (2191624740)

- Opens with permission for about 23 seconds and lets the person decide whether to continue. The hook describes likely sales bottlenecks and asks which is more relevant: more appointments or better closing.
- The prospect describes developer-career and podcast coaching. Dylan listens, clarifies the real offer, buyer experience levels, price tiers, existing podcast audience and mailing list rather than forcing the initial generic pitch.
- He identifies the prospect's actual issue: converting the existing audience and getting the messaging right, not simply finding more names. He then connects the relevant platform, messaging and list-building capabilities to that need.
- Books a specific time, reconciles Mountain and Eastern time, sends the calendar invitation during the call and confirms the next meeting's purpose.
- Debrief: one booking from the first pickup is not a normal guaranteed rate. Listening and summarizing the fit mattered. Some days may contain many dials without a conversation. The example's offer and numbers belong to the caller/prospect.

### Live Cold Calling Demonstration 2 (2191624741)

- These are calls to opt-ins and prior contacts, not an untouched cold list. The stated purpose is both appointment setting and understanding why ad viewers opted in but did not book.
- First conversation: trade-show business owner. Dylan builds rapport, clarifies the company's actual work, current PPC/newsletter/cold-email channels and the small sales team. He connects appointment setting with timely form/reply follow-up and targeted outbound. A specific Friday meeting is booked and the invitation confirmed; additional decision makers may join.
- His speed-to-lead statistics are spoken claims in the recording, not verified universal rates. The operational lesson is quick notification and prompt response to an expressed inquiry.
- Second conversation: early-stage coaching business with insufficient cash. He explains his placement price and a coaching-first option, then agrees to revisit later, creates a task and offers a follow-up email with proof. No sale is claimed.
- Third conversation: owner with multiple businesses and existing inbound/educational sequences. Dylan clarifies the needed triage and follow-up role, addresses a bad previous experience, explains training/replacement support and discusses price. The prospect cannot justify the cost; Dylan acknowledges that and leaves information rather than claiming a booking.
- Final conversation: young agency serving electricians, with another niche client and an existing mentor. He explores current acquisition activity, explains a possible future path, accepts the current mismatch and ends courteously.
- Debrief: one booked meeting plus useful qualification and ad-market feedback. Not every opt-in is ready or suitable. Hiring prices, guarantees and service terms in these calls are Dylan's, not DRM's offer. No hiring action was taken.

<a id="coaching-section-121"></a>
## YouTube

### YouTube Content System (2191624876)

Produce one useful weekly long-form video and repurpose its subpoints into text posts. Seek buyer-relevant search questions rather than broad influencer views. Demonstrated research uses vidIQ, related questions and keyword tools; the instructor favors scores around 65+ for topic selection. Outline clear steps and record a straightforward screen tutorial with a visible, well-lit face. Add a short offer plug naturally within the first 30% and a link. He teaches a roughly 40+/50 optimization score, bright readable thumbnail, 8% click-through as a minimum target, 10% ideal and about 30% average viewing. Those are his targets, not universal YouTube requirements.

### Recording and Editing Your Videos (2191624878)

Use a clear camera, good microphone and front-facing light. Google Docs can hold the outline and become a useful linked resource. Start with a visible face, then show the actual process. He demonstrates Camtasia: import the main recording and offer plug, set 3840x2160/30fps, split at a natural break within the first 30%, insert the plug and export MP4. Simple useful instruction matters more than elaborate editing. Tool purchases and recorded pricing are not requirements executed in this review.

### Additional Recording Ideas (2191624880)

Riverside interviews provide separate high-quality tracks and options for vertical clips; the demonstration removes background noise and normalizes audio before export. Phone Shorts can be recorded in short held-button segments, switching between face and demonstration. Fancy captions are not a prerequisite in this lesson. These are alternate recording methods, not new mandatory channels.

### YouTube SEO (2191624882)

Use a relevant title, useful description including the destination link, and relevant tags. Demonstrated tools are vidIQ and Rapidtags, with irrelevant tags removed. He favors a detailed description and a strong optimization score, then measures thumbnail click-through and watch percentage. Bright contrast, a clear face and a few readable words are the thumbnail approach. Choose specific buyer topics and use sufficient performance data before changing thumbnails. His claims about descriptions increasing watching/SEO remain attributed to him.

### OBS Setup (2191624883)

OBS is presented as a free, configurable recording tool, with Loom preferred for quick shareable client messages. Learn scenes, sources, audio mixer and transitions. The walkthrough uses hardware encoding where available, a 1080p/60fps canvas, MP4 output, the correct microphone, a full-camera scene and a screen/window scene with camera overlay. It discusses reducing recording bitrate if performance suffers, keyframe interval two, high-quality encoding and audio-track selection. Some bitrate units are unclear in captions, so consult the visual settings rather than treating those caption units as exact. Fit sources to the canvas, position the camera above the screen source, test recording and locate the output file.

### Using VidIQ (2191624885)

Review daily ideas, keyword demand/competition, existing channel search terms, competitor topics and audience timing. Make the title accurately describe the video. Add relevant description/keyword matches, clean duplicate or irrelevant tags and use the optimization score as a checklist. The example reaches about 48/50; that score alone does not establish business results. End cards and scheduling support discovery. Trend ideas should be evaluated for relevance to the channel's buyers.

### YouTube Masterclass with Helmi (2191624886)

- Distinguish an entertainment channel earning ad/affiliate revenue from a service channel designed to lead viewers to an offer and a call. Language, topics and proof should fit the actual customer.
- Funnel: useful video, organized channel/playlists, landing page with VSL/proof/CTA, then sales call. Competence plus personality can sell before the call without a huge audience.
- Build bottom-of-funnel proof first, such as genuine cases/results/testimonials; then several middle-of-funnel tutorials, comparisons and practical guides; then broader stories, opinions and trends. His steady-state example mix is 40% top, 40% middle and 20% bottom.
- A channel can cover a broad service with industry-specific playlists. Use a VSL as channel trailer where appropriate. Clearly communicate the business result in the banner and link to the relevant page.
- Plan a comprehensive flagship guide and turn sections into individual videos. Useful resources can support the lessons and become a lead asset.
- Research search questions and unusually strong videos from smaller channels. Study why an outlier worked and adapt the framework with your own expertise, not another creator's claimed results. A separate research viewing account can focus recommendations.
- Thumbnail teaching includes a clear before/after, mechanism or visual connection, face and few words. Do not confuse illustrative thumbnail design with evidence of a client result.
- Script with a structured outline: hook, audience, benefit/credibility, clear body points and a next action. Docs, Gamma, Notion, Miro or physical notes are options. Speak naturally from experience rather than reading like a newsreader.
- Basic editing removes dead air, filler and retakes; Descript, CapCut and DaVinci are discussed. Phone plus good light can be enough. Weekly consistency is viable; more videos only help if useful and sustainable.
- Repurpose the long-form script into newsletter, LinkedIn/X posts and short clips or new phone takes. A body point can become one short video.
- Another company's analysis is a teardown, not your own client case. Podcasts can support relationships but need relevant guests/topics. Affiliate programs are merchant arrangements, not the core service-channel goal.
- Helmi's preference for limiting outbound links and keeping viewers watching differs from Daniel's repeated offer-plug method. Both are preserved instead of silently selecting one for DRM.
- The private Miro board and promised future flagship example were not acquired. The full lesson captions are preserved.

### d100-26-prompt-document

---

<a id="coaching-section-125"></a>
# **Marquee Method AI Outreach — Prompting Guide**

### **By Christian Bonnier | Client Ascension**

*Use this doc with Claude (claude.ai) to find prospects, research them, write hyper-personal outreach, and create Marquee Method deliverables in minutes.*

---

<a id="coaching-section-126"></a>
## **HOW THIS WORKS**

There are 4 prompts in this doc. Run them in order:

1. **PROMPT 0 — Find Your Marquee Prospects** → tells you exactly who to target and where to find them  
2. **PROMPT 1 — Research the Prospect** → paste in the prospect's info and get a full intel brief  
3. **PROMPT 2 — Write the Cold Email / DM** → turns the research into a hyper-personal outreach message  
4. **PROMPT 3 — Create the Marquee Method Deliverable** → builds the actual asset to send after they reply

Each prompt builds on the last. Don't skip steps.

---

<a id="coaching-section-127"></a>
## **BEFORE YOU START — Know Your Offer Level**

| Level | What It Means | Example Offers | Strategy |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| **Level 1** | Prospect KNOWS they need this | Podcast placement, speaking gigs, book publishing | Direct CTA — go straight for the call |
| **Level 2** | Prospect needs it but doesn't know why yours | Cold email, ads, email marketing, YouTube content | Lead magnet \+ risk reversal |
| **Level 3** | Prospect doesn't think they need it | Web design, SEO, Facebook ads, IT | Free work deliverable upfront |

**Rule:** The closer you are to Level 3, the more free work you lead with.

---

<a id="coaching-section-128"></a>
## **PROMPT 0 — FIND YOUR MARQUEE PROSPECTS**

> Run this first. It tells you exactly who to target and where to find them.

```
You are a Marquee Method prospecting strategist. Your job is to help me build a targeted list of 
ideal prospects to reach out to.

Here is my business info:
- My service: [WHAT YOU DO]
- My offer level: [LEVEL 1 / 2 / 3]
- My ideal client: [DESCRIBE WHO YOU WANT TO WORK WITH — e.g. "e-commerce brand owners doing 
  $50k-$500k/mo", "agency owners doing $3k-$10k/mo", "B2B SaaS founders"]
- My lead magnet: [FREE THING YOU'RE OFFERING]
- My best case study: [YOUR STRONGEST RESULT — e.g. "helped X go from $2k to $93k/mo"]
- Niches I want to target: [LIST ANY SPECIFIC NICHES — or say "suggest some for me"]

Do the following:

1. DEFINE MY MARQUEE METHOD CRITERIA
   - What does my ideal prospect look like? (revenue range, team size, content activity, 
     platform presence, engagement level)
   - What signals tell me someone is a QUALIFIED prospect vs a waste of time?
   - What are 3 red flags that disqualify someone immediately?

2. SUGGEST WHERE TO FIND THEM
   For each of the following platforms, tell me exactly how to find qualified prospects:
   - LinkedIn (search filters, company pages, post engagement, etc.)
   - Instagram (competitor followings, hashtags, "For You" lists, tagged posts)
   - Twitter/X (lists, threads, engagement on competitor accounts)
   - Podcasts (shows in my niche, recent guests who match my ICP)
   - Newsletters (Substack, Beehiiv — writers in my niche)
   - YouTube (channels in my niche, comment sections)
   - Communities (Facebook Groups, Slack groups, Discord servers, Skool)

3. BUILD ME A SCORING SYSTEM
   Create a simple 1-10 scoring rubric I can use to prioritize prospects. 
   Include factors like: audience size, content activity, offer alignment, 
   engagement rate, and likelihood to need my service.

4. OUTPUT A SAMPLE PROSPECT LIST
   Based on my ICP above, give me 10 example types of prospects I should be targeting 
   (real or hypothetical). For each one include:
   - Type of business/person
   - Why they're a good fit for my offer
   - Where I'd likely find them
   - What my hook angle might be
```

---

<a id="coaching-section-129"></a>
## **PROMPT 1 — RESEARCH THE PROSPECT**

> Once you have your prospect list, run this for each person you want to reach out to.

```
You are a world-class sales researcher. Your job is to build a complete intelligence 
brief on a prospect I want to reach out to.

Here is the prospect's info:
- Name: [FULL NAME]
- Company: [COMPANY NAME]
- Role: [THEIR TITLE / ROLE]
- Email: [EMAIL IF YOU HAVE IT]
- LinkedIn: [LINKEDIN URL]
- Website: [COMPANY WEBSITE]
- Any other links (podcast, YouTube, Twitter/X, Instagram): [ADD ANY]

Search everything publicly available on this person. I need you to find:

1. ONE specific, impressive, verifiable achievement or public statement they've made 
   (a LinkedIn post, podcast quote, case study result, revenue milestone, etc.) — 
   this will be the hook for my outreach
2. Their current offer / what they sell
3. Who their target customer is
4. Any pain points, bottlenecks, or problems they've publicly talked about
5. Their content style and tone (how do they talk — casual, formal, data-driven, 
   story-driven?)
6. Any recent news, launches, or announcements about them or their company

Format your output as:
- BEST HOOK: (the one thing I'll open my email with — be specific, include the quote 
  or stat)
- OFFER SUMMARY: (what they sell in 2 sentences)
- ICP: (who their ideal customer is)
- PAIN POINTS: (what problems they've talked about publicly)
- TONE/STYLE: (how they communicate)
- RECENT NEWS: (anything notable happening with them right now)
- OUTREACH ANGLE: (your recommended angle for my cold email based on all of the above)
```

---

<a id="coaching-section-130"></a>
## **PROMPT 2 — WRITE THE COLD EMAIL / DM**

> After running Prompt 1, paste the research brief into this prompt along with your offer details.

```
You are an expert cold email copywriter trained on the Marquee outreach method.

Here is the research brief on my prospect:
[PASTE OUTPUT FROM PROMPT 1 HERE]

Here is my offer:
- My service: [WHAT YOU DO]
- My lead magnet: [FREE THING YOU'RE OFFERING — e.g. "50 free leads", "a sample script", 
  "a free homepage mockup", "a free video"]
- My offer level: [LEVEL 1 / 2 / 3]
- My best case study or result: [E.G. "helped X go from $2k to $93k/mo in under a year"]

Now write me THREE versions of a cold outreach message:

VERSION 1 — Cold Email
- Lowercase subject line (2-4 words, question or curiosity-based)
- 3-5 sentences max
- Open with the BEST HOOK from the research — make it feel like I did my homework, 
  not like a compliment
- Reference my lead magnet naturally in the body
- End with a soft "mind if I share it?" CTA — the ONLY goal is to get them to raise 
  their hand
- No fluff, no formal language, write like a peer texting a peer

VERSION 2 — Instagram / LinkedIn DM
- 2-4 sentences max
- Even more casual than the email
- Same hook, same lead magnet, same CTA
- Could open with a genuine observation about their content or a recent post

VERSION 3 — Voice Note / Loom Script
- 30-45 second spoken script
- Open with the hook
- Explain the lead magnet in one sentence
- End with the CTA
- Write it exactly how you'd say it out loud — no formal language

Rules for all three versions:
- NEVER use the word "I" to start a sentence
- NO corporate buzzwords (synergy, leverage, robust, etc.)
- NO compliments that could apply to anyone ("love your work", "big fan")
- The hook must be SPECIFIC — a real stat, quote, or post they made
- The lead magnet must be mentioned — never pitch a call as the first ask
```

---

<a id="coaching-section-131"></a>
## **PROMPT 3 — CREATE THE MARQUEE METHOD DELIVERABLE**

> Use this AFTER they reply positively. This builds the actual asset to send after they reply.

```
You are an expert [INSERT YOUR SERVICE — e.g. "YouTube scriptwriter / cold email 
strategist / web designer / email marketer"].

A prospect just replied positively to my outreach. They are interested in seeing 
the lead magnet I promised them.

Here is everything I know about them:
[PASTE THE RESEARCH BRIEF FROM PROMPT 1]

Here is what I promised to send them:
[DESCRIBE YOUR LEAD MAGNET — e.g. "a sample YouTube script in their voice", "a cold 
email campaign written for their business", "a homepage mockup", "a 5-email welcome 
sequence"]

Now build the actual deliverable. Make it:
1. Specific to THEM — use their brand name, their audience, their offer, their tone
2. Immediately usable — they should be able to implement it with zero extra work
3. Impressive enough that they feel they NEED to get on a call to get more of this
4. Finished, not a template — no [brackets] or placeholders in the final output

Also include at the end:
- A short follow-up message I can send WITH the deliverable (2-3 sentences max)
- One sentence explaining why this deliverable will work for their specific business
```

---

<a id="coaching-section-132"></a>
## **THE 3-STEP FOLLOW-UP SEQUENCE**

**Email 1 (Day 1\) — Original outreach** *(Your message from Prompt 2\)*

**Email 2 (Day 3\)**

> still have \[LEAD MAGNET\] pulled up for you. mind if i send it over?

**Email 3 (Day 7\)**

> last follow up on this — \[LEAD MAGNET\] is ready to go whenever you are. worth a look?

**Rule:** Same message, three times. Don't add more info. Don't apologize for following up. Don't change the offer.

---

<a id="coaching-section-133"></a>
## **QUICK REFERENCE — OFFER ANCHORING**

❌ "We help businesses grow their YouTube channel" — not anchored to anything

✅ "We can get you 1 video a week — scripted, edited, posted" — anchored to a deliverable

✅ "I put together a sample YouTube script for you in your voice" — anchored to a lead magnet

✅ "We helped \[Name\] go from 0 to \$43k in clients from YouTube in 2 months" — anchored to a case study

✅ "I put together a sample script AND a list of 10 video topics for your audience" — anchored to lead magnet \+ specificity

---

<a id="coaching-section-134"></a>
## **EXAMPLE — FULL RUN-THROUGH**

**Prospect:** Daniel Fazio — Co-Founder, Client Ascension \+ ListKit **Offer:** Organic YouTube content (1 video/week, scripted, edited, posted) **Offer Level:** Level 2

**RESEARCH HOOK IDENTIFIED:** Daniel publicly posted he signed \$43k in clients from YouTube in 2 months — off just 500–1,500 daily views.

**COLD EMAIL OUTPUT:**

Subject: `quick question`

> saw your linkedin post where you mentioned signing \$43k in clients from youtube in just 2 months — off 500-1,500 daily views.

> that's an insane ROI for a channel that size.

> i put together a sample youtube script for you — "the exact cold email that took me from \$0 to \$100k/mo" — written in your voice, based on your story.

> if you like it, all you have to do is record. we'll handle scripting, editing, and posting every week.

> mind if i share the script here?

**DELIVERABLE CREATED:** Full YouTube script written in Daniel's voice, structured with hook → problem → breakthrough → formula → CTA, ready to record.

---

<a id="coaching-section-135"></a>
## **TIPS FOR YOUR STUDENTS**

* **You don't need to know everything about the prospect before you start.** Just drop their LinkedIn URL and website into Prompt 1 and let Claude do the research.  
* **The lead magnet doesn't have to exist yet.** Only build it if they reply. This saves you hours of wasted effort.  
* **The hook is everything.** If you can't find one specific, impressive, verifiable thing — dig deeper. Check LinkedIn posts, podcast appearances, YouTube comments, and their blog.  
* **Don't overcomplicate the CTA.** "Mind if I share it here?" is enough. The only goal of the first message is to get them to raise their hand.  
* **Match the tone to the platform.** DMs are more casual than emails. Voice notes are even more casual than DMs. Looms sit in between.  
* **Volume is a vanity metric.** 10 hyper-personalized messages will always outperform 500 generic ones. Use the scoring system from Prompt 0 to stay focused on the right people.

---

*Built for the Marquee Method AI Outreach Training | Christian Bonnier | Client Ascension*

### Preserved resource: 2191624884-equipment-guide.md

**How to Get That YouTuber Setup Look**

First things first, what does a YouTuber video setup look like?

Depends on which ones you watch, but generally, we’re talking about a few key elements

1: High-quality camera with a shallow depth of field (blurry background)  
2: High-quality microphone and audio (that podcaster sound)  
3: High-quality lighting (key lights \+ coloured lights)  
4: Recording and streaming software

Imagine a setup similar to Iman Gadzhi or Sebastian Ghiorghiu

All of this sounds complicated and expensive but you can do it cheap as hell if you know what you’re doing 

Check out this quick video I recorded below to get an idea of my setup

[**CLICK THE THUMBNAIL**![][image1]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1_yWcoGSwM4)

I’m going to briefly explain WHY each piece of equipment matters and what it does, most importantly what you SHOULDN’T buy

I’ll then list equipment-buying guides based on budget \- note that you can find many of the items I list second hand in extremely good condition and I recommend searching around for the best price although Amazon links will be provided

**Camera**

Arguably the most important part of this setup is the camera

You can spend \$200+ to get a decent webcam or you can just upgrade to a DSLR camera

If you insist on a webcam, just get the Logitech Brio but a DSLR is recommended

A DSLR is a significantly better investment as not only will it make your videos look better but it can be used for all types of content creation

Going on a business trip? Make a vlog. A client sends you a product? Take a high-quality picture. Want to get into YouTube content? Use the camera

Not only will a DSLR generally give you a higher-quality image, it will allow you to swap out lenses on the camera

A lens with a low aperture (how much light the lens allows into the camera) will give you that nice blurry background look in your videos

Lens apertures generally range from f1.4 up to as much f6. Lower aperture lenses will cost more

If you want to learn more about aperture settings, [go here.](https://photographylife.com/what-is-aperture-in-photography)

Aside from that you’ll have to choose between a mirrored or mirrorless camera setup. Mirrorless cameras are generally smaller, more compact, and often faster at taking photos

DSLR cameras will not plug directly into your computer and will need a device called a “capture card” to be displayed in your recording software. The CamLink 4K is the best option for this.

Popular camera brands include Canon, Sony, Nikon, and Fujifilm, but for the price lists I will be focusing on Canon and Sony as they are the most versatile of the few and the ones I personally have the most experience with

**Microphone**

**DO NOT BUY THE BLUE YETI**

Just putting that out there to start. The Blue Yeti is not a terrible quality microphone, but for the price of the Blue Yeti you can do a lot better and will sound a lot more professional 

There’s two types of microphones that we care about:

1. Dynamic  
2. Condenser

There’s many difference between these two but theres only a few we care about

**Dynamic microphones** pick up **less sound** around you, which is one of the reasons they’re so popular in broadcasting and podcasting

They give you that much more isolated vocal sound that we’ve grown used to hearing on the radio

In the video at the start of this article I am using the Shure SM7B, which has been an industry standard vocal mic for some time

You’ll probably recognize it as the mic used on *The Joe Rogan Experience* and *Impaulsive* podcasts

**Condenser microphones** pick up **more sound** around you. This means that you can sit further away from the microphone but it also means that it’s going to pick up more sound in the room that you may not want

The Blue Yeti is a condenser microphone that is known in the YouTube and streaming world for its annoying background hiss and unwanted sound pickup

Condenser mics can be a good choice if you’re in a relatively quiet environment but I would argue that for 99% of the work that the people reading this are going to be doing, just get a dynamic mic and you’ll immediately sound better

I’ll list some dynamic and condenser mics in the price list but I would lean towards suggesting dynamic mics for any professional calls / recordings

There is two common types of computer microphones \- USB and XLR

USB microphones plug directly into a USB port on your computer

The upside of this is they’re much handier to use \- the downside is that they often have an annoying electrical background hum as the same cable that is capturing audio is also transmitting power to the microphone

XLR microphones require an audio interface that can connect to your computer

A cheap option is the Scarlett Solo II USB which has more than enough functionality for most people

XLR microphones generally sound better than USB but can be more of a hassle to set up

I would previously have suggested only using an XLR microphone but with the introduction of microphones like the Elgato Wave and Shure MV7, there’s a ton of great options these days

**Lighting**

This is regularly overlooked but it doesn’t matter how sick or expensive your camera is if no one can see you on it

Lighting can be done for a few bucks or for the cost of a new car, it really depends what you’re looking for

There’s some primary lighting practices you’ll want to follow, again these are the basics and you can find much more info about this online if you wish to delve into it but we’re aiming to just get you started with a sick setup

For that YouTube look we’ll need three types of lights:

1. Fill light  
2. Key Light  
3. Colored background lights

Now there is a standard lighting setup called a “3-point” setup that we will slightly modify to get the look we want

Check out the diagram of a 3-point setup below:

![][image2]

In this setup the object in the centre \- that would be **you** \- has 3 lights pointed at it

A key light, a fill light, and a back light

In my experience, coloured lights can act as your back light, adding some ambience to your scene and making it slightly more interesting

Your key light is usually your brightest light, this is what primarily lights the scene and shows the most detail. 

As you can see in the diagram, it is to the front right of the object

I would also suggest raising the light slightly and even point the light at a reflective surface like a white wall to soften it slightly depending on what light you use

The Fill light essentially fills in the shadows created by the key light

This light is usually not as bright as your key light and helps to give your videos a softer, more professional look

In the below picture, on the left there is no fill light. On the right, a fill light is turned on

![][image3]

Here is another diagram to give you an idea of how to set up your key lights and fill lights. For backlights, I would suggest coloured lights positioned in a way that suits your setup the best and provides the most interesting background

![][image4]

**Software**

Loom is great for hosting quick videos to send to clients but we need to stop using it for long form videos when ther is much more powerful free software available

Enter: [**Open Broadcaster Software**](https://obsproject.com/)

Open Broadcaster Software (OBS) is the gold standard for screen recording and capturing video

It is also COMPLETLEY FREE and open source, you will NEVER have to pay for OBS

There are millions of tutorials from streamers and YouTubers on how to use OBS but I will give a quick overview in the video below

[**CLICK THE THUMBNAIL**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i5rmeBu1Alw)  
[![][image5]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i5rmeBu1Alw)

OBS can stream to livestreaming services or record directly to your computer in higher quality than Loom and allows for insane levels of customization

There’s even a [whole forum dedicated to OBS plugins](https://obsproject.com/forum/resources/categories/obs-studio-plugins.6/)

You can use your OBS scene as a webcam and share your desktop on calls without having to request access to do so in Zoom, you can display graphics on top of your stream, you can remove a greenscreen behind you, you can transition from a closeup to a wide shot, and even more 

For an example of just how insanely powerful OBS is, [all of this was done live in OBS](https://youtu.be/QFvv6J_UPgc)

Check out some tutorials below:

[OBS For Brand New Streamers (Creating Scenes, Adding Custom Widgets, and MORE)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EuSUPpoi0Vs)

[How to Use OBS Studio - Complete Tutorial for Beginners\!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-puA85ciDEM)

[Ultimate OBS Studio Full Setup Guide and Tutorial for Streaming and Recording](https://youtu.be/tQhIaNbnhNk)

3. **Lights**

   4. Light Stands
