# Detailed lesson notes — Onboarding, Operations & Systems

These are source-based summaries. Business adaptations are labeled separately. Full source transcripts are preserved beside this document. Hiring is excluded by user instruction, including implementation of hiring recommendations embedded in core lessons.

<a id="coaching-section-146"></a>
## 1. Quick intro — Andre Haykal Jr

Source post 2195864082; 8.2 minutes. Automatic transcript reviewed, with the opening 180 seconds repaired in short audio segments and reviewed separately. Automatic transcription can mishear names; it is not a verbatim certified transcript.

Andre describes three support channels: study the course, attend his weekly coaching calls, and use his AI clone between calls. The recording says Thursday at 2 p.m. Eastern; verify the current members-only schedule before creating a calendar event. He says the general course addresses approximately 80% of common issues; live coaching helps tailor the remainder to the actual service, team and client. Return to relevant lessons as bottlenecks change. Avoid treating Slack DMs to him as the primary support route.

Resource: https://ai.clientascension.com/chat-with-andre

The repaired opening emphasizes that operations is an evolving discipline, not a one-time fix. Andre frames the transition from signing clients to delivering consistently as a milestone. His business-volume examples are his reported experience, not DRM's scale.

<a id="coaching-section-147"></a>
## 3. Client Fulfillment, Operations & Systems

Source post 2190822223; 94.7 minutes. Full published transcript and linked workbook reviewed. The core framework is marketing → sales → fulfillment. Operations protects the ability to continue acquiring clients and deliver consistently.

### Sales velocity and client journey

Andre defines sales velocity here as consistently signing new clients without switching marketing and sales off to catch up with delivery. His illustrative 10% monthly client churn requires one replacement for ten opening clients, or five replacements for fifty, just to stay level. These are examples, not a benchmark assumed for DRM. Track the actual cohort, client count and revenue separately: one large lost account can matter more than several small ones.

The journey is onboarding → implementation → optimization → growth. The first 24 hours should remove uncertainty and buyer's remorse through acknowledgement and specific next steps. Three things clients dislike: unknowns, negative surprises and repeating information already provided. Pass sales-call context into onboarding instead of making the client start over.

### Three onboarding pillars

1. **Remove friction:** concise steps, familiar tools, plain language, visual instructions where helpful. Finish communications with the next action, its owner and timing. If practical, help complete intake/book kickoff while the client is still on the sales call.
2. **Show early value:** agree what the client values, then make meaningful progress visible before renewal. Approved targeting, working tracking, approved creative and a launched campaign can be progress milestones before a commercial result arrives. Progress is not booked revenue and does not replace the promised outcome.
3. **Reward useful participation:** acknowledge the client's prompt access, feedback or training completion and explain how it helps results. Discounts, bonus credits and gift cards in the lecture are optional examples; none became DRM policy.

### Weekly engagement

Send wins/KPIs, completed and in-progress work, and upcoming actions. Consistency matters more than a flashy portal. Use the method the client actually responds to: email, Slack, Loom or calls. Keep communications personal. Celebrate small wins when they happen; raise underperformance before the client must ask, with the corrective action attached. Client responsibilities are part of the process and must be explained in terms of their desired outcome.

### Systems, quality and time

Begin with a real 72-hour task audit. Classify time, energy, value and client-facing/internal work. Remove unnecessary steps before automating. For repeatable work, document trigger, start/end, actions, decision points and quality standard. Use training and examples for judgment-heavy tasks instead of attempting to script every decision. Review completed work and call recordings, collect feedback, and fix recurring causes rather than repeating cleanup.

The recording suggests grouping meetings, deep work and communication instead of constantly switching. Andre's 9 a.m.–1 p.m. meeting block is his example, not a sensible automatic four-hour daily requirement for Brandon's 10–20-hour week. Set weekly objectives early in the week and review Friday. Establish realistic response boundaries and push back constructively on scope creep, impossible deadlines or requests that undermine the client's desired outcome.

### Workbook actions and Q&A

- Within seven days: map onboarding, prepare/use a weekly update, conduct the 72-hour audit.
- Within thirty days: automate three genuinely repetitive processes and create a client-health tracker.
- Establish recurring reviews and quality checkpoints. Hiring tasks are excluded by the user's instruction.
- Q&A favors simple Trello + Google Docs + Slack for an agency at the discussed stage; a separate elaborate onboarding website is optional.
- Prioritize according to the real problem: weak onboarding, clients at risk, or unclear time use. The audit helps when the priority is uncertain.
- AI assists delivery and judgment; a written automation specification is not a running integration.

DRM adaptation: six-list private Trello template, industry-specific activation paths, written weekly updates and client-health fields. No current client is being onboarded. Actual client sends, milestones and audit observations remain future execution, not checked-off claims.

<a id="coaching-section-148"></a>
## 4. World-Class Service & CSMs

Source post 2196853990; 115.2 minutes. Automatic transcript reviewed. Service portion runs approximately 0:00–1:02:25; later hiring discussion is excluded from implementation. Some audience questions in the automatic transcript are unclear, so no precise claims depend on those garbled passages.

### Client service framework

Service has a **front stage** (communication, expectations, onboarding and relationship) and a **backstage** (campaigns, creative, lists, delivery). Strong technical work alone does not show the client what is happening. Establish the starting point A, desired point B, and roughly five activation milestones in between. Favor milestones the agency/client can actually complete rather than only outcomes that cannot be scheduled precisely.

Around 6:50–10:30, Andre describes mapping activation points and shortening time to value. His cold-email example progresses through campaign launch, meaningful sending volume, iteration from replies and improved campaign performance. His SaaS examples concern connecting a sending tool and buying a domain. These examples illustrate identifying behaviors associated with retention; they are not universal instructions to buy tools or send 10,000 emails for every DRM client.

### Joint accountability and onboarding

Around 13:50–30:00, the lesson calls for clear deliverables and explicit client responsibilities. Signed scope precedes onboarding; each client must know what the agency does and what they need to provide. The welcome should recognize the investment, personalize the reason for joining, and answer “what happens next?”

Complete intake before kickoff so the call can present a prepared plan. Collect business details, baseline, desired state, relevant proof and assets. Compare goals with what was agreed during sales. An aspirational number written in intake is not automatically an accepted promise. Where appropriate, existing warm leads may provide an early opportunity, but using or contacting those leads is a separate campaign action.

Prepare from sales-call transcript plus intake, then build rapport, present the timeline/activation points, explain both parties' responsibilities, resolve questions and confirm next steps. Ask candidly whether the onboarding experience gives them confidence in the decision. Record the call appropriately and produce a personalized recap with actions/owners/dates. Offer help completing intake when a client stalls instead of merely repeating reminders.

### Ongoing management

Around 31:00–45:00, the recurring update has three essentials: what we did, what comes next, and what we need from the client. Recognize real activation milestones. When a problem appears, acknowledge it before the client does and explain the correction already underway. Use a call for emotionally charged or complex issues; text can obscure tone. A brief unscheduled check-in is the coach's example, not a call placed by this review.

Set and consistently honor communication expectations. The coach gives one business day as an example. DRM's actual response promise must match availability and agreement. Offer a monthly one-on-one review. When churn signals appear, review the work and proactively present an updated plan. After cancellation, seek honest feedback and feed it back into onboarding/delivery improvements.

### Retention metrics and expansion

Around 45:00–56:00, the newer lesson promotes **net revenue retention (NRR)** as the revenue-focused measure alongside client churn. For the opening recurring-revenue cohort: (opening MRR − churned MRR − contraction MRR + expansion MRR) / opening MRR. Exclude new customers from that cohort calculation. The recording's simplified formula omits a separate contraction term; this adaptation includes reductions so retained revenue is not overstated. If opening MRR is zero, NRR is unavailable.

Example from the lecture: five clients paying $2K each, one lost, another increased to $4K → $10K retained revenue and 100% NRR, even with fewer clients. Offsetting lost **client percentages** with upsold **client percentages** is insufficient unless the dollar effects match. Also track monthly client churn, feedback/NPS, testimonials, referrals and upsells. NPS is a likelihood-to-recommend question; with one client it should not be presented as statistically robust evidence.

Offer expansion when genuine value or a milestone reveals a relevant need, not only at contract expiry. Options include more of the existing service, continued access, or a complementary service solving the next bottleneck. Reactivation is a separate stage for past clients; one example checks in 30 days after churn. No upsell or reactivation messages have been sent for DRM.

The coach recommends *Unreasonable Hospitality* and *Excellence Wins*. No book purchases were made. The closing actions are to map activation points, process-map fulfillment and implement the obvious gaps without over-planning. Hiring/compensation/recruiting tasks remain excluded.

<a id="coaching-section-149"></a>
## 2. Basic Finance: Accounting, Tax, Investing

Source post 2190019481; 45.6 minutes. Daniel presents basic accounting before investment topics. Main operational instruction: track money coming in, money going out and cash remaining. A simple business can start with a simple sheet; complexity is not the objective.

### Accounting framework taught

- Revenue less direct delivery costs equals gross profit. Subtract operating expenses for operating/net results as defined in the sheet; keep tax and owner withdrawals explicit rather than muddling categories.
- Gross and net margins express profits as a percentage of revenue. Break-even means revenues cover expenses.
- A balance sheet lists assets, liabilities and equity. Cash flow records actual movements of money; booked sales or unpaid invoices are not cash collected.
- Separate business receipts/spending from personal activity. He recommends a business account/card and consistent transaction tracking.
- Compare fixed costs (owed regardless of sales) with variable delivery costs (increase with work). Daniel prefers a lean variable-cost structure for resilience when revenue falls. The lesson also acknowledges that fixed-cost models can gain operating leverage as revenue rises.
- Budget from after-expense and after-tax resources, not top-line revenue. His emergency-fund example uses six months of personal living expenses before deploying surplus into long-term investments.

### Tax/investing portions — coach's examples, not implemented decisions

The recording discusses sole proprietorships, LLCs, S-corporation elections, reasonable salary, distributions, income/self-employment taxes, brackets and capital gains. It uses simplified US examples and historical figures. It proposes discussing an S election around $75,000 yearly profit. That number is the coach's heuristic, not a verified trigger for this business. No entity election, salary, tax reserve rate or filing has been changed.

Daniel emphasizes long holding periods and automatic contributions over trading. He discusses VOO/S&P 500 exposure, reinvested dividends, compound-growth illustrations, Robinhood, M1 and Coinbase; he describes his personal VOO/Bitcoin allocation. His return assumptions and very large future balances are scenarios, not guaranteed outcomes. Broad claims about never losing over a ten-year period or always outperforming every alternative are not independently established by this review. The notes preserve the lesson without turning those claims into promises or initiating investments.

The business takeaway for DRM is a reliable cash/profit dashboard tied to actual sources. The user's $20,000 monthly profit goal remains unchanged; the coach's motivational income targets do not replace it. Financial setup still requires actual balances, revenue, costs and accountant-approved tax assumptions.

Resource: https://gamma.app/docs/Basic-Finance-Accounting-Tax-Investing-symx1ewot1h1t5s

<a id="coaching-section-150"></a>
## 5. Client Contracts

Source post 2190536825; 8.1 minutes. The lesson supplies two examples, not a universal agreement: (1) a retainer without a refund guarantee; (2) a retainer plus performance fee and conditional refund guarantee. Daniel explicitly says the templates require tailoring to the actual offer and deal terms and that his examples are not legal advice.

The process taught: copy the example, adjust parties/scope/deliverables/timeline/client obligations/payment and guarantee provisions, export the document, map signers and their name/date/signature fields in e-sign software, and retain the executed agreement. He mentions DocuSign and PandaDoc; pricing remarks are historical and have not been used to select a paid subscription.

Important fields: project start conditions (payment and required assets), revision limits, ownership transfer, confidentiality, termination, liability provisions, governing law, and any software requirements in an appendix. A performance arrangement additionally needs the result definition, period, client eligibility obligations, proof requirements, fee basis and payment due dates. His sample amounts/three-client guarantee are illustrations, not DRM terms. Do not copy a no-refund clause into a DRM offer that promises a refund or guarantee. Do not carry his suggested deletion remedy into an operational automation.

Resources:
- https://docs.google.com/document/d/1LmspqXY_okkNtspr-QbDl_AsfjmRArU6Ix1uIkPpSNo/edit?usp=sharing
- https://docs.google.com/document/d/1q-PB4k_IWUDhGYqO3ky3rgDmIwOaHB3ZigKsQq3PuPc/edit?usp=sharing

Both documents were exported and read. The no-refund example has two revision rounds, $200/hour additional revisions, seven-day termination notice and Florida governing law. The performance example uses $5,000/month plus 10% of a specially defined revenue base, three new clients/month, $10,000/month ad spend, a 15% close rate and eight hours/day of availability. These are the coach's example terms only. Its phrase “Gross Revenue” is explicitly defined as cash collected minus ad spend, so it must not be confused with ordinary gross revenue. None of those figures, its account deletion remedy, or its guarantee conditions was adopted for DRM. Actual current industry terms must be used at future client onboarding.

<a id="coaching-section-151"></a>
## 10. Effective Client Communication

Source post 2189331031; 58.3 minutes. Full published transcript reviewed, including the middle section separately to avoid output truncation.

Retained clients need evidence of results and a good experience. Communicate in short, clear, conversational messages rather than essays. Capture baseline metrics during onboarding; otherwise even improvement is hard to demonstrate. The lecture's rhythm is a Monday/Tuesday check-in, useful updates or wins during the week, and a Friday KPI report. Vary the wording to reflect real context; the coach discourages a robotic repeated check-in message.

For a cold-email service, the example reports positive replies, booked calls, reply-to-call conversion and a pipeline-value estimate. Pipeline estimates are not cash or guaranteed revenue. DRM reports the applicable industry's contracted result, with its numerator/denominator and period, instead of forcing every client into cold-email metrics.

When performance is good, contextualize against baseline and the agreed goal. When it is poor, state the numbers and the corrective plan, then use a live call when explanation or tone matters. Do not make the client ask for bad news. Ask how the client perceives the service and what success means to them; reconcile unreasonable expectations directly.

Live review structure: where we started → where we are → ahead/behind the agreed goal → where we are going → action plan. Ask questions throughout; a monologue is not alignment. Conclude with named next actions and follow-up. A short 5–15-minute alignment call can be separate from a strategy-heavy kickoff if too much information would overload one meeting. Monthly or biweekly review calls often allow more meaningful progress than automatic weekly meetings; retain weekly asynchronous contact.

Ask for referrals when the client is happy and value has been demonstrated. The coach's $500 referral-discount example was not adopted as DRM policy. Email is acceptable when a client will not use Slack. Use actual client feedback to improve intake and access instructions.

<a id="coaching-section-152"></a>
## 11. AI To Increase Fulfillment Capacity

Source post 2190822671; 49.2 minutes. Full published transcript reviewed. The coach treats AI as assistance that improves capacity and quality, with humans retaining strategy, relationships, judgment and final review.

Begin with the 72-hour audit and ask daily what slowed the work. A company AI Slack channel gathers opportunities, experiments and results. Implement one actual bottleneck at a time; measure time and quality rather than collecting tools.

Four demonstrations:
1. Slack task capture/reminders with Chaser: owners and deadlines extracted into follow-up. The lesson's pricing is historical; no paid app installed.
2. An offer-drafting bot trained on expert calls and examples, using intake context. The reported capacity improvement is the coach's result. DRM's existing offers are not being rewritten.
3. Onboarding preparation from the sales call, emails, intake and CRM so the call starts informed and clients do not repeat themselves. A reusable preparation prompt is included in the implementation pack.
4. Recorded-call review against a 1–5 rubric, with examples, then personalized follow-up drafts. Review low scores and compare ratings against human judgment; a model's score is not automatically reliable.

The proposed drafting workflow is initial draft → critique → synthesis → human final QA. Examples such as Fathom, Fireflies, Typeform and Poppy.ai show possible tools, not a requirement to buy every product. Team/hiring/pay recommendations and experimental spending cards remain excluded. The internal private `drm-ai` channel was created with an experiment-recording description; no client data or call transcripts were uploaded to a new external AI tool.

<a id="coaching-section-153"></a>
## 12. Retain Clients FOREVER

Source post 2190822580; 64.7 minutes. Full published transcript reviewed. The title is aspirational, not a guarantee that clients never leave.

**Phase 1 — offer:** believe in the service, prioritize a valuable result and ask whether you would buy it yourself. Results can be a usable finished app/video as well as numerical business performance. Define success with the client. This does not require abandoning DRM's existing industry offers.

**Phase 2 — first impression:** acknowledge the agreement/payment promptly, explain the next steps and then update the client as work progresses. If a tailored welcome must be assembled manually, a brief immediate acknowledgement can bridge the gap. Payment terms can differ; an acknowledgement of a signature must not falsely claim a paid invoice. The first 24 hours establish confidence, while the first 30 days should demonstrate a credible roadmap and delivery progress. A personal welcome Loom can walk through the email and tools.

Kickoff introduces roles, maps the process, answers questions, realigns expectations and ends with actions. When strategy consumes the meeting, a short separate alignment call can clarify expectations. The coach illustrates conservative expectations with lower lead forecasts and earlier-than-expected delivery. Existing written DRM guarantees and signed deadlines are not silently lowered by this technique.

**Phase 3 — ongoing management:** prioritize results and proactive communication. Explain why a genuine win matters. Raise problems with a proposed solution. Admit a communication gap, explain the specific improvement and invite feedback. Difficult conversations belong on a call when written tone would be ambiguous. Use cancellation/exit feedback to improve the service. For a one-time project, a later check-in can learn how the delivered asset was used and reveal a legitimate follow-on need.

Optional value additions include relevant education, introductions and thoughtful personal touches. These are not purchases, introductions or new deliverables automatically committed for DRM. Ask what success looks like in 30/60/90 days, agree realistic expectations and report against those consistently.

**Phase 4 — pricing:** price increases should accompany demonstrated value and better service. The coach's agency grandfathered current clients; this is his practice, not a new DRM policy. No prices changed.

**Phase 5 — operations:** the recording refers viewers to the separate task-audit/optimization lesson instead of teaching the whole phase. The audit is the starting point when existing operations feel messy. Hiring implementation remains excluded.

<a id="coaching-section-154"></a>
## 14. When Clients Are Getting Results

Source post 2190822638; 22.7 minutes. Full published transcript reviewed.

A case-study interview can reinforce the featured client's progress, teach other clients, and give prospects evidence. Ask after a real win, congratulate specifically, and find a useful story angle or objection the story resolves. The suggested interview is 20–30 minutes. Riverside is a recording example; no new subscription is required merely to prepare the interview.

Questions: who they are and what they sell; how they found the agency; prior situation and struggle; why they acted; what was different about working together; precise outcomes and timeframe; what they did that helped; advice for another client; what they would tell a prospect. Follow up naturally instead of reading a rigid list or feeding them the answer.

Use an approved interview on YouTube, the website, social content, sales follow-ups or a VSL where relevant. Repurpose the actual evidence without changing industry, timeframe, attribution or annual/monthly units. An upsell is appropriate only when there is a relevant next need.

DRM already has six website case studies approved by the user for reuse and a proof deck from the acquisition work. An interview-preparation outline is included in this pack. No clients were contacted, no quote was invented and no interview was marked recorded.

<a id="coaching-section-155"></a>
## 15. Step Into the CEO Role

Source post 2192204022; 64.8 minutes. Full published transcript reviewed. Hiring implementation excluded. The recording combines operational frameworks, reported student/business results and the speaker's personal leadership beliefs.

Set a wildly important goal and be able to explain why it matters personally. Distinguish lag measures (outcomes) from lead measures (actions contributing to them). DRM's existing goal remains $20,000 monthly profit; the personal reason and deadline have not been supplied and are not invented.

Use a CEO dashboard organized around marketing, sales and fulfillment. Review/update weekly, typically Friday; examine the previous month and set next month's objectives. Track roughly three or four meaningful metrics per function:
- Marketing examples: outbound activity, replies/positive replies, content and booked calls. Calls booked is the lecture's primary agency acquisition output.
- Sales examples: call reviews, follow-ups, show/offer/close rates, deals and cash collected. Closed deals and cash are distinct.
- Fulfillment examples: completed updates/calls, case studies, reviews, referrals, upsells and churn. Lesson 4 adds NRR as the broader revenue-retention view.

For more useful meetings, gather wins, critical issues, improvement ideas and top three objectives beforehand so live time addresses the actual bottleneck. Avoid spending the day continually clearing Slack messages. The lecture's leadership portion stresses clear direction, consistent standards, communicating concerns early and making decisions that have been postponed. Its “be → do → have” framing and religious interpretation are the speaker's perspective, not business measurements.

DRM adaptation: one named owner (Brandon), an operational dashboard, a Friday review worksheet and one prioritized improvement. No new hires, employee scorecards, compensation plans, staff monitoring or team meeting invitations were created.

<a id="coaching-section-156"></a>
## 6. Onboarding Process For New Clients

Source post 2189330978; 51 minutes. The central point is to reduce uncertainty immediately after a sale through a repeatable, visible process. Andre's Trello is an example; he explicitly accepts Notion/ClickUp or another tool that provides the same functionality and insists on adapting to the actual agency.

### Sequence demonstrated

1. Obtain the signed agreement and create the client project from a reusable template.
2. Store the executed PDF; record contract-sign date, first campaign launch date and invoice due dates. Those dates let the agency measure actual onboarding speed.
3. Create/verify the billing customer, issue the agreed initial invoice and confirm payment. A signed contract does not prove payment. Avoid starting unpaid fulfillment just because the team is excited.
4. Set up the client board, shared recording/resource folder and client communication channel. Invite only the participants for that client.
5. Add the client to internal scoreboards/invoice tracking and assign an actual delivery owner.
6. Send a tailored onboarding email the same day if possible. It explains what was set up and gives four client actions: complete intake, schedule kickoff after intake, join Slack, and join the project board.
7. Make the portal easy to understand through short client-facing tutorials. Internal SOPs alone are insufficient: clients also need instructions.
8. Collect intake answers, prepare the specific service, obtain necessary client approvals, conduct kickoff, complete readiness checks and launch.

### Board structure and information

General resources: signed agreement/dates, communication link, shared folder and account-access information. Educational resources: timeline, how to use the board, how to use Slack, how to provide feedback. Campaign resources: intake answers, target/list details if relevant, approved scripts/assets, continuing client-supplied resources and performance feedback. To-do and completed tasks visibly show progress. Clearly distinguish agency tasks from client tasks through labels or lists.

The coach stores account credentials in example cards. DRM adaptation retains its existing access-notes approach and records invitations/access status; secret passwords are not needed in a client-visible checklist.

His cold-email example includes warming inboxes, building lists, approving scripts, configuring Calendly/Zapier and launching sequences. Those tasks belong only to a matching service. They should not be assigned automatically to a dental ad client, an ecommerce client or a SaaS-only customer.

### Client involvement and feedback

Give meaningful homework that helps delivery. Ask for a feedback loop after results: for an appointment service, whether the prospect attended, quality score and explanation. Use that feedback to improve qualification, targeting or copy. Explain why the input matters. Leave a place to add new case studies, exclusions and changed information after the initial form.

The example agency's seven-day launch claim is its own capability, not a new DRM promise. Set the actual client's launch date after prerequisites are known. A polished first impression comes from fast, accurate communication and visible progress rather than purchasing a particular software stack.

Template inspected: https://trello.com/b/SIFIKgGU/client-x-knowledgex . This is a shared course board with many members. Do not edit it or put DRM client information there.

<a id="coaching-section-157"></a>
## 7. Slack Channels For Client Fulfillment

Source post 2189330979; 16.2 minutes. Andre recommends one agency client workspace, an announcements channel for general updates, and a private conversation channel per client. Keep client-specific discussions isolated. More channels create friction; add an extra result-notification channel only when a real integration needs it.

Announcements are intended for agency-wide notices; he recommends admin-only posting. A client channel should clearly explain its purpose and include only the client team and relevant agency participants. Introduce the channel during onboarding, explain where questions go, and keep all project context easy to find. Slack may support files, audio/video clips, huddles and integrations; feature/plan details in the recording may be dated.

Action: configure the existing DRM workspace instead of creating another account. The existing general/random/demand-flow channels are not being deleted just because the example removes defaults. A channel template/description can be prepared before a client is identified. Client invitations require the actual intended participants.

<a id="coaching-section-158"></a>
## 8. Create Your New Client Onboarding Form

Source post 2189330984; 41.2 minutes. Start from the fulfillment process and ask which steps require information from the client. The intake is the best early chance to get detailed answers that the whole team can reference later. Do not shorten it so much that delivery requires repeated follow-up for basic facts.

Three parts taught: contact/account information; business/offer/targeting details; baseline and goals. Use clear wording and explanatory examples so the client understands why each answer matters. Customize branding. Google Forms, Typeform or an existing website form are all acceptable; enable response visibility/notification and preserve responses in the client project.

Question categories:
- Contact, billing/business details, location/timezone, website and relevant profiles.
- Required account access and whether required tools already exist. The old example collects passwords; DRM's existing forms explicitly request access notes rather than passwords.
- Who the client helps; result offered; timeframe; mechanism; ideal customer/service area; qualification criteria and exclusions.
- For B2B outbound specifically: titles, company size/revenue, industries, hiring/technology signals, keywords, existing target lists and suppression lists.
- Exact services/products, typical pains, prospect questions, differentiation, guarantees and evidence. Capture case studies as baseline → result → timeframe with a concrete explanation of work performed.
- Baseline performance, desired performance and the single outcome that would make the relationship a success.

Study the answers before kickoff, resolve ambiguities live, and keep them current. The coach recommends testing the form yourself and with another person; his reference form takes at least roughly ten minutes. That is guidance to encourage thoughtful answers, not a reason to add irrelevant fields. DRM industry branches should ask only questions needed for that offer. A client goal is not automatically a contractual promise; clarify alignment at kickoff.

<a id="coaching-section-159"></a>
## 9. Structure New Client Onboarding Calls

Source post 2189331029; 26.5 minutes. Schedule after payment, intake and access preparation. Prepare by reading the submitted information and identifying gaps. Typical meeting is 30 minutes, sometimes 30–45. Record and store the call when appropriate.

Agenda taught:
1. Introduce each participant's delivery role, even if the client already met Brandon during sales.
2. Hear the client's present situation and desired success; reconcile expectations with the actual service/agreement.
3. Screen-share the project board and show where information lives. Review the work prepared so far and obtain relevant targeting/copy/asset approvals.
4. Resolve missing information or access issues while the client is present.
5. State remaining actions, their owners, dependencies and launch sequence. Explain where results and feedback will appear after launch.
6. Set communication/review expectations and answer questions. The example uses an initial 60-day review plus calls when needed; tailor to the actual offer rather than copying a cadence blindly.

End with both parties able to state their next actions. Practice the agenda with a mock call or Loom. A written agenda/script can be prepared here; Brandon's actual speaking rehearsal and client attendance cannot be marked complete by writing a template.

<a id="coaching-section-160"></a>
## 13. 72-Hour Task Audit

Source post 2195465883; 10 minutes. Track everything for three consecutive days with start/end times, including personal activities if the user chooses to apply the full exercise. The coach recommends Clockify or a simple log. Slow down enough to record accurately; the temporary inconvenience is the point of using a bounded audit.

Classify each task by whether it gives or drains energy. For draining tasks, mark repeatable and/or teachable; these labels can overlap. Repeatable work may be automated (his example: signed client → onboarding email/workspace tasks). Teachable work may be delegated. Rank by dollar/hour value and start with lower-value burdens. He cautions against handing off sensitive billing/financial control indiscriminately. Hiring/delegation implementation is deferred per user request; automation analysis remains in scope.

DRM application: prepare a 72-hour log and classify only after Brandon supplies actual time/energy observations. The known 10–20 available hours weekly is capacity, not an audit result. Potential recurring work to inspect includes intake completeness, access reminders, project creation and weekly reporting. No fictional timestamps or claimed savings.

PDF linked in lesson: https://learn.clientascension.com/courses/downloads/2163358542/how_to_optimize_operations_3_-pdf

<a id="coaching-section-161"></a>
## 16. CEO Dashboard

Source post 2192265324; 20 minutes. A monthly sheet is reviewed weekly, with one owner and one clear data source per metric. General measures: income, profitability, bank balance. Choose a few business-specific north-star metrics and three to five useful measures for marketing, sales and customer success; start smaller if needed.

The coach's examples include leads/calls, show and close rates, upfront cash collected, content/outbound activities, client retention, testimonials/referrals, and fulfillment response time. SaaS examples add MRR, new users, conversion, failed payments and expansion revenue. Avoid copying CA's target volumes or tracking numbers nobody uses.

Update the data before the weekly review. Investigate red/off-track items first, then yellow risks; assign an action to the bottleneck instead of merely coloring a sheet. Also study green metrics to learn what works. Duplicate for the next month and adjust metrics as the business changes. Cash collected is separate from deal count. Ratios need real numerators/denominators; unavailable data is not zero.

DRM application: retain $20,000 monthly profit as a goal, track service outcomes separately by industry, and use existing GHL/Instantly/payment records as sources. One paying client is user-reported, not a fresh CRM count. No actual current financial balances have been supplied.

Template: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1B-hWGoN7XhL7rFEdg4aoWkrW5RtGYePibXHVk8Uzn4A/edit?usp=sharing

<a id="coaching-section-163"></a>
# Dead River Management — reusable onboarding and operations pack

Prepared September 27, 2026 for Brandon, brandon@deadrivermanagement.com. No client is being onboarded. This applies the coaching frameworks to DRM; industry-specific examples below are implementation drafts, not claims that the coach prescribed DRM's offers. Current signed scope governs deliverables, pricing, timelines and guarantees. Growth Partner is obsolete. Hiring and Whop are excluded.

<a id="coaching-section-164"></a>
## What is set up

| Item | Verified state |
|---|---|
| Private Trello board | 31 cards with saved instructions across six lists; reusable normal board, not a paid native template |
| client-announcements Slack channel | Created with description; no clients invited; restricted posting and automatic membership not enabled |
| drm-ai Slack channel | Private internal improvement channel created with description |
| Operations workbook | CEO Dashboard, 72-Hour Audit, Client Health; formulas checked, actual business figures remain blank |
| Core lessons | All 16 reviewed through published or automatic transcripts; hiring implementation excluded |
| Client communications | Reusable drafts below; nothing sent |
| Automations | Three specifications below; not activated |
| Live onboarding forms | Inspected existing implementation; no website changes made |

Board: https://trello.com/b/A2TClpoG/dead-river-management-client-onboarding-template

Slack announcements: https://deadrivermanagement.slack.com/archives/C0C4CL4UFRD

Internal improvement channel: https://deadrivermanagement.slack.com/archives/C0C4XMMRDGC

<a id="coaching-section-165"></a>
## Completed worksheet answers and honest unknowns

- Business: Dead River Management; marketing and SaaS with separate industry offers.
- Responsible person: Brandon. Goal: $20,000 monthly profit. Available time: 10–20 hours per week.
- Stage: one paying client previously reported; no active onboarding requested now.
- Delivery tools: existing Slack, Trello, GoHighLevel and Loom. Use existing accounts rather than adding tools for their own sake.
- Journey: signed scope and payment → intake and access → kickoff → implementation and approval → launch → optimization → results review.
- First-24-hours plan: acknowledge purchase; give one ordered next-step list; transfer known sales context; identify contact and kickoff path. Execute only for a future actual purchase.
- Client communication method: private client Slack plus Trello task ownership; email if that client's preferred method. Loom explains complex updates. Do not force duplicate reporting.
- Weekly update structure: wins/KPIs; completed and in-progress work; next steps with owner/date; blockers and decisions.
- Existing delivery capacity, actual churn, current profit, task duration and whether sales pauses during delivery: not established. Do not invent worksheet answers.
- Seven-day exercises: reusable onboarding flow prepared; weekly update prepared but not sent; actual 72-hour observations still to be recorded by Brandon.
- Thirty-day exercises: client-health tracker prepared; three automation designs prepared but not running. Hiring exercises skipped as requested.

<a id="coaching-section-166"></a>
## Onboarding SOP

**Trigger:** a real client has agreed the current offer and the required initial payment is confirmed. **Owner:** Brandon until another owner is expressly assigned. **Finish:** launch readiness is verified and the client knows how progress will be reported. Sources: lessons 3, 4, 6–10.

1. Confirm exact industry/plan, signed deliverables, exclusions, payment state, commercial terms, client dependencies and key dates. Save links to the actual agreement and invoice. Do not substitute course-example terms.
2. Copy the private Trello board for that client. Replace template references with the client name, owner and agreed dates. Verify board privacy before inviting anyone. Keep Completed empty until evidence exists.
3. Create the client folder and private communication space using the contacts the client authorizes. Store invitations/access status, not passwords, in the board. Do not automatically invite every workspace member.
4. Send the personalized welcome with a concise sequence: intake → required access/assets → kickoff. Bring forward information already obtained in sales. Assign a clear next action.
5. Review submitted information before kickoff. Resolve contradictions in goals, geography, capacity, qualification and baseline. Ask only for missing information rather than repeating every form question.
6. Hold kickoff using the agenda below. Record agreed success definitions, responsibilities, approvals, communication rhythm, first five milestones and next dates.
7. Complete the relevant delivery setup and quality checks. Test tracking and handoff end-to-end. Record test evidence; verify targeting, messaging, assets and client approvals.
8. Launch only after the agreed prerequisites are satisfied. Communicate what launched, what is being measured, what to expect next and the first review point.
9. Send concise weekly reporting with source-linked results and a corrective plan for underperformance. Ask for downstream outcomes that DRM cannot observe directly.
10. Maintain client health and the improvement backlog. Review results, scope fit and the next bottleneck. Request a case interview when a substantiated win exists.

### Completion evidence

Every Trello task should end with a link, recorded decision or completed check: signed scope, confirmed payment, submitted intake, accepted access invitation, kickoff recap, approved asset, tracking test or published campaign. A task title or draft is not evidence that onboarding occurred.

<a id="coaching-section-167"></a>
## Five activation milestones by delivery path

These are DRM adaptations of lesson 4's five-milestone concept. Select the row matching what the client actually bought. Commercial outcomes remain measured separately from operational progress.

| Path | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Home services | Service area, job types and capacity confirmed | Lead routing and booking tested | Targeting and assets approved | Campaign live with verified tracking | First quality review completed with booking/attendance feedback |
| Dental | Accepted treatments, location and patient capacity confirmed | Inquiry-to-appointment process tested | Treatment messaging and assets approved | Campaign and routing live | Lead quality, booked/attended appointments and patient outcomes reviewed |
| Med spas | Treatment economics, capacity and offer confirmed | Booking and revenue attribution tested | Creative and treatment claims approved | Campaign launched | Appointment quality and attributable revenue reviewed |
| Ecommerce | Products, margins, inventory and baseline confirmed | Purchase tracking and reporting reconciled | Campaign/creative plan approved | Campaign live | Spend, net economics and test decisions reviewed |
| Real estate | Geography, property/client criteria and availability confirmed | Lead routing and appointment process tested | Messaging and targeting approved | Campaign launched | Qualified and attended appointments reviewed against agreed definition |
| SaaS / Demand Intelligence | Actual purchased plan and use case confirmed | Account/access ready | Required data or integrations connected | First intended workflow completed | User demonstrates repeat use and resolves initial friction |

Do not turn these into universal guarantees or blend industry offers together. A launched campaign is progress, not proof of a revenue result.

<a id="coaching-section-168"></a>
## Intake form question library

Prepared for a future form revision. Existing site forms contain legacy plan definitions, so this library has not been blindly connected to those routes.

**Shared questions:** business/legal trading name; website; main contact and authorized decision maker; purchased offer/plan; locations/service geography; desired outcome in the client's own words; current baseline and its date/source; prior attempts and what happened; sales/fulfillment capacity; required launch timing and constraints; approved assets; current CRM/booking/reporting tools; who grants access; who approves creative; client responsibilities; preferred communication and availability.

**Home services:** accepted/excluded jobs; service radius; minimum job value if relevant; crew capacity; call-answering/booking process; definition of a qualified appointment; booked/attended/sold outcome reporting.

**Dental:** treatments to prioritize; new-patient capacity; booking and follow-up owner; locations/hours; approved treatment claims and assets; how booked appointments and new patients are counted. Operational setup does not require patient-level health records.

**Med spas:** treatments, pricing and capacity; approved offer; booking/deposit workflow; existing lead follow-up; definition/source of attributable revenue; approved creative and claims.

**Ecommerce:** store/platform; priority SKUs; inventory limits; product economics, shipping, refunds and contribution-margin definitions; ad accounts; purchase tracking; baseline revenue/profit and attribution convention.

**Real estate:** market and client type; accepted/excluded inquiries; availability and response process; qualification/attendance definitions; downstream outcome owner.

**SaaS:** actual plan; intended workflow; primary user; required connection/data; first useful output; activation success; training/support needs.

Before publishing a form, prefill known sales information, remove irrelevant branches, check mobile usability, test required fields and verify the saved submission reaches the correct existing workflow.

<a id="coaching-section-169"></a>
## Reusable communications

Fields in braces are intentionally unfilled because there is no client onboarding now. These are drafts for future use, not sent communications.

### Welcome

Subject: Welcome to Dead River Management — your next steps

Hi {first name}, welcome aboard. We're working toward {agreed outcome} through {purchased offer}. I'm Brandon, your point of contact.

Please complete {intake link}, provide the access/assets listed at {board link}, and choose your kickoff at {booking link}. We've already carried forward {known sales context}, so you don't need to repeat it. Your next action is {action} by {agreed date}. I'll review everything before kickoff and flag any missing items. We'll use {private channel/email} for questions and {board} for task status.

### Weekly update

Period: {dates}. Outcome we're working toward: {agreed outcome}.

Results: {metric, actual, comparison, source}. Wins: {substantiated progress}. Completed: {work and links}. In progress: {work, owner, next checkpoint}. Blocker/decision: {specific request, owner, date}. Next week: {priority and expected checkpoint}.

If results are below plan: {observed issue}; we're testing {change} because {evidence}; we'll review {metric} on {date}. Please share {lead quality/attendance/sales feedback needed} so the next decision uses the full picture.

### Scope or timeline change

To deliver {agreed outcome}, we need {dependency}. The current scope covers {included item}. Your new request adds {difference}. Here are the effect on timing and the available options: {options}. Please confirm the chosen path before we change the plan.

### Kickoff recap

We agreed: {success definition and baseline}; {first five milestones}; DRM owns {actions}; your team owns {actions}; approvals come from {person}; reporting occurs {cadence/channel}. Next action: {owner/action/date}. Open decision: {decision and due date}. Reference: {recording/notes/board}.

<a id="coaching-section-170"></a>
## Kickoff agenda and welcome Loom outline

Sources: lessons 6, 9 and 10. Prepare from sales context and intake before the meeting.

1. Confirm why the client bought and what success means; resolve mismatched expectations.
2. Confirm scope, baseline, responsibilities, access and constraints.
3. Walk through the first five milestones and what is required to launch.
4. Explain where work, questions and approvals live; agree realistic response/reporting expectations.
5. Demonstrate any client-critical process, especially lead response and outcome reporting.
6. Resolve questions, recap decisions, and finish with an owner and date for the next action.

Welcome Loom outline: personal greeting → restate agreed outcome → show the actual client board and first tasks → demonstrate intake/access steps → explain kickoff and communication → state the next action. Brandon's personal recording is not fabricated or marked complete.

<a id="coaching-section-171"></a>
## AI-assisted preparation and quality review

Sources: lessons 11 and 13. Supply only material appropriate for the chosen tool and task. These prompts are reusable drafts; no private client content was uploaded by this setup.

**Kickoff preparation prompt:** “Using only the supplied sales notes, purchased scope and intake, create a kickoff brief with confirmed facts, baseline/source, desired outcome, responsibilities, missing information, contradictions, five proposed activation milestones and prioritized questions. Label every inference. Do not invent results, access, prices, guarantees or dates. Reuse answers already provided. Finish with a human verification checklist.”

**Call review prompt:** “Review this call against the agreed scope and kickoff checklist. Identify expectations confirmed, unresolved decisions, client responsibilities, commitments with owner/date, and moments where we failed to answer clearly. Cite the supporting passage or timestamp. Separate explicit statements from interpretation. Draft a concise recap for human review.”

**Task audit prompt:** “Group these actual task observations by repeated workflow. Calculate time from supplied entries. Identify unnecessary work first, then simplification and automation candidates. For each candidate show trigger, inputs, steps, exceptions, quality check and expected time saved as an estimate. Do not invent observations. Exclude hiring recommendations.”

**Internal improvement entry:** task → current effort/evidence → what slowed work → proposed change → quality check → measured result. Use the private drm-ai channel for internal process discussion when appropriate; none has been posted automatically.

<a id="coaching-section-172"></a>
## 72-hour audit and weekly operating rhythm

Log actual start/end dates and times, task, client/internal category, energy, value, repeatability and teachability in the workbook. Include interruptions and context switches. Do not reconstruct invented precision from memory. After three days, total the repeated work, remove avoidable tasks and choose one clear improvement. Hiring is excluded.

For Brandon's 10–20-hour week, choose realistic blocks within actual availability: brief priority planning at the start of the week; grouped client communication; protected delivery/acquisition work; Friday KPI and client-health review. The coach's personal daily meeting schedule is not imposed. No calendar events were created without available times.

Friday review: update a small set of useful measures; verify sources and cohort definitions; find the weakest result; choose the controllable action most likely to improve it; assign owner/checkpoint; study what is working too. Profit is revenue less direct costs and operating expenses, not cash receipts or account balance. NRR excludes new customers; keep contraction and expansion in the same opening cohort. Capacity of 240 emails/day is user-reported infrastructure capacity, not a required target or achieved sending count.

<a id="coaching-section-173"></a>
## Client health, recovery and results capture

Sources: lessons 10, 12 and 14. Use evidence instead of assuming a silent client is happy. Review progress toward the actual outcome, participation/approvals, feedback, blockers and commercial risk. Green = progressing with shared expectations; yellow = emerging blocker or missed checkpoint with a plan; red = material unresolved delivery/relationship problem. These labels are a DRM implementation convention, not an automatic judgment based on missing data.

For risk: clarify the gap, establish its cause using evidence, agree the recovery action and owner, set a review date, and communicate proactively. If a client leaves, record the actual reason and process improvement rather than treating every cancellation as the same cause.

For a real win, conduct a short case interview: situation before; why they sought help; what had failed; experience implementing; specific change/results with timeframe; what they would tell someone in the same situation. Verify numbers, source and permission before reuse. The user's existing website case studies are approved for reuse; do not invent new results or testimonials.

<a id="coaching-section-174"></a>
## Three automation specifications — prepared, not live

These apply the lesson 3 exercise. Activate only after the actual existing integration and record mapping are tested. There is no current onboarding event to execute.

1. **Onboarding preparation:** trigger = verified signed scope plus required payment for an actual client. Match existing contact/client ID. Create a private board copy and internal checklist; attach verified scope/intake links. Stop duplicate creation with a stored event/client ID. Missing offer or contradictory data routes to Brandon for review. Do not automatically invite/send. Test: duplicate trigger, missing scope, failed board creation and correct industry path.
2. **Intake readiness:** trigger = valid intake saved in the existing system. Match to the correct client; check only required fields/access for that purchased offer; update internal readiness and draft missing-information request. Human checks before client communication. Test: incomplete submission, wrong identity, repeat submission, revoked access and saved notes failure.
3. **Weekly reporting preparation:** trigger = scheduled internal review once actual clients and data sources are mapped. Pull date-bounded metrics; record source and freshness; draft weekly update and flag missing inputs. Human reviews interpretation and sends via the chosen client channel. Test: empty/late data, zero denominators, attribution mismatch and duplicate report period.

Acceptance for any live automation: documented owner; correct trigger; correct client/industry; private destination; no duplicates; failure visible to Brandon; appropriate human review; successful test and rollback/disable method. Draft specifications are not counted as three running automations.

<a id="coaching-section-175"></a>
## Contract and form alignment checklist

Lesson 5's two contracts are examples. For a future deal verify: correct parties; purchased industry/plan; scope/exclusions; payment and dates; client dependencies; approved result definitions; current cancellation/renewal provisions; actual agreed guarantees; signature and record storage. Preserve approved current terms. Do not copy retainer/performance example terms or obsolete Growth Partner/Whole River terms into a new agreement by default.

<a id="coaching-section-176"></a>
## Future execution, not missing setup data

Actual time audit, personal welcome recording, real client-specific access, signed terms, kickoff, reporting figures and live client automation tests require real events/observations. They remain intentionally unexecuted because the user said no one is being onboarded. The reusable system can be reviewed now and copied when needed.

# **Client Fulfillment, Operations, & Systems**

[*Capturing The Value of Your Sales Velocity*](https://gamma.app/docs/Client-Fulfillment-Operations-Systems-4dmxhj488x68woh)

**By Andre Haykal Jr**

---

<a id="coaching-section-179"></a>
## **🚀 PART 1: SALES VELOCITY & WHY OPERATIONS MATTER**

✅ **Keep Selling—Always**

* Sales velocity \= consistently signing clients without pausing.  
* Don’t stop sales to “catch up” on delivery—it breaks momentum.

✅ **Avoid the “Agency Flywheel of Death”**  
 ☐ Do you pause sales when you feel overwhelmed?  
 ☐ Do you rely on you alone to deliver client results?

👉 *If yes, you need systems NOW.*

---

<a id="coaching-section-180"></a>
## **🧭 PART 2: CLIENT ONBOARDING – THE FIRST 24 HOURS**

✅ **What To Do Immediately After Payment**  
 ☐ Send intro email from Sales to Fulfillment  
 ☐ Share onboarding form \+ key info from sales call  
 ☐ Set up Slack/email channel  
 ☐ Schedule kickoff call  
 ☐ Grant access to any resources or training

✅ **3 Pillars of Onboarding**  
 ☐ Remove Friction → Use step-by-step guides  
 ☐ Deliver Quick Wins → Focus on first visible result  
 ☐ Reward Good Behavior → Celebrate when clients take action

---

<a id="coaching-section-181"></a>
## **🔁 PART 3: WEEKLY CLIENT ENGAGEMENT**

✅ **Use the Weekly Update Formula**  
 ☐ Wins & KPIs  
 ☐ Work status (Done vs. In Progress)  
 ☐ Next Steps / Timeline

✅ **Pick a Delivery Method**  
 ☐ Slack  
 ☐ Email  
 ☐ Loom video  
 ☐ Live call

✅ **Avoid Client Ghosting by YOU**  
 ☐ Over-communicate  
 ☐ Celebrate small wins  
 ☐ Address problems before they complain

---

<a id="coaching-section-182"></a>
## **⚙️ PART 4: BUILDING FULFILLMENT SYSTEMS**

✅ **Do a 72-Hour Task Audit**  
 ☐ Track what you do and how long it takes  
 ☐ Tag: "Gives Energy / Drains Energy"  
 ☐ Tag: "High / Low Value"

✅ **Systemize and Automate**  
 ☐ SOPs \= Step-by-step for repeatable tasks  
 ☐ Training \= Teach judgment for unique scenarios  
 ☐ Use tools: Zapier, ChatGPT, Trello, ConvertKit

✅ **Maintain Quality Without Micromanaging**  
 ☐ Set review checkpoints  
 ☐ Create feedback loops  
 ☐ Call reviews for client-facing teams

---

<a id="coaching-section-183"></a>
## **🛡 PART 5: MANAGING CLIENTS & PROTECTING YOUR ENERGY**

✅ **Design Your Daily Flow**  
 ☐ 9am–1pm for meetings  
 ☐ 1pm–3pm for deep work  
 ☐ Friday: Review & Adjust Weekly Plan

✅ **Set Boundaries With Clients**  
 ☐ Define response time expectations  
 ☐ Say “no” to unrealistic or out-of-scope requests  
 ☐ Use: “To deliver quality, here’s what we need…”

---

<a id="coaching-section-184"></a>
## **👥 PART 6: BUILDING YOUR TEAM**

✅ **Signs It’s Time to Hire**  
 ☐ Quality slipping  
 ☐ Turning down sales  
 ☐ You’re stuck doing low-value work

✅ **What to Hire First**  
 ☐ Client-facing role (CSM or VA)  
 ☐ Admin support (PMs, reports, scheduling)  
 ☐ Delivery specialists (writers, designers, ops)

✅ **Use the 5-Step Hiring System**

1. **Define** the role: scorecard with KPIs  
2. **Source** from referrals \+ online  
3. **Screen** using the ACE Framework  
4. **Test** using sample tasks or mock scenario  
5. **Onboard** with structure, daily check-ins, quick wins

---

<a id="coaching-section-185"></a>
## **🧰 BONUS: YOUR IMPLEMENTATION STARTER PLAN**

### **In The Next 7 Days**

☐ Build your onboarding flow  
 ☐ Send your first weekly client update  
 ☐ Complete your task audit

### **In The Next 30 Days**

☐ Automate 3 processes  
 ☐ Write your first role scorecard  
 ☐ Create a basic client health tracker

### **In The Next 90 Days**

☐ Hire your first support role  
 ☐ Launch performance-based pay  
 ☐ Implement team meeting cadence

---

✅ **Final Reflection**  
 ☐ What’s the next role you’ll hire for?  
 ☐ What’s one task you can delegate or automate this week?

<a id="coaching-section-186"></a>
# **THIS IS AN EXAMPLE CONTRACT**

<a id="coaching-section-187"></a>
# **Performance-Guaranteed Marketing Agreement**

This Agreement (“Agreement”) is entered into as of \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ by and between:

Client: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Agency: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

<a id="coaching-section-188"></a>
## **1\. Scope of Work**

Agency agrees to deliver:  
\- Funnel Build – Custom-built lead generation and/or sales funnel  
\- Email Flows – Automated email sequences for nurturing and conversion  
\- Ads Management – Ongoing management of paid advertising campaigns (Facebook, Instagram, Google, etc.)

<a id="coaching-section-189"></a>
## **2\. Performance Guarantee**

Agency guarantees that the Client will sign at least 3 clients of their own per month, provided that the Client strictly adheres to the Eligibility Requirements outlined in Section 3\.

If the Client does not sign at least 3 clients in a given month and requests a refund, the terms in Section 4 apply.

<a id="coaching-section-190"></a>
## **3\. Eligibility Requirements**

To qualify for the performance guarantee, the Client must:  
1\. Spend at least \$10,000 per month on ad spend (paid by Client, not Agency).  
2\. Maintain a minimum 15% sales call closing rate on all calls booked by the Agency.  
3\. Maintain an active ad account in good standing throughout the Agreement.  
4\. Maintain at least 8 hours of availability each business day for sales calls scheduled by the Agency.

Failure to meet any of these requirements voids the performance guarantee.

<a id="coaching-section-191"></a>
## **4\. Refund Policy**

If the Client requests a refund due to failure to sign 3 clients in a month, the following conditions apply:

\- Client must provide:  
  1\. Proof of ad spend of at least \$10,000 for that month.  
  2\. Sales call recordings of all calls booked by the Agency.  
  3\. Proof that the ad account is active and in good standing.  
  4\. Login access to their sales call scheduling tool.

\- If the Client cannot provide all four items, the refund request is denied.  
\- Refunds are limited to the last 30 days of work only.  
\- Performance fees paid are non-refundable under any circumstances.

<a id="coaching-section-192"></a>
## **5\. Payment Terms**

\- Base Fee: \$5,000 per month.  
\- Performance Fee: 10% of Gross Revenue generated from Agency’s activities.  
  \- Gross Revenue is defined as cash collected from Agency’s efforts minus ad spend.  
\- Due Date: Performance fees are due within 7 days of the first of each month.

Failure to pay within:  
\- 7 days: Agency reserves the right to pause all advertising activity.  
\- 14 days: Agency reserves the right to delete the funnel created for the Client.

<a id="coaching-section-193"></a>
## **6\. Client Responsibilities**

The Client agrees to:  
\- Provide all requested assets, account logins, and approvals promptly.  
\- Maintain accurate reporting of revenue generated from Agency-driven leads.  
\- Maintain open lines of communication and provide feedback as needed for optimization.

<a id="coaching-section-194"></a>
## **7\. Intellectual Property**

\- Funnels, ad creatives, and email sequences remain the property of the Agency until all fees (base and performance) are paid in full.  
\- Upon full payment, ownership of deliverables transfers to the Client.  
\- Agency retains the right to showcase results as portfolio or marketing material unless otherwise agreed in writing.

<a id="coaching-section-195"></a>
## **8\. Confidentiality**

Both parties agree to maintain strict confidentiality of all proprietary and sensitive information unless required by law.

<a id="coaching-section-196"></a>
## **9\. Limitation of Liability**

Agency’s liability under this Agreement shall not exceed the total amount paid by the Client in the last 30 days. Agency is not liable for indirect, incidental, or consequential damages.

<a id="coaching-section-197"></a>
## **10\. Governing Law**

This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of Florida, without regard to its conflict of law principles.

<a id="coaching-section-198"></a>
## **11\. Entire Agreement**

This document represents the full agreement between the Client and Agency and supersedes all prior discussions, agreements, or understandings.

Signed and Agreed:

Client: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_  Date: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Agency: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_  Date: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

<a id="coaching-section-199"></a>
# **THIS IS AN EXAMPLE CONTRACT**

<a id="coaching-section-200"></a>
# **Marketing Funnel Build Agreement**

This Agreement (“Agreement”) is entered into as of \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ by and between:

Client: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Agency: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

<a id="coaching-section-201"></a>
## **1\. Scope of Work**

Agency agrees to deliver the following:  
\- Marketing Funnel – Complete build of a lead generation and/or sales funnel.  
\- Email Flows – Automated email sequences for nurturing leads and driving conversions.  
\- Ad Creative & Campaign Setup – Copywriting, creative design, and ad account setup for agreed platforms (e.g., Facebook, Instagram, Google).

All deliverables are detailed in Appendix A – Project Specifications. Any work beyond this scope requires a signed change order and may incur additional fees.

<a id="coaching-section-202"></a>
## **2\. Timeline**

Project will begin upon:  
\- Receipt of initial payment (see Section 4\)  
\- Client submission of all required information and assets

Estimated completion: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ weeks from the project start date.

Delays due to the Client’s failure to provide necessary information or approvals will extend the timeline accordingly.

<a id="coaching-section-203"></a>
## **3\. Client Responsibilities**

Client agrees to:  
\- Provide all requested brand assets, copy, logins, and necessary information within \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ of request  
\- Review and approve deliverables in a timely manner (within 3 business days unless otherwise agreed)  
\- Ensure ad accounts and email platforms are in good standing

<a id="coaching-section-204"></a>
## **4\. Payment Terms**

\- Ongoing Fee: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ per month.

<a id="coaching-section-205"></a>
## There are no refunds for any reason.

<a id="coaching-section-206"></a>
## **5\. Revisions**

\- Includes \[2\] rounds of revisions for each major deliverable (funnel, email flows, ads)  
\- Additional revisions billed at \$200 per hour

<a id="coaching-section-207"></a>
## **6\. Intellectual Property**

\- Upon final payment each month, all deliverables become the property of Client.  
\- Agency retains the right to showcase completed work and results generated in its portfolio and marketing materials.

<a id="coaching-section-208"></a>
## **7\. Performance Disclaimer**

Agency will deliver the assets as outlined but does not guarantee specific results such as lead volume, cost per lead, sales, or revenue unless explicitly stated in a separate written agreement.

<a id="coaching-section-209"></a>
## **8\. Confidentiality**

Both parties agree to keep all business, financial, and technical information confidential, except where disclosure is required by law.

<a id="coaching-section-210"></a>
## **9\. Termination**

Either party may terminate this Agreement with 7 days written notice.  
\- If terminated by Client, all work completed to date will be billed at the agreed rate, and all unpaid invoices are immediately due.  
\- No refunds for work already completed.

<a id="coaching-section-211"></a>
## **10\. Limitation of Liability**

Agency’s total liability under this Agreement is limited to the amount paid by the Client. Agency is not liable for indirect, incidental, or consequential damages.

<a id="coaching-section-212"></a>
## **11\. Governing Law**

This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of Florida, without regard to its conflict of law principles.

<a id="coaching-section-213"></a>
## **12\. Entire Agreement**

This Agreement, including all appendices, constitutes the entire agreement between the parties and supersedes all prior agreements or understandings.

Signed and Agreed:

Client: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_  Date: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Agency: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_  Date: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

<a id="coaching-section-214"></a>

\- Email software: \[Klaviyo / ActiveCampaign / etc.\]  
\- Key pages: Opt-in, Thank You, Application, Calendar, etc.  
\- Deadline for asset delivery: \[Date\]

# AI Development & Workflows — Dead River Management

Reviewed September 27, 2026. **All 41 lesson transcripts reviewed**: 9 Claude, 11 n8n starter, 13 advanced n8n, 6 Poppy and 2 bonus workshops. Review used 38 published caption transcripts and 3 local automatic transcripts. This does not claim every visual frame was inspected. No downloads are needed from you for the lesson review.

<a id="coaching-section-219"></a>
## Start here

- [Detailed lesson-by-lesson notes](lesson-notes.md) — coaching explanations, examples, exercises and limitations.
- [What's built and what still needs connecting](implementation-status.md).
- [Claude workspace](claude-workspace/CLAUDE.md) — business context, approved proof, Brandon's voice and six reusable skills.
- [Three-working-day time audit](claude-workspace/goals/three-day-time-audit.md).
- [n8n First Win setup](n8n/first-win-setup.md) and [inactive error workflow](n8n/drm-error-alerts.json).

- [Completed historical reporting exercise](claude-workspace/projects/historical-report-exercise/report.md).

<a id="coaching-section-220"></a>
## Cliff notes from the coaching

1. Understand the work and what a good output looks like before automating it. Record three working days to identify actual time drains.
2. Keep company context, project context and reusable reference material in organized files so each task has the right inputs.
3. Make one useful deliverable, inspect it, then turn its repeatable steps into a skill. Do not attempt the whole business in one prompt.
4. Use agents for research, writing and production; use n8n for structured triggers, transformations, connections and error handling. Validate data mappings and test failures.
5. Poppy's important mechanism is connected context: training, company, voice and output rules. Dream 100 work also needs actual prospect context and a real useful asset.
6. Reuse existing tools and review client-facing outputs before delivery. The workshop's human-review step is part of the coaching itself.

<a id="coaching-section-221"></a>
## Using the Claude workspace

Open the `claude-workspace` folder with your installed Claude Code. Project skills live in `.claude/skills` and can be invoked as `/drm-dream100-research`, `/drm-dream100-deliverable`, `/drm-dream100-package`, `/drm-sales-call-brief`, `/drm-weekly-report` and `/drm-content-brief`. Provide the actual task inputs. Skills have been structurally checked, but are not a claim that every downstream service is connected. [Official Claude skill documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills).

<a id="coaching-section-225"></a>
## What the coaching suggests doing first for DRM

The coach asks for an actual time audit and a single useful repeatable output before broad automation. Apply that by measuring work for three working days, then choosing one recurring bottleneck. The existing Dream 100 research → asset → Gamma/Loom package process is a candidate because its tools and proof already exist; it is not asserted to be your biggest bottleneck without the audit.

Reuse GHL, Slack and Trello. Keep industry offers separate. Give the agent company, task, voice and output context. Inspect the result. Convert successful steps to skills. When a process needs explicit triggers, mappings and error handling, use n8n. These are applications of the lessons, not a recommendation to purchase every product demonstrated.

## Reviewed: 1 — Intro + Claude Code Setup (2195707265)

22:53; full published captions reviewed. Lucas begins with a prerequisite: understand how the agency delivers the service and what a good output looks like before trying to automate it. An agent does not remove the need to judge the work. His examples include first understanding/writing a VSL and the fulfillment process manually.

The original setup is private GitHub repository → local project folder → OpenCode → Claude subscription connection. Apply the VS Code correction above to the interface. The private repository stores versions and project work; public repositories are not the default for client files. The lesson uses separate sessions for separate tasks and a shared filesystem for the resulting artifacts.

Exercises: build a fictional Fresh Fitness ads dashboard with explicitly mock data; build a landing page from supplied intake and sales context; inspect the HTML in a browser; then back up project files. The landing-page process researches the existing brand, uses its relevant imagery, writes copy from supplied context and produces a responsive page. The coach suggests scaling only after the single example works, using a CSV of prospect names, websites and context.

Useful planning prompt structure: state the desired outcome, proposed steps, expected deliverable and ask which tools/access are needed or whether a better process exists. The video demonstrates this rather than requiring technical terminology from the business owner. Model/pricing comparisons in the recording are historical examples; no new subscription was purchased. Claims that an agent can do essentially anything are the coach's broad characterization, not verified capability guarantees.

<a id="coaching-section-229"></a>
## Reviewed: 2 — Claude Code Workspace Setup (2195708738)

6:58; full published captions reviewed. The starter workspace organizes work into inbox, projects, areas, resources, archives and goals. Inbox is temporary unsorted material. Projects contain client folders, client.md context and specific deliverables. Areas hold ongoing responsibilities such as operations and recurring work. Resources hold reusable reference/training/templates/tools. Archives hold completed/inactive work. Goals holds strategy and weekly/daily plans.

CLAUDE.md describes how to operate within this structure. The coach distinguishes guidance from hooks that enforce specific behavior. The initialization checks supporting tools, prepares an environment file, excludes secrets from Git, and connects a private repository. Client-wide facts belong in client.md, so the next project does not depend on remembering a chat. A session should load only relevant context. Do not confuse the course's fake Acme/Globex examples with actual DRM clients.

Steps: research brand/products, select source assets, build image prompts, submit requests, wait for completion, save outputs and report file paths. Optional gallery creation is removed from repeat runs. Store configuration separately so the API key does not need repeating. Validate the skill on another brand and inspect the actual images. A successful API request alone is not visual quality review.

## Reviewed: 5 — MCPs, CLI tools & email design (2195742751)

20:51; full published captions reviewed. MCP is an interface for the agent to operate another service/app. Lucas favors selected integrations rather than loading many unrelated tool descriptions. He describes context-window consumption and compaction, then uses Paper's desktop MCP for editable design. Context limits and prices shown are those of the recording.

Email design example: research brand → define design system → generate eight hero images using fal → construct eight editable welcome-flow artboards in Paper → inspect screenshots → fix layout/copy issues. The lesson then retrieves a YouTube transcript using an MCP, converts the operation into a local CLI in resources/tools, tests it, disables the redundant MCP for that demonstration, and verifies a second transcript retrieval through the CLI.
