- Record name and available business email/social URLs. ListKit and Apollo are demonstrated/discussed with his preferences. Missing a particular social account does not prevent outreach if another relevant contact exists. He recommends doing initial qualification personally to learn the market.
- Communities: contribute, attend relevant calls, ask concise genuine questions, form peer relationships and share useful knowledge. Do not turn the group into a pitch fest. Trust may convert months later.
- Trello setup: lead in, first message, successive follow-ups, meeting booked, pipeline/undecided, won and lost. Card contains contact links, context, due dates and meeting notes. Reassign the next due date after each touch. Free-card dates work even if a calendar view requires a paid tier.
- Message examples give a completed script or content asset first, offer the remaining production work and explain the next practical step. Include a short written summary with Loom because not everyone watches. He now generally dislikes voice-note openers unless the recipient prefers them or can read a transcript.
- Follow up at the time the prospect requested: three weeks, one month or next quarter in examples. One busy contact was deliberately given space and later returned. Do not confuse persistence with ignoring a stated timeline.
- Demonstrates winning a paid engagement by producing usable scripts, editing, thumbnails and SEO quickly, then discussing terms after the free sample. The $9k three-month example and personal growth claims are his historical cases, not DRM pricing.
- Work that requires no new prospect recording can reduce friction, such as repurposing existing videos or making thumbnails. If recording is necessary, provide clear instructions and follow up on that dependency. Set a sustainable production target and keep all activity/outcomes organized.

### Hiring Scorecards (2193817939)
- Hiring implementation remains deferred. This section records the teaching only.
- Define who is needed and what success means before recruiting. Scorecard structure: mission, outcomes/KPIs including daily/admin execution, competencies, position description and actual compensation. Examples are adaptable starting points, not fixed templates.
- CSM mission: retention and lifetime value. Responsibilities include clear onboarding expectations, timely accurate answers, check-ins, team updates and Friday recaps. Competencies include empathy, communication, emotional intelligence, problem-solving, initiative and personalization.
- Include check-ins, end-of-day reporting and relevant team meetings so the hire participates in the operating system. Describe schedule, location, time-off process and pay rather than leaving expectations implicit.
- Operations manager example covers onboarding, strategy, campaign/team/client coordination, deadlines, SOP creation and workflow improvement. Appointment setter example ties revenue goals back to price, closing/show rates and required calls, plus follow-up and community/inbox work.
- Copywriter example combines cold-email writing with performance analysis and improvement. Community manager focuses on engagement/student success, check-ins and digest communications. Student-success coach adds proactive guidance, depth/speed of support and renewals.
- Qualitative roles still require clear observable responsibilities; sales roles have more explicit numerical outcomes. Define five-to-ten relevant competencies with what they look like in practice. Start with one needed role and submit the completed scorecard for coaching feedback. No DRM hiring or compensation decisions were made.

### Systemize Your Hiring Process (2191192596)
- Treat recruiting as a pipeline like sales. Demonstrated Trello columns: new applications, screening scheduled, assessment assigned, culture-fit interview, final interview, hired and disqualified. Resources column holds application, assessment and booking links.
- A Google Form/Zap creates applicant cards with contact details and response links. Review before scheduling. A candidate may be disqualified at any stage; retain context so the process is repeatable.
- Application explains role, expected earnings and appeal, then asks contact/location/time zone, source, company knowledge, motivation, relevant experience, career goals, availability and start date. Include a small role-relevant task. Andre calls Loom optional but says he usually filters out submissions without it; preserve that distinction rather than representing it as an explicit form requirement.
- Screen first, assign realistic scenarios, assess reasoning rather than expecting untrained candidates to know every internal process, obtain a second team member's perspective in a roughly fifteen-minute culture conversation, then final decision-maker review.
- Feed the funnel through relevant community posts, social channels, email and referrals. Hiring posts sell the actual opportunity and may use real company proof. No application or recruitment campaign was created for DRM.

### Designer / Project-Based Hiring (2191966676)
- Example funnel: specific social hiring post, short Loom explaining role and expectations, written practical brief, submitted work, evaluation and offer. The demonstrated project tests the same work the person would actually deliver.
- Sample task: design a lead-magnet opt-in experience with entry page, usable opt-in and thank-you path toward booking. Provide brand inspiration without requiring copying, deliverables, estimated effort, deadline, submission method and evaluation criteria.
- Requested deliverables include a live shareable Framer prototype, Figma/static designs and an explanation of layout, flow and conversion reasoning. Example allowed two-to-four hours of work with a two-day deadline.
- Applicants with inaccessible links or only Figma when Framer was required were rejected. Winner supplied working links, clear communication, relevant prior examples and a process recording. Instruction-following and accessibility mattered alongside visual quality.
- Instructor proposes per-deliverable compensation for design work while defining his example 'full-time' as responsive availability. This is his commercial model, not a legal worker-classification determination or an approved DRM employment arrangement.
- A large personal audience helped attract candidates quickly. Alternatives mentioned: community referrals, content coach network and the course-associated recruiter. No paid recruitment, test project or hiring was commissioned.

### A-Player Hiring Funnel Example (2192203856)
- Ali Abdaal example: concise social post and short pitch video lead to a detailed Notion role page, then an application with a role-specific video assessment, then selective interviews.
- Sell the genuine mission, impact, role, requirements, remote/full-time status, compensation, team and benefits. Repeat essential details at each step so applicants understand before investing time.
- Sample assessment asks for a five-minute introduction/motivation and ideas for taking over TikTok. Evaluate effort, reasoning and creativity, not perfect knowledge of internal systems. Screen applications before interviewing everyone.
- Andre's claims about dramatically improved candidate quality and likely rapid hiring are his expectations, not measured guarantees. Some distribution channels described for Ali are explicitly the instructor's guesses, not observed actions.

### Service Provider Agreements / Contractor Examples (2195106196)
- Documentation review only. Andre shows Knowledge X inbox-manager and project-manager agreements, followed by onboarding email, form and workspace integration, mirroring client onboarding.
- Agreement sections: parties/date, detailed services, availability/expected effort, compensation/payment cadence, termination, nondisclosure/nonsolicitation, relationship of parties, liability, confidentiality/return of materials and severability. Customize the actual role rather than copying unrelated responsibilities.
- Examples: inbox manager paid $50 per booked appointment, project manager $40 per assigned client per month; monthly payment and fourteen-day termination notice. These are historical source terms, not DRM pay decisions or market benchmarks.
- Define responsibility and communication clearly, account for outages and require timely notice of problems. Store signed agreements and manage return/deletion of confidential work/access at the end of the relationship.
- Source expressly says these are not legal advice and asks students to have agreements reviewed by a lawyer. His use of labels such as 'service provider' or 'generally available' and his 'loophole' characterization do not establish legal classification or enforceability. The notes preserve the business process without adopting those legal conclusions.
- One-off projects can test working fit before a continuing arrangement. Electronic-signature tools mentioned include DocuSign, PandaDoc, HelloSign and others. No contract was drafted, signed or altered during this review.

### Onboarding a CSM in About 23 Days (2190814733)
- Instructor's staged framework, dependent on service complexity and hire experience. Master client onboarding before handling clients; train in the sequence work occurs: onboarding, ongoing meetings, then renewals/expansion.
- Prepare business/offer documentation, client journey, SOPs, recordings, case studies, tool tutorials and assessments. Include mundane setup such as calendars, recording, Slack, email and who pays for tools. Explain mission, market, packages, contract length, expected milestones and first-win expectations.
- Days 1-7: structured foundational learning with daily manager contact, explicit daily goals and knowledge checks. Watching videos is not proof of comprehension. Self-rated confidence below seven merits attention; verify with actual assessment. Later checklist suggests a 90% knowledge score.
- Days 8-15: study three-to-five onboarding recordings more than once, explain why questions are asked, conduct live pause-and-explain reviews, and practice progressively harder mock calls. Start friendly, then skeptical/complex, then a clearly announced demanding-client scenario. Shadow as many useful live calls as feasible.
- Practice confirming understanding, taking notes, setting expectations and ending with next actions. Source explicitly says not to promise unsupported outcomes, skip discovery, argue about the client's situation or omit follow-up.
- Days 16-23: supervised real calls with manager guidance, debriefs and increasing independence after demonstrated competence. Continue regular one-to-ones, assess communication, technical skill, business understanding, client management and strategic thinking. Do not promote independence solely because the date arrived.
- Instructor estimates forty-to-fifty hours of intensive training/practice across the period, especially for a first CSM. Record good training sessions to improve the next hire's resources. Correct missing SOPs promptly.
- Continued development: basic independent delivery first, more complex problem-solving and expansion work around months three-to-six, strategic-advisor maturity around month seven in his experience. These are expectations, not guaranteed learning times.
- Keep communication concentrated in an agreed channel where possible. Measure quality, documentation and client feedback; sample satisfaction target is above eight out of ten. Pair constructive feedback with genuine recognition. The slide's total-ten-sessions claim is explicitly corrected verbally as too low. Hiring remains deferred.

### Managing CSMs (2190805530)
- Instructor advocates proactive operating rhythms rather than investigating only after a complaint. Claimed retention/turnover improvements in the introduction are not sourced in the spoken lesson and should not be used as verified statistics.
- Weekly example: Monday one-hour focused execution session, Tuesday individual development meetings (roughly thirty minutes, longer for new hires), Wednesday sixty-to-ninety-minute team training, Friday leadership/team alignment. Founder participation on Friday communicates company direction and recurring client issues.
- Power hour selects a concrete task such as health updates, reactivation or review collection, works on it together and closes with outcomes/notes. Training can review recorded calls, methods, tools, new offers and problems shared across accounts.
- Review sampled calls for clear communication, diagnosis, relationship quality, process adherence, notes and next steps. Give specific feedback linked to the recording. Instructor suggests calls per week of 15-25 high-touch, 10-15 mid-touch and 5-10 low-touch, with length/service-dependent capacity.
- End-of-day form, sent before work ends: accomplishments, urgent clients, proof/referrals collected, challenges, process suggestions and tomorrow's priorities. Manager reviews urgent flags daily and patterns weekly.
- Audit Monday/Wednesday/Friday client check-ins for substance, replies and response time. Ask about the client's actual agreed work, not generic greetings. Also reconcile failed/missing payments and renewal status rather than continuing unpaid work unknowingly.
- Biweekly client-health sheet before the one-to-one: client/owner, package/value, remaining term, stage, last call, engagement, results/implementation progress, 1-10 health, challenges, opportunities and next actions. Four or lower is his red-risk example; orange needs improvement; green requires evidence of progress, not optimistic labeling.
- One-to-one order: portfolio overview, red/orange root causes and interventions, then green-client expansion/referrals/proof and replicable practices. Alternate health reviews with call-quality reviews and check whether prior actions helped.
- His generalized targets include 75% client retention, 80% net revenue retention, average health eight, NPS +70, 95% calls completed, 90% documentation quality, replies under two hours, three check-ins weekly, two case studies monthly and referrals from roughly a quarter of clients. Periods/denominators are not consistently specified; preserve as sample targets, not a ready-made DRM scorecard.
- Example progression: junior under one year, senior around twelve-to-twenty-four months, lead beyond two years, based on competence as well as tenure. Example team sizes of one CSM for 25-50 clients and larger teams thereafter depend on service intensity.
- Tools are flexible: recorded calls, forms, calendar and a CRM/Sheet/task system. He estimates eight-to-ten weekly management hours and claims 25-40% performance improvement; that uplift is a source claim, not verified evidence. No meetings, automations or hiring were activated.

### Getting Rich Through Other People / Team Workshop (2190824701)
- Transcript quality: the published caption text repeats one sentence through a substantial middle section. A separate local audio transcription recovered the missing discussion, including the delegation choices, T1/T2/T3 model and worked objective examples. Keep both source versions and treat automatic wording/names cautiously.
- Speaker describes his own growth, burnout and rebuilding. Core exercise: define the desired monthly income and date, plus the work you want to stop doing. Then distinguish work that can stop entirely from necessary work that must be delegated. Find people who are good at and motivated by the work the founder should no longer own.
- Three team levels: T1 decision makers, paid to think and set direction; T2 managers, responsible for execution, time, budget and quality; T3 implementers, responsible for the assigned work. Hiring only implementation help does not remove the founder's decision burden.
- Translate objectives into two-to-three key results and each result into roughly three-to-ten assignments. Results have outcomes and constraints; assignments are concrete activities/deadlines. Build sufficient capacity into the results to support the objective rather than stating an aspiration alone.
- Recovered example: target 180,000 customers over three years, with monthly acquisition channels totaling 7,500 and a stated acquisition-cost recovery constraint. Assignments include a book-funnel deadline, eight ads monthly and a challenger funnel. Another example uses sets, completed calls and close rate, supported by daily dialing, coaching and review. These are workshop illustrations, not DRM forecasts; subscriber/customer definitions and unit economics must match before using the arithmetic.
- Fit model: person, personality and position. Team assessment: attitude (culture, communication, teachability), competency (skill, resourcefulness, follow-through), experience (decision-making and experience at the intended next stage). He suggests recruiting relevant experience from businesses about three-to-five times current scale rather than radically larger organizations.
- Culture is described as shared beliefs, reasons and strength of commitment. The speaker advocates high standards and intentionally stretched capacity/lean staffing to promote creativity. Preserve this as his management philosophy, not a measured universal claim or a DRM staffing change.
- Founder role: hire, train, equip and hold accountable, then focus on valuable work the founder enjoys. Equipping includes tools, resources and real decision authority, with room to learn from mistakes. Add managers when leaders can no longer oversee implementation effectively.
- Q&A covers repeated vision communication, caution about promoting beyond demonstrated ability, attracting talent through mission and using profit-share/bonuses for senior roles. His personal priority order is self-care, family, business/team, then other relationships, with concrete recurring commitments.
- Follow-up exercise: identify energizing work, one objective with results/assignments and a team-fit audit. Hiring implementation is still deferred. The linked team playbook is a separate resource, not automatically reviewed by this lecture review.

### Hiring a Customer Success Manager (2190814841)
- Andy distinguishes proactive client success (adoption, outcomes, retention and expansion) from reactive support and from hands-on account fulfillment. His stated 73% failure statistic and expected financial returns are not independently evidenced in this lecture.
- Preferred first hire combines relevant CSM experience and industry/product knowledge. If choosing between them, he favors CSM experience plus learning the business over training both competencies from scratch. Sales, negotiation, technical literacy and demonstrated retention/expansion results are valuable.
- Interview structure, up to about sixty minutes: business/market preparation, realistic scenarios, deep examples of prior work, then fit and questions. Seek specific research and evidence rather than generic 'people skills' statements.
- Scenarios include ignored implementation advice, disputed expectations, refund requests, accidental billing mistakes, a client asking for another CSM and learning an unfamiliar service. Look for diagnosis, empathy, clear boundaries, transparent correction, documented next steps and a careful handover rather than defensiveness or unsupported promises.
- Ask about client-health analysis, meaningful results, priorities and learning style. Candidate questions about journey, goals, tools, team, first ninety days and support indicate curiosity. Evaluate substance rather than charm alone.
- Compensation examples: performance model roughly $60-$150 per client plus 8-10% of generated backend revenue and example bonuses; salary roughly $3k-$5k with expansion incentives; hybrid roughly $1k-$2k base plus smaller per-client pay and backend share. He favors meaningful backend incentives and says not below 5% in his model. These are source examples, not approved DRM pay rates.
- Tradeoffs: variable pay aligns with client portfolio but fluctuates with acquisition and can discourage non-client tasks; salary offers stability but requires accountability and sufficient recurring revenue; hybrid balances both. Accurately track earned compensation and define responsibilities.
- Match intensity to service: low-touch up to about one hundred clients, mid-touch roughly fifty-to-seventy, high-touch roughly twenty-to-thirty-five with more strategic calls. These are workload examples, not universal staffing limits.
- Score competencies in technical/process ability, relationships, strategy and fit. Suggested rating bands: 90-100 excellent, 75-89 strong, 60-74 needs substantial training, below 60 reject. Predicted ramp times are the instructor's estimates and do not replace demonstrated readiness.
- Recruit with a clear role scorecard, source through relevant networks/boards/referrals, screen, interview, check references, run a practical scenario or Loom, obtain another team member's assessment and make a final decision. Prepare supervised onboarding and ongoing feedback. Hiring remains deferred for DRM.

## Hiring Masterclass | 2190823311
Source: https://learn.clientascension.com/products/ai-assisted-agency/categories/2158060095/posts/2190823311
Full transcript reviewed, including workshop Q&A. Hiring implementation remains deferred for DRM.

- Andre organizes hiring like acquisition: role offer, candidate traffic, onboarding, retention, expansion. Use an energy audit and fulfillment capacity/quality constraints to decide the role; do not hire simply because a revenue milestone was reached.
- Build a role scorecard with mission, responsibilities, measurable outcomes, time commitment, compensation and future growth. Sell a credible company vision and meaningful role. Specific titles can attract better candidates, but preserve recognizable search terms. His cold-email systems engineer is an onboarding role, not a software engineer.
- Example compensation: $1,500 base plus up to $2,000 in bonuses tied to churn, net revenue retention, launch time and call volume. These are his company examples, not DRM pay or targets. Review progress weekly so employees can course-correct before month end. Sales example increases commission from 7% to 10% through required follow-up, CRM, attendance and reporting behaviors.
- Source through referrals, existing customers/team/peers, personal and company social audiences, relevant communities, recruiters, job boards and targeted outreach. His geographic preferences and sourcing results are personal examples. A detailed external application filters better than counting one-click applicants. Ten qualified candidates can be more useful than thousands of unqualified applications.
- Five-stage screening: application to eliminate mismatches; 15-30 minute conversational culture interview; realistic homework/mock work; scorecard interview confirming responsibilities, KPIs, time and pay; optional colleague/team interview when choosing between strong finalists. More senior hires can require more team input. Ask why this company and why this role. Inspect preparation, questions, effort and submission timing, not interview charm alone.
- The lesson usually reveals compensation at the scorecard stage, but says disclose a range sooner when expectations clearly conflict. This differs from other lessons that publish compensation early. Do not silently combine these into one universal rule.
- Andre describes intentionally delaying candidate replies to test follow-up and an anecdote about rejecting a candidate to test their response. Retained as his screening tactic, not an action taken for DRM.
- Onboarding: signed agreement, personal welcome and next steps, kickoff covering ambitions, company email, software permissions, SOPs, external training, regular check-ins and experienced teammates. Supply examples of excellent actual work: successful calls, ads, scripts or completed campaigns.
- Readiness progression: shadow work/recordings; perform with an experienced person present; perform independently with recording/work review; then remove unnecessary oversight while remaining available. For campaigns, inspect client labels, source-list counts, assigned inboxes, copy formatting and settings against a launch checklist. Sample ongoing work so standards stay consistent.
- Management: outcome-linked compensation, end-of-day reporting, weekly KPI meetings and work review. Four EOD prompts: what I did; what I am working on; what I need help with; how I rate my day and why. Route the form into Slack. Review personal context as well as output.
- Team meetings start with wins, then progress against the exact metrics used in compensation. Aim for 30 minutes; split departments or increase frequency if agendas routinely overflow. Peer call reviews can provide training and recognition without the owner reviewing every recording.
- Underperformance: identify specific missed expectations, create a written 30-day improvement plan, meet weekly and genuinely help. Also check whether the role or targets are wrong. Workshop example moves an overwhelmed support employee into operations coordination, where she succeeds. Ask the team whether bonus thresholds are achievable; unrealistic targets undermine incentives.
- Retain strong people through career goals, recognition, one-on-one time, upside and promotion. Look for initiative, independent problem solving, exceeding outcomes and constructive disagreement. Trial a player-coach role before full management; create an internal wins channel. Do not spend all leadership time rescuing underperformers while ignoring strong performers.
- Leadership framework is his quoted combination of being respected, feared and liked. His political illustration is a speaker opinion, not evidence or DRM policy. Operational examples: model standards, keep commitments, communicate, train yourself, help in the work when necessary and address issues early.
- Q&A: hire when capacity prevents growth or rushed work reduces quality; retain a candidate pipeline; reconsider fit before dismissal; communicate changes and reasonable standards to the relevant team. His usual 14-day transition and payment practices are company examples, not universal employment requirements. Budget may rise before revenue when capacity is built. Scope changes and substantial additional responsibilities should trigger an explicit role/pay conversation.

<a id="coaching-section-366"></a>
## Three things that make ads run on easy mode, Evan | 2199140506
Full  workshop transcript and Q&A reviewed. Source lesson ID 2199140506 in Ads, Funnels & Copywriting. Automatic transcript has errors; named tools and numerical anecdotes should be checked against visuals before implementation.

1. Expand the addressable market where the same core problem and delivery process apply. An agency is not permanently limited to the industry in its first case study. Different front-end offers can serve different readiness levels, such as improving existing ads versus building an initial funnel. Expansion should not break fulfillment. This supports a possibility, not a directive to change DRM's chosen offer.
2. Sell an outcome the market wants, with the deliverable as the means. Thirty creatives is a commodity unless the buyer understands the result. Research repeated language in actual sales calls, using Manus to analyze recordings; if unavailable, interview salespeople and survey customers/community. Write the complete offer first, then condense the headline and use the subheading for supporting detail.
3. Test creative formats as well as angles. The same winning message may reach different people as a selfie, whiteboard, screen share, skit, podcast, AI animation, static or carousel. Do not produce poor ads merely to claim diversity or volume.

### Eight-part offer checklist
- Easy to understand immediately (cognitive fluency).
- Solves a significant existing problem.
- Easy for the customer to implement, with minimal required work.
- Clear delivery/result timeframe.
- Clear desired outcome rather than only tools or process.
- Clear explanation of how the outcome is produced.
- Believable outcome backed by context, explanation and proof.
- Shifts some risk to the seller through terms or structure.

Risk reduction need not mean a guarantee or free trial: examples include half upfront/half delivery, fixed-duration sprints, one-time setup, low-risk front-end work and pay-per-result. The workshop critiques huge unsupported outcomes and vague named blueprints. Merely naming a mechanism does not explain it.

### Examples and exercises
- Cold email example: 30-50 calls/month during a 90-day sprint, campaigns live in 10 days, reaching decision makers across the addressable market.
- Other examples include AI content charged per thousand real views, local-search offers, qualified inbound insurance calls, roofing estimate coaching, free ecommerce emails and hiring/automation roadmaps. These are speaker/client examples, not promises or deliverables added to DRM. Evan explicitly does not know the view-validation mechanics of the pay-per-view example.
- Failed positioning example centers on repeat purchases and scaling at break-even without a clear desirable outcome or timeframe. Improved examples use actual buyer language, such as label-ready music tracks and paid gigs.
- Exercise: turn one winning ad into ten intentionally chosen formats; write ten new ads and choose formats that best explain each angle. The linked 47-format SOP contains examples and production instructions; discovery is not full review of every nested example.
- Curate a separate research feed around the buyer's interests; save relevant ads and organic posts, recording verbal hooks, visual hooks and format. Preserve disappearing story examples with screenshots/recordings. A platform feed trick described in the recording is time-specific, not verified current functionality.

### Low-budget call funnels and Q&A
- Evan's model describes Meta moving between audience pockets based on ads, page, targeting, history, objective and returned conversions. This is his explanatory model, not direct access to Meta's internal algorithm.
- Under roughly $500/day, few daily booked calls can make results volatile. His approach combines a larger relevant market, stronger offer/creative/page and fewer application restrictions while retaining basic industry fit. He relaxes revenue gates before niche fit, then tightens at higher spend. A low reported revenue can mask a funded new business.
- He explicitly describes reporting some unqualified in-ICP applicants as the optimized conversion, including Schedule even when routed to a confirmation/triage page without a booking, to increase event volume. This tactic is preserved accurately as taught; it has NOT been installed in DRM's tracking. It would make that event different from a literal count of booked meetings, which must be kept distinct in reporting.
- To protect calendar space he uses triage or a shorter deprioritized calendar. Alternative lead-form, low-ticket and webinar funnels bring different tradeoffs, not an automatic fix.
- Judge costs from offer economics, close rate and fulfillment costs, not a universal cost-per-call target. On very small budgets, allow enough spend/time to observe results; his example is 5-7 days when daily spend is below expected call cost. CBO may get a new campaign/new ads; ABO a new ad set, depending on whether the existing campaign still works.
- More mediocre creatives do not solve weak message/format. Use readable offer/pain overlays, good light and intentional movement for talking-head ads. For weak VSL engagement he tests a YouTube-style hook and visual teaching aids; his quoted play/retention rates are one example, not universal targets.

## Cold email and agency operations, Nick Abraham | 2199140508
Full keynote and Q&A reviewed. Automatic transcript preserved. Speaker's results, platform availability and costs are recording-time examples, not promises or verified current product specifications.

### Acquisition and offer
- Nick contrasts a generic list plus booking CTA with a useful service lead magnet: a real deliverable relevant to the buyer and the eventual service. Examples: 1,000 ICP-fit leads, a trial outbound campaign, five LinkedIn posts with relevant proof, or mapping an agency's operations on a call. A PDF is not what he means by service lead magnet.
- Choose a usable, affordable lead platform with bulk exports rather than overspending on data or obsessing over brands. Industry filters are imperfect; qualify sites against the actual ICP, then enrich one useful field such as specialty/sub-niche that makes the message meaningfully specific.
- Verify exported emails even if the source says valid. Separate SMTP-valid and independently validated catch-all segments. He cites MillionVerifier and catch-all validation vendors. Untouched catch-all/public-email segments are his opportunity hypothesis, not a guarantee of deliverability.
- He describes prioritizing historical positive responders, including a pooled multi-client reply database, and suppressing hostile/opt-out contacts. The claimed nine-percent reply result is one campaign. No client data pooling, recontact or outreach was implemented for DRM.
- Maintain a weekly campaign-building rhythm. Layer lower-volume signals over broad relevant volume: hiring ads for roles your service can replace, relevant content engagement, company followers, and competitor sales reps' new connections. Followers/connections are clues, not proof of a purchase or sales conversation. Qualify and deduplicate before outreach; he says not to name-drop the monitored competitor/person in the message.
- Signal examples: smaller firms hiring Salesforce/HubSpot admins offered outsourced help; niche-influencer audiences; SMB public email addresses. He describes vendors/avatars for company-follower extraction and stacking Sales Navigator licenses/borrowed or purchased profiles for InMail volume. These are preserved as his methods, not adopted account practices. He notes providers can stop working and recommends vendor redundancy.

### Delivery and response handling
- His infrastructure preference is managed Google/Microsoft inbox setup, warmed reserve capacity, and replacement rather than prolonged repair when a domain fails. Do not treat his low historical domain prices or Google/Microsoft comparison as current verified facts.
- When reply rate is below his usual roughly one-percent floor, compare inbox placement of actual campaign copy against neutral copy. Neutral copy failing suggests infrastructure; only campaign copy failing suggests wording/content. He cites EmailGuard and another placement tool; ASR spelling is uncertain. Domain assessment example uses 4,000-8,000 emails/month, not a required sending target.
- Smartlead for API automation or Instantly for UI ease, according to his experience. Tool claims do not compensate for a bad list or offer.
- Positive reply goes automatically into CRM. Enrich phone if available and create a call task; otherwise create a manual email-reply task. Prioritize qualification before booking: budget, authority, need and implementation timing.
- His example benchmarks: 50% positive-reply-to-booked, 70-80% show, approximately 19-20% close. These are targets from his experience, not DRM forecasts. B2B outbound often needs more than one sales call.
- First seven days: three calls and three emails in his process, then a lower-priority weekly nurture sequence for about a year. He builds nurture topics from real objections and voice notes with Claude. This cadence is recorded, not enabled for DRM.
- After-hours experiment: AI inbox/voice agents after human SDRs log out, citing Close Chloe and Master Inbox/Calendly. His disclosure-law comments are his own speculation and were not validated as legal guidance.
- Stabilize one acquisition channel before adding another. InMail and cold calling are his next channels. Parallel dialer example Salesfinity; qualify rather than rewarding raw booked volume. Calls are harder to scale because staff burn out. Learn the process yourself before delegating and review recordings.
- His presales follow-up includes multiple emails/texts and SDR/AE touches, with acknowledged complaints/drop-off from overcontact. This is not silently imported into DRM.
- Log outbound touches in CRM to see delayed attribution. Cursor-built server workflows sit on existing CRM APIs; he explicitly says not to rebuild the entire CRM. His claim AI never forgets is speaker rhetoric, not a reliability guarantee.

### Operations and delivery
- Operations always need improvement. Consolidate handoffs where an empowered account manager plus good tooling can own the work. His 75-100-account example is for a productized service with lead delivery, not managing every prospect reply or a universal staffing ratio.
- Use AI to draft client email, with human edits and sending. Batch communication blocks; the fulfillment lead helps when someone is overloaded. Front is his shared inbox; two-hour response is his reported operating standard.
- Automate one process per week rather than attempting a full rebuild in one weekend. Approved campaigns can be assembled through API, then inspected and launched by the responsible person.
- Project management is the operational memory: map each trigger to an assigned task and attach submission/review context. Examples: onboarding form creates inbox, copy and kickoff tasks; campaign 75% exhausted creates replacement-campaign task; underperformance creates investigation task. For DRM, payment remains the user-selected start trigger, not automatically changed to form completion.
- Relate team, client and campaign tables so an event resolves the correct client and owner. Draft milestone touchpoints when onboarding finishes, first lead arrives or sending reaches a milestone. He automates drafts, NOT their final send. Staff review both incoming messages and prepared drafts.
- Negative client sentiment creates a call task. Address the issue directly rather than long defensive email exchanges; leave a message if unavailable and respect a client's request for written documentation. His preference is client email rather than Slack at his service level; internal Slack remains. This differs from other coaches' client-Slack model.
- Onboarding explicitly asks expected lead volume, overall expectations and what success means, then records answers. Completion requires that discussion. He does not claim proven retention uplift from this alone, but says it clarifies later expectation disputes.
- Client portal centralizes reporting and reduces status requests. Start with low-code while learning the process; custom development follows stable, proven workflows. His Airtable/Lovable example is being rebuilt because of customization limits, not an instruction to replace DRM's tools.
- AM compensation: base plus quarterly revenue-under-management bonus influenced by churn and non-negotiable behaviors. Example: ask for ten upsells and ten testimonials per month; distinguish asks from completed sales/reviews. Reactivation and appropriate existing-client offers can support slow months.
- Scheduled skills/reporting: balances and margin forecast, send volume, reply rate, churn investigation across emails/calls/campaigns. His 150,000 daily sends reflects his large agency and is NOT DRM's volume. A churn analysis should distinguish team execution from fit/client factors rather than assume one cause.
- Preserve structured operational history and relationships for future automation. His three-to-five-year AI forecast is an opinion about the future.

### Q&A detail
- Productized lower-price delivery suited his preference better than founder-heavy large bespoke accounts; it is not a rule that DRM should lower prices.
- Standardize repeatable LinkedIn plays such as first-degree connections and content engagement instead of reinventing each client's process. He cites Aimfox; vendor functionality needs verification before use.
- Scheduled scrapes need a deduplicated database. Inspect the first ten enriched records manually and refine false-positive rules, such as not treating any booking button as proof of telemedicine. His 90-95% enrichment accuracy aspiration is not a guarantee. Faster tools do not automatically make classification more accurate.

<a id="coaching-section-368"></a>
## Turning $3k ecommerce clients into $100k relationships | 2198112636
Full guest workshop and Q&A reviewed. Guest describes his growth-advisory practice and client anecdotes; ASR renders some names inconsistently. $100k primarily refers to lifetime relationship value, not a promise of $100k monthly fees.

- Three moves: uncap the offer, change positioning, expand the relationship. Recurring loop: prove value, earn trust, expand scope, reprice. Retention keeps this loop possible. Getting results alone does not automatically increase fees.
- Three pricing levers: base plus managed-ad-spend percentage (often declining tiers as spend grows); base plus performance upside on a measurable outcome you influence; additional base for genuinely additional scope. The base ordinarily covers delivery costs. Do not finance a struggling business through pure performance. In Q&A he allows a low-base/performance-heavy exception for beginners seeking initial proof; preserve this distinction.
- His hourly-fee story illustrates results rising much faster than hours/income. A luggage-brand example ties upside to companywide year-over-year growth, not only Google attribution. A supplement/telehealth example starts around $3k plus 10% spend and later moves to declining tiers. These are his client arrangements, not DRM's pricing or results. Verify name spelling from slides before citing publicly.
- Illustrative spend percentages decrease from 10% toward 7%, 5%, 3% at larger budgets; no exact universal tier boundaries. Existing high-spend brands may start lower. Choose a metric and structure appropriate to that actual client.
- Positioning progression: vendor executes tasks; consultant diagnoses/recommends; advisor joins strategic decisions. Report the whole business first: revenue, customers, then margin/profit and constraints. A strong channel ROAS alongside declining company revenue is not automatically a good business week.
- Each review cycle bring one numbers-backed recommendation outside the narrow paid scope. Ask the owner's primary growth constraint and listen. Recommendation structure: observed metric/change, opportunity or risk and estimated size, two or three steps, optional offer to help. Do not offer execution when you lack the ability; seek specialist input or refer.
- Advice against your own financial interest can build trust, such as recommending against unnecessary spend or an unsuitable partner even when a referral fee is available.
- Add adjacent scope gradually. Own accountability without personally executing every specialty; use a competent client team, partner, contractor or agency. Guest prefers direct specialist referrals and strategic coordination over white-labeling everything after earlier attempts consumed too much time.
- New scope gets new terms; old scope can retain its original price. A client declining expansion can remain on the existing arrangement. Referral/coordination does not automatically justify a separate execution fee; agreed spend/performance upside may already compensate it, or propose an explicit new advisory scope.
- Best proposal moments: after a significant win or when the client articulates an important unresolved constraint. Give the useful recommendation first, then discuss expansion on a review call. Do not confuse repeatedly giving unpaid full execution with strategic recommendations.
- Workshop worksheet: actual client name; spend/results/scope structure; one recommendation to send; next area you have earned trust to own (or result needed to earn it); next review/proposal date; proposed monthly value. No real client expansion or contract change was performed in this review.
- Q&A: understand whether the client wants in-house help, one accountable partner or several agencies. Introduce specialists for an audit and jointly evaluate fit. A limited trial of a new service can have explicitly agreed success/payment terms and return to old scope if unsuccessful. His suggested $10k minimum for extensive advisory responsibility is his opinion, not a universal price or DRM offer.
- Claimed client growth, approximately $46k average 12-month LTV and industry comparisons are speaker-reported, not independently verified. They must not become DRM case studies.

<a id="coaching-section-369"></a>
## AI-powered Dream 100 machine, Jake | 2198142042
Full guest presentation, demonstration transcript and Q&A reviewed. Automated transcript begins with repetitive filler; substantive presentation follows. This is a build overview, not a supplied finished production system.

- Validate before automating: watch Evan/Dan's Dream 100 modules, manually create a strong deliverable and Gamma package, get coach feedback, preferably see positive prospect responses, then automate. Do not spend weeks scaling an unproven package. Dream 100 work also prototypes eventual fulfillment.
- Three components: repeatable deliverable, personalized presentation page, operator interface. Build each separately before joining them.
- First make one high-quality asset by hand/with AI, then turn it into a controlled template. Change only necessary prospect-specific data while retaining genuinely relevant content and quality. His example is a quiz funnel plus ten static ads; it is not the only required deliverable.
- Stack: Claude Code builds assets/pages/operator app; GitHub stores code; Vercel deploys/hosts; optional Anymail Finder locates email and OpenAI generates ads. External specialist tools may be connected through APIs. Tool choice follows the deliverable, not the other way around.
- Convert the proven Gamma/PDF package into an HTML template once, refine it, then populate prospect data. Keep it professional and personal, with their branding and a relevant note, rather than making a generic enterprise-looking website that feels mass-produced.
- Prefer one hosted project/custom domain with prospect-specific paths instead of a new deployment project/domain for each prospect. This simplifies tracking and makes links more recognizable. Vercel pricing/compute figures are recording-time examples; hosting is not necessarily free or cheaper than Gamma. He is exploring alternatives and suggests retiring old unused projects over time.
- Operator form collects contact, business, site, LinkedIn, logo, positioning/research and relevant service-specific inputs. Generation builds the asset and page, inserts the asset, deploys, and records status. Keep edit/redeploy and links accessible. Record the personal Loom and insert it after generation.
- Pipeline/Kanban tracks prospects, generation/deployment, views and follow-ups. Tracking design: page-view ping to server, server records event in database, board updates and Slack alerts. His analytics were still being refined; do not describe the demonstration as a fully verified analytics product.
- Demonstrated workflow: LinkedIn connection, confirm ICP fit, enter prospect data, generate, record roughly five-minute Loom, email package, then personal LinkedIn video notification. He reports 5-10/day in roughly 1-2 hours and imagines 20 with further focus. His 25 daily connection figure is his operating practice, not a verified universal platform limit.
- Cold calling and fully autonomous prospect research/form entry through an agent are proposed next steps, not completed functionality. The human Loom remains the personalized step in his envisioned flow.
- Example assets: ads/funnels including quiz, VSL or webinar page; finished static/video creative; ecommerce welcome-flow design; LinkedIn banner/profile/posts before-and-after; public-data chatbot or working automation demo. Visual working outputs are stronger than merely describing the proposed work.
- Cold email is harder to demonstrate upfront. His speculative example books a meeting and adds a prospect with a how-it-was-done document; retain as an idea rather than a proven workflow or permission to represent another business. AI automation often needs private process/access context, so use available public data or a limited prototype honestly.
- Q&A: establish consistent image/design output before connecting generation API. GoHighLevel hosting was suggested by an attendee and acknowledged as worth testing, not demonstrated or confirmed. Cloudflare was also an attendee suggestion. His under-ten-hour build estimate assumes a validated deliverable and prior Claude Code familiarity, with ongoing refinement.
- Training dependency: Lucas's Claude Code modules. Main lesson reviewed; every external example/tool page is not thereby reviewed. No DRM outreach, hosting migration or new machine was executed in this notes pass.

## AI content studio demonstration, Ryne | 2199713089
Full guest demonstration transcript and Q&A reviewed. This is an early personal tool and potential offer, not a proven deployed client service. ASR inconsistently spells his name and several model/editor names; retain source uncertainty instead of inventing precise product names.

- Starts from his real bottleneck: consistent content production for an AI automation offer. Describes the desired end-to-end outcome to the coding assistant, asks it to interview him, separates must-have/nice-to-have/later, then builds and iterates. Lucas calls this reverse prompting: goal first, then jointly determine implementation.
- Studio combines his voice, reference creators, format examples and content research. Inputs can be an original idea or reference post; outputs include short clips, YouTube, carousels/how-to/ranking formats. Use references to explain the desired structure and visuals; his claims of matching top creators' expertise are personal assertions, not measured equivalence.
- Pipeline: idea/research, building, ready to record, editing, ready to publish. Generated script/teleprompter has speed/input controls and can be edited or paraphrased. After recording, generated B-roll is aligned to actual speech. Human reviews timing, framing, overlays and music, exports MP4 and posts.
- Editor supports aspect ratios, crop/face positioning, clip trimming, B-roll and text. Defaults differ for short versus long format. Custom projects such as a VSL can enter the same library. His timeline editor was built from scratch; he agrees an existing open-source component could have saved work.
- He manually posts because he wants native platform music and exact cover selection not available through his tested scheduler flow. Drive/Slack can move completed assets to the phone or archive. This is not a verified statement that every scheduler lacks those features.
- Captions are formatted separately for Instagram, YouTube and LinkedIn. ManyChat keyword comments trigger a resource message and voluntary email collection into the newsletter. Analytics track views, engagement, followers and submitted opt-ins. Plausible/YouTube API are cited; exact cross-platform attribution was not independently tested here.
- Backend initially exposed through an ngrok-style URL, with always-on computer/server; AWS migration was ongoing. Do not equate a tunnel address with the full compute/hosting architecture. Editor migration and feature parity remained incomplete.
- Uses Claude/coding tools, Whisper for speech-related work, optional model routing/OpenRouter/Hermes, Higgsfield for his likeness/avatar visuals, Runway for other visuals. First make the system work, then measure and reduce per-task/model costs. Daily spend report proposes cheaper appropriate models. Model names rendered as Fable/Kimi variants are ASR-dependent, not verified product specifications.
- Build took roughly two to three weeks of intensive work and refinement. Hardest parts: natural voice, useful on-brand B-roll, teleprompter and editing. Human feedback is central; a first generated version is not finished.
- Talking-head recording remains real: he tried full avatar narration but did not like the result and preferred a real personal presence. His claim of roughly 90% automatic assembly still includes human review/editing and recording.
- Twin-character format exists as a planned/partially built option, not a completed example. Cold email/Dream 100 integration and multi-tenant onboarding were still being developed. No clients were using the studio at the time of the talk. Possible future offers: done-for-you, supported access/done-with-you, or lower-price software.
- Long-form problem: too many separate takes. Lucas advises keep recording, pause and repeat a bad line, then use transcript-aware editing to remove failed takes/silence. This was proposed improvement, not shown fully integrated into the guest studio. Editor names in ASR should be checked against linked resources before choosing tools.
- Business positioning lesson: a specific visible solution such as a content studio makes an automation offer easier to understand than a broad promise to automate anything. The guest's reported posting/follower counts are an early personal example, not proof of client acquisition results.
- No new studio, account, paid subscription, posting or outreach was executed for DRM during this review.

<a id="coaching-section-371"></a>
## Ultimate Dream 100 Implementation Guide, Evan Seech | 2194588802
Source: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1URDbBlASf95Z2o9Hu23_AtNQq5555CzNJJqw6IO0yBs/edit?tab=t.0
Entire linked guide exported and read. This lesson is a written resource, not a missing video. Original Markdown retained as sources/2194588802-guide.md.

- Intended audience: agencies, freelancers and B2B service providers. The guide's whale-client objective is an aspiration, not a guaranteed result.
- Ten operating rules: non-salesy outreach, valuable personalization, useful follow-ups, consistent 100-day cadence, at least 100 packages before pivoting, remove document fluff, use multiple relevant channels, tie to the buyer's actual desired outcome, personalize follow-ups as well as initial contact, and deliver a quick win near revenue/leads/time saved.
- Step 1: define the core result the customer wants. Booked calls that become retained clients matter more than ad production or CPM alone. Explain the connection between the free sample and that outcome.
- Step 2: list your service deliverables, audit the actual prospect, then choose something valuable they need and can use easily. Different prospects may need different assets. Finished creatives can be easier to use than scripts requiring filming. The guide's posting/DM-management and prebooked-call examples are examples, not authorization to access or represent a prospect.
- Step 3 is optional: an attention-grabbing attraction offer/risk reversal attached to the sample. Its example guarantees and cash payments are not automatically part of DRM's offer.
- Step 4: build an initial 100-person prospect list. Suggested fields are name, email, phone and Instagram/LinkedIn/Twitter. Manually inspect relevant niche micro-influencers' followers/following, often under about 15k followers, rather than assuming a huge general audience fits. Check ICP and potential benefit; enrich missing contact details. Tools are optional.
- Step 5: set new-package and value-follow-up targets for 100 days, including weekends in this guide. Evan describes protecting 4-6 outreach hours/day and an example of 15 new packages plus 35 follow-ups. His 15 landing pages/day used a designer and a library of 15 templates, not fifteen bespoke builds by a solo beginner. These differ from earlier smaller-cadence lessons and exceed DRM's stated 10-20 total weekly hours; no schedule was imposed.
- Step 6 pipeline: prospect list; deliverable in progress; ready to send; initial outreach sent; short-term follow-up; long-term follow-up; call 1 booked/no-show; call 2 booked/no-show; won/lost. Add dated next-action tasks per prospect. After about 14 days without progress, use more spaced follow-up, for example seven days later. Tool may be Trello, Close, Monday or another suitable system.
- Step 7 package: short personalized headline/subheading; Loom walkthrough; actual free asset; concise explanation of benefit, optionally a clear financial model; reason to attend an implementation call; optional relevant case studies. Prospect branding and minimal copy. Gamma, Docs or a landing page all work. The guide's per-prospect domain suggestion differs from Jake's newer single-domain/path approach; retain both with context.
- Step 8 first message: relevant research observation, what you made, why it helps. First objective is opening/consuming the asset, not forcing a booked-call CTA into the message. Default email or the prospect's most active social channel. The document itself can contain the implementation-call reason.
- Step 9 exact example cadence: day 0 initial plus social selfie; days 1 and 2 useful follow-up on original channel; day 3 add another channel with the asset; day 4 follow up and add another platform; day 5 secondary-channel follow-up plus selfie; days 7 and 9 useful follow-up; day 12 useful follow-up across channels plus selfie; day 14 onward long-term. Recorded as teaching, not an activated sequence.
- Step 10 first call: help implement the free work and obtain a useful result. Do not immediately convert the whole call into a pitch; discuss service if the prospect opens that conversation. Book the next meeting before ending and make both parties' next actions clear.
- Worksheet actions preserved for later use: core outcome, deliverable menu, optional attraction offer, 100-person list, sustainable cadence, pipeline, first package, initial message/channel, follow-up tasks and implementation-call plan. Current request was review and notes, so none of these external actions were executed.

Normal coaching pricing is somewhere around $5,000 for the coaching package. Normal close rates are around 20%. The cost per qualified call is normally around $250. The show up rate is normally around 60%. We're also using an opt-in, where before they book a call, they opt-in with their name email and phone. This is what we consider a lead, and we are able to add them to our newsletter and text and call them in order to get them to book a full sales call. If there's anything else you're unsure about before you make the ROI calculator in order to make it correctly, please ask that now

Claude Response:

Great! I'd love to help you create an effective ROI calculator. Before I build it, let me ask a few clarifying questions to ensure it's as accurate and compelling as possible:

Your Service Pricing: What do you charge for your VSL funnel build + ad management service? Is it a one-time setup fee plus monthly retainer, or how is it structured?
Lead to Call Conversion: What's the typical conversion rate from opt-in lead to booked call? (Since you mentioned people opt-in first, then book)
Cost Per Lead: What's the typical cost per lead (opt-in) you achieve, separate from the $250 cost per qualified call?
Ad Spend Range: What's the typical monthly ad spend you recommend or work with? (e.g., $5,000-$10,000/month)
Timeframe: Should the calculator show ROI for month 1, first 3 months, first year, or multiple timeframes?
Recurring Revenue: Do your clients' coaching programs typically have any recurring/continuity component, or is it all one-time $5,000 packages?
Other Value Metrics: Besides direct ROI from sales, should we factor in:
Value of the email list being built
Value of leads that don't immediately convert but may buy later
Any upsells/downsells in the funnel
Input Variables: What should prospects be able to adjust in the calculator? (e.g., their price point, close rate, ad budget, etc.)

What's up, guys? My name is Evan Siech. I run an agency called Sell More Online, where we focus on basically helping people make more money online through advertising. So we focus on paid ads and funnels, and that's our main bread and butter.

But primarily what we focus on is just driving leads, driving book calls, driving purchases, you know, depending on what type of funnel we're doing through paid ads. That's our main thing. And of course you need to be able to actually warm those leads up through different marketing methods before they actually show up to a sales call. So you can actually sell them properly. So from A to Z, what you're going to be doing on, you know, a day to day basis, we're going to get into it much more detail in a little bit here, but essentially you're helping people run ads profitably.

You're going to be making landing pages, making funnels. You're going to be helping with emails on the backend too. Pretty much everything in the paid acquisition system from click to close besides taking sales calls. If you actually want to do this right, you should be focusing on, you should be helping your clients with, it shouldn't just be you sitting down, looking at the ads manager for a couple hours a freaking day, clicking buttons and all that stuff.

No, you're directing the creative. You're directing the angles of the ads. You're directing the copy on the landing page. You're directing what type of funnel, what the funnel looks like.

You're making landing pages. You're building backend email flows and everything like that. And you're seeing where the bottlenecks are in the funnel and in the paid acquisition system. And you're going all hell bent on that to fix that.

So let's talk about what makes a good ad in the first place. So the first thing is, of course, the messaging in the ad. So what should your ad actually talk about? Your ad should be calling out the real-time pain points, desires, situations, and circumstances that your target prospect is experiencing right now.

It has to be hyper-contextual to what they're experiencing right now. It should be something like if you're talking about wanting an iPad, that's where you want essentially you to get served an ad with an iPad. So it's like you want to be in that position. We can run back that.

Your ads need to be hyper-contextual to what the prospect is dealing with right now in real time. So what I mean by that is, for example, if they're struggling with show rates, you want to call that out. You want to articulate that problem better than they can. You want to call out, hey, are you struggling with show rates?

Not stuff where it's like, hey, are you struggling with sales? It's way too broad. You want to get very specific to these pain points in your copy and in your messaging. That's what's going to get ads that hit.

So it's very crucial that in your copy and when you're writing these ads, you need to get very, again, granular with these problems people are experiencing and these dream states that they want to be in, these desires that they have. Nothing is too specific. Not nothing. You don't want to go super broad.

You don't want to be very generic like coaches, agencies, and consultants. I'm going to help you four to five X your lead flow by fixing your sales. That doesn't work anymore. The call outs don't work anymore.

You need to articulate the pain points, the desires, the real situations that your prospects are in right now and the circumstances that they find themselves in in your ads. So the flow of a good ad that I like to follow is you have the hook, of course, hit the body and you have the CTA. Now the hook is articulating that problem. So calling out the problem like, hey, are you struggling to get your show rates above 75% or, hey, are you struggling to get prospects to show up to your sales calls actually warm and ready to buy?

Because every time they show up, shoot, if they do at all, they're super cold guarded and just thrown out objections. You see how more specific that hook is than something like, hey, are you struggling to actually get sales through ads? Terrible, right? So the hook will call out the pain points, the problem, or the desire someone has.

Or it could also call out proof to like one of the ones that we shot over with list kit, or like one of the ones we shot with Christian over at list kit was, we sent, you know, 150,000 cold emails or something crazy like that, generated x appointments, x revenue, x sales calls, all that stuff. It was super proof led. Also, some like case study ads do really well with this logic too, where you basically call out, hey, we got this person, this result, here's how we did it. And then the body supports that and talks more about that, right?

So then the body, what we like to do is essentially give support to the hook. So if you talk about a pain point, you want to talk about, you know, why that occurs, like why that pain point or problem is occurring. The solutions to it, which essentially is guess what, your product or service. And then the outcome slash proof, which is where you can weave in some CTAs and also talk about the outcome they're going to get of, you know, using your product or service as the solution.

And then we go into the CTA, which the CTA, we just want to be very direct and tell people what to do next. And also what's on the next page. So what I like to do for our CTA is not click the learn more button down below and you'll, you know, go to a page and you book a call. I like to say, click the, you know, if this is interesting to you and you want to fix your show rates, click the learn more button down below.

You're going to be taken to a quick page that has a five to 10 minute video on there that explains everything about our offer in detail and how we can help you. And then on that page too, you can click a button, fill out a quick application, schedule a call, and you'll hop on a call with me to see if this is a fit for you, right? I like to be very direct and tell them what's going to be on the next page and just make sure that they're not jarred when they get to there. We want to pre-frame them before they get to there.

Um, I am defaulting lately to having longer ads that have more context and more, a little bit more education in them, but these do work pretty good too. Just a very direct one. So that's essentially what you want to follow. Uh, when you're writing ads is the hook needs to be very articulate and needs to hit on their pain points, their problems, their desires, or show some really hard proof.

All right, let's talk about what actually makes a good winning funnel and really what separates a winning funnel from a losing funnel. So first off, I just want to make it very clear when I talk about what a funnel is, is I talk about everything from click to close. So most people look at funnels like it's just a landing page. You know, you'll talk to a client like, yeah, we have a funnel.

And you know, they just pull up like their main landing page and stuff like that. So I look at a funnel as the entire experience, pre-click and post-click that somebody goes through, right? So from click to close, they see your ad, then what happens next on the funnel, the landing page, all that stuff, what happens in the sales process, what happens after they book in a call, everything from click to close. So that's what I look at in terms of being a funnel.

So and again, by being able to have eyes on that entire thing and input on that entire thing and influence over that entire process from click to close, you become more valuable to your clients. And you can also get them better results because you can find different bottlenecks throughout that entire funnel. And you can actually get them again, good results because you're acting like a marketer. You're not just some low level media buyer who's pressing buttons in the ads manager.

So anyways, what makes a good funnel, right? So from click to close, we have the ad, then we have the landing pages that we drive them to, which essentially, you know, is quote unquote, the funnel that a lot of people refer to. Then we have the backend systems. So like think email flows, think content remarketing, stuff like that.

Then we have the sales process. And then we got where you collect that cash, that cheddar right on the backend. But pretty much from there, what makes an actual good funnel from a bad funnel? So the first is congruency with messaging.

So think about it this way. If I had an ad that said, Hey, I'm going to help you fix your show rates. And then the landing page, I drive you to says, Hey, we're going to help you fix your close rates in your sales process. That's not too congruent, is it?

Right? Let's even think of another example. Say you run an offer that helps people stop smoking and say the ad says something along the lines of, Hey, look, you know, you might just have some family history of, you know, smoking addictions and stuff like that. But you know, right now you're just maybe enjoying one or two cigars a month.

And you're like, I just want to get a grip on this and ensure that this doesn't turn into a big nicotine addiction and a big problem, right? Something very light like that on the ad level. And then say, you know, it drives you over to a landing page that has something like, yeah, you're a chronic smoker, you're a chain smoker, you're going to die. You have really terrible family history and stuff like that, right?

It's too jarring and it's not congruent messaging. So you want to make sure that your ad says one thing, your landing page says the same thing. Then your backend systems, like all your emails says the same thing. Then your sales process and what the actual, you know, setters and closers reach out with in terms of messaging and different trust assets and sales assets says the same thing.

It's fully congruent. And then ideally on the sales call to the initial discovery is about that same thing too. And then from there, of course you can branch off into other aspects if it deems fit, but congruency is huge. I re I see some people's funnels where the ads say one thing and then the landing page says another thing and they try to like fit too many characteristics in the copy on the landing page.

And the VSL is like this whole big thing, right? It's the power of one. That's a big thing that I like to really focus on when we're writing copy, making ads and funnels is the power of one. So what exactly is that now the power of one means I'm writing for one avatar.

I'm focusing on one message I'm focusing on one pain point and I'm focusing on one solution. I'll give you another example of this. So we had a client who is running challenge funnels. And it was just really like convoluted, confusing and weird, right? It's like too many things.

There's too many ideas. There's not one central through line, not one central idea. So what we did was we just slashed the tax end because we looked at their sales call recordings and we looked at why people were joining their program in the first place and ascending and why people would show up to the event in the first place. And it was just because they wanted to find their first multifamily property.

That was it. So all the messaging was centered around this one idea of saying, Hey, during this three day workshop, we're going to help you find your first multifamily property that you can get cash out that you can, that you can invest in and get passive monthly cashflow on. That was it. That's the power of one, right?

It wasn't this weird convoluted, double ended sort of offer and messaging and this confusing thing. It was just centered around one idea and now it's just, it's just now centered around one idea of helping you find your first multifamily property that you can buy and invest in with little cash down. So way easier to write all the copy, the through lines easier. The ads say the same thing.

So put the time and effort into making it custom branded and also making sure that it's mobile optimized. That's a huge thing.

Is your headline here? If you have a VSL here, you know, your sub headline, is it clean to read? Is your button above the fold, your CTA above the fold, right? You want to make sure all this stuff on mobile is above the fold, all the key elements, and just make sure it doesn't look again, scammy, confusing, blocky, all this stuff.

You want to ensure that design is very crisp and clean. So that's something that a lot of people overlook, but it really can help the conversions a lot. So, and the third thing in making a winning funnel is making sure that you pair the right conversion mechanism slash funnel type, which essentially are the same thing with the right offer. Okay.

So if you have an offer that needs a lot of educating and it's not necessarily something like super intuitive, like a staffing company or something like that, like maybe it's this new sort of business opportunity that really not a lot of people have heard about. That's where I would do some sort of funnel, like a webinar funnel or some sort of funnel, even like a challenge funnel. Now, obviously challenges you can't run too, too continuously. These are more like bi-monthly or quarterly events, but that's where I would pick some sort of mechanism, like a webinar funnel to where, Hey, I need to spend more time educating these people on my process or this opportunity in order for them to convert.

And with the call funnel, I just don't necessarily have that time. Unless of course you have the backend systems in place, but that's more advanced. This is where you could experiment with something like a webinar. So I see some people trying to just jam this convoluted, crazy, confusing offer through a call funnel without any backend education or backend sales processes.

And if they just switched to a webinar funnel, they would find much much more, uh, you know, just much better results overall. And on the flip side too, I see some people who are trying to run a webinar funnel for a just straightforward service that they don't necessarily need to run that type of conversion mechanism with. They can just switch to something more simple, like a call funnel, and then add some backend processes like content remarketing, good education manually in the sales process, backend email flows to essentially educate them, to essentially educate the prospect and why their specific service in general, why they're different, their process, why it's different, why they get results.

But instead, you know, they're doing this like longer kind of webinar, which look is cool. You can still make it work, but sometimes you're, uh, just, but sometimes you just have the wrong essentially, but sometimes you're just adding more friction and you're running more of a, uh, more taxing funnel, like a webinar funnel when you could just run a call funnel on that point and be perfectly fine. So simple offers go for a call funnel or something like that, a much more lower friction funnel. And if you need something that need, and if you have an offer that needs a lot of educating before the actual conversion point, that's where you can explore something like a webinar funnel.

And then finally, number four, two real quick is just having a good offer and offer that cold traffic once. So that is the main thing. It has to be cold traffic optimized. And of course, Mr.

Fazio talks about this all the time. So go through his training for sure on the offer side, but having a cold traffic optimized offer, something that cold traffic actually wants is going to make your funnels convert super, super well. So these are four things to keep in mind when you're building these funnels and just implementing these four things will get you to a point where you can get good results through your ads and through your funnels.

Message from Daniel:

Important note that's mentioned at the end of the video: for using pixel codes on Clickfunnels 2.0 pages specifically, the event codes need to go inside the FOOTER of the individual pages.

Again, for clarification: the base pixel code (not event code) goes in the Header code for the entire funnel in the settings of the whole funnel (not an individual page). For the EVENT CODE that you want to trigger on specific pages, those must go inside the FOOTER of that individual page.

This is counter to what you do on every single other platform. Normally, on ANY other page builder, the event codes also go in the header. This is not the case with Clickfunnels 2.0

BONUS: Evan's Dream 100 Course
Important Message from Daniel:

In this video you'll hear Evan say that Dream 100 deliverables could take 1-3 hours each. This is not entirely accurate anymore - as many of the deliverables can be created near immediately with AI. Let's take an example:

Example:

You're an Ads/Funnels Agency. Your Dream 100 deliverable are ad scripts. And the target market you're going after is coaches/consultants.

Step 1: You build an ad scripts brain based off of already successful coaches/consultants running ads. You go onto the Facebook ad library and transcribe what they're saying in their video ads. You dump all of these ad scripts into a Google Doc. You get between 5-10 ad scripts.

Step 2: You download that Google Doc as a TXT file with all of the scripts, and upload them to ChatGPT, Claude, or Manus.

Step 3: You input the following prompt:

You've been given access to transcripts of successful video ads from coaches/consultants. Your job is to be a professional ad script writer. Inside this conversation I will be be providing you a description of a different person's offer in each message. Once I've done that, your job is to come up with new direct response ads for me. The formate by which you should deliver these ad scripts are as follows: 5 hook variations in front of 1 body. A hook is defined as the first 1-5 sentences of an ad. Each hook should logically and grammatically flow into the body in a cohesive manner. This combination of 5 hooks and 1 body is what we will call and adset.

When you're writing these ad scripts, imagine you are a direct response copywriter who is a professional at human psychology, persuasion, and has made billions of dollars across hundreds of different offers ranging from business opportunity courses, b2b services, consulting offers, b2c offers, and all forms of information marketing or courses and coaching programs. You should also reference the provided successful ad scripts that have been uploaded into your knowledge, however, you do not need to exactly follow them. You should simply use them as foundational understanding for what has worked recently for that person's specific offer.

Now, make me 5 different ad sets. Here is a description of the offer I want you to do it for: [Description of the Offer]

Step 4: This will spit out the adsets. You will only need to revise them. Once you've done so, you can deliver them as the Dream 100 deliverable.
