Right? Cold email is marketing just like paid ads. And so marketing requires creative input and testing volume to simply find what works. Right?

Like we said in the very beginning, cut the losers, double down on the winners. And really at the end of the day, it's just more shots on goal. It's the whole game with marketing and of course, with cold emails. So the cadence that I shoot for, and this is also for running my own internal cold email campaigns.

The cadence that I shoot for is a minimum of one campaign launch per week, especially in the beginning when you have zero data on what works. We've all experienced that before.

Don't settle. Don't get complacent once you found, quote, unquote, a winner. Keep pushing the envelope to try to find a winner that makes that winner look like a loser. And more volume sold means more campaign angles per week to maximize sends.

So if you sold someone on a thousand email sends per day, it doesn't require as many new campaign angles per week as two thousand email sends per day or ten thousand email sends per day. If you can respond back to them within five minutes, they're most likely still going through their email inbox, and they can continue the conversation with you right then and there. Otherwise, you miss them, and then you have to wait until they go to check their email inbox. Alright. So getting into module number six where we're gonna talk about communication with your clients, reporting, and also just staying in. So the number one thing that'll help you to keep your clients for longer, keep them from churning, is to just never let the relationship go stale. And we're gonna get into really specific ways of how you can do that.

And the main way of doing that is to narrate the work, not just the results. If you wait until you get results to then communicate to the client, the communication is gonna be far and few between, which is not good. And so what you should do instead is every time you're about to start a new campaign, tell them what you're launching, why you're launching it, how you think it's gonna benefit them, or at least increase the results from the previous campaigns, when you expect it to go live, and how long until you're gonna be able to draw a conclusion from the data. Right?

The client wants to see you working on this every single day, not just stats after the fact. Right? Don't just show them the results. Show them the inputs.

Show them the amount of work that's going into their account because they're gonna appreciate it. Even if it's not generating the results that you or the client is hoping for, at least you show them that you're not sitting on your hands doing nothing. Right? So narrate the work, not just the results.

Communicate even in the silence. This is one thing people have, trouble with for whatever reason. Some clients are not gonna respond. Like, if you post these things that I'm telling you to post in your shared Slack channel and the client's just not responding, post it anyways in detail every single time.

Don't get discouraged if your clients are not responding. Keep posting it because, again, this is gonna create a paper trail. So if your clients come back and start complaining that things haven't been working and you're not getting results and they want a refund or this ad and the other thing, you have a paper trail to say, hey. Look.

We were sending updates. We were putting in real work, and you were nowhere to be found. You weren't helping the situation. You weren't giving feedback.

You weren't approving our new campaign ideas. And so we were never gonna be able to make this work because you weren't doing your part. And doing your part goes back to the onboarding call where you talk about here's what we're responsible for doing as the agency owner, and here's what you're responsible for doing as a client to make this relationship wildly successful. So make sure to communicate even into silence, even if it feels like nothing's happening and it's it's not gonna be for anything good.

Then you have the Friday KPIs report. So every single week, what we'll send on Friday is how many new campaigns were launched, how many total emails have been sent across all campaigns, how many total replies were generated, how many total positive replies, how many total calls booked, and how all the compares to the last week. Then the part that actually matters, which is your analysis. And, basically, what are you doing about it?

So these are the KPIs, but what are you doing about the KPIs? Are you launching new campaigns? Are you turning off old campaigns? Are you testing new angles, doubling down on winners, cutting losers?

And what I'll say, just like in the onboarding email, a short Loom video beats a written summary every single time. And so make sure you capitalize by showing your clients your face and your voice on these Friday KPI reports rather than just sending a Slack template that looks the same each and every single week. They wanna hear from you. And you can do it in the form of a short Loom video, literally just following exactly what's in this slide.

It it it lays it all out there for you very clearly.

And then what do you do more than weekly? Well, report campaign wrap ups, celebrate every win, highlight everything. Right? So we can go into each and every single one of these.

Like, when a campaign ends, send the wrap up stats for that campaign specifically. Every single time there's a win, put it in front of them and celebrate it. If there's a positive reply, if there's a call booked, if there's a deal closed, all of it gets highlighted and shared within the the Slack channel we have with the You're literally training the client to connect the inputs of your service to the results in their business that happened later on because there's a correlation between inputs and outputs. The only reason it's difficult for us and the clients, of course, to see it is because there is the time delay.

Right? There's a time delay. You reap what you harvest, but you don't know when you're going to reap what you harvest. So if you send a bunch of emails now, you might reap from that work three months down the line. And so if you just get into the habit of training your clients to connect the inputs of your service on a daily and a weekly basis to the results that show up in their business every month or so, you're you're gonna set yourself up for a successful client relationship. And the ListKit analytics page gives you a clean breakdown that you can actually share directly, which is helpful, if you don't wanna come up with your own custom reporting. Like, the ListKit analytics page, even if you wanna come up with your own reporting, you can take the results or the stats from the ListKit analytics page to then put into your own custom branded report or whatever works best for you.

And then you wanna stay plugged into their business too. Like, businesses are always changing. Right? I mean, I run businesses that are constantly coming up with new lead magnets, constantly producing new case studies, constantly testing new target markets and offers.

Like, businesses do everything but stay stale. If a business is staying stale, then they're most likely not gonna stay in business. That's pretty much the the general rule rule of thumb. So your success is not solely about whether cold email works or not.

It's largely based on the health of the business you're emailing on behalf of. Like, this is this is such an important understanding. A lot of times people are like, well, I can't get results for this client. And it's not necessarily that cold email doesn't work.

It could just be the health of the business you're trying to get cold email results for. And so stay in lockstep on things like new initiatives and pivots, wins, challenges, and bottlenecks, results from other channels. Like, maybe they're running paid ads. Maybe they're doing LinkedIn outreach.

Maybe they're cold calling. Like, there's insights you can gain from those other channels that can help make the cold email campaigns more successful. Maybe they're producing new assets like case studies, lead magnets, VSLs, ad creatives that can be super helpful in the actual campaigns themselves, but also in inbox management. Same with sales team trainings and new close one call recordings.

You can learn how to objection handle and what selling points actually resonate with their target market. And then just in general, new target markets and offers, like what they're actively testing because businesses will change offers, change target markets quite often. So stay in lockstep and stay plugged into their business because, again, it's not always whether or not cold email works. It's largely based on the business you're emailing on behalf of.

So you need to become an expert at their business as much as you are an expert at doing cold email. It's just as important of a part of the equation.

Then you wanna feed their sales process rather than just mine it. Mining it means we take the sales call recordings from their sales team and we take the transcripts and we figure out how to reverse engineer the selling points and the objection handling into our script strategies, our campaign strategies, and, of course, our inbox management.

And that's what most agencies do, if that sometimes they don't even do that. They don't extract learnings. But most agencies, if they extract learnings, they stop there. But go the other way too.

Meaning, share feedback and insights from your campaigns with their sales team. Because market response data is so valuable to them, and it surfaces new target markets and offers worth testing that maybe opens up again a new target market offer that they weren't gonna test before until you gave them this insight on how some campaigns are performing that all of a sudden hits home. Like, they found product market fit with this brand new target market and offer that they didn't have when you guys first started working together, and now all of a sudden you're booking calls nonstop. Right?

There's been offers where we've booked dozens and dozens and dozens of calls each and every single month just from them pivoting slightly their target market and their offer. So if you can be part of that feedback process with their sales team, like, now become valuable to their sales process rather than you're just good for if you book calls or not. So this is how to become irreplaceable as a cold email lead generation agency is to feed their sales process rather than just mining it. And and, again, it's just that cold email is their testing ground.

Cold email is a great testing ground, and it's a big value add on its own if you understand how to frame it. And if you put this in front of your client, right, before you launch a new offer or market full scale, just have them test it in cold email first. So always ask your clients, hey. Is there any new ideas, new target markets, new offers that you wanna just test to see if it's worth doing full scale across the business?

We can do this in the form of a cold email campaign. Like, offer your clients to do that on a monthly basis because chances are they're gonna find more value in you being able to go out and test new ideas. And then maybe one of these new ideas hits, and all of a sudden, can scale it. Right?

Scale the winners, cut the losers. And all of a sudden, you're booking a ton of calls from this new campaign angle that would have never existed if you didn't put it in front of them as an idea in the first place. So the moment your strategy goes stale is the moment your results do the same.

That's really it with cold email. You always have to be thinking on your feet. You always have to be reinventing yourself, innovating, and coming up with new creative ideas just like you do with any other form of marketing. Right?

So testing cold email first, validate new offers and markets before the company then full scale launches. This will be a super valuable thing, for them to understand that they have access to through your service. Keep the strategy fresh, continuously iterate, innovate, reinvent yourself because stale strategy means stale results, and then deliver compounding value by positioning cold emails and ongoing strategic asset, not just a channel that books a handful more calls for their sales team. And this module that goes through client communications, proper reporting, and just staying in lockstep with your client covers exactly how you can do that.

So I'm excited to see you guys implement this one because it's gonna really set you apart in the agency game if you do this properly.

And so those are really the pipeline stages that you wanna ask a client for. Hey. Do you have any people that booked a call but never closed? Do you have any people that are closed lost? Alright. So let's talk about scaling and churn. So you wanna scale volume before you scale services. This is a common trap that most agency owners and especially cold email agency owners fall into.

The most natural expansion is the simplest one, which is to just send more emails. A lot of people, for example, try to expand services by saying, oh, we'll do your sales. We'll, set up a CRM for you. We'll do cold calling. We'll do LinkedIn outreach. But the easiest and the most natural expansion is to just send more cold emails. So one bundle, as you know, from ListKit is one thousand email sends per day or roughly ten thousand net new leads contacted per month.

If you scale to a hundred fifty bundles, I know it's an extreme example. Sure. But businesses legitimately just it's about scale. And they run a business that sends a hundred thousand emails per day.

So a hundred bundles would make sense for some clients. Especially if it's working, you scale what's working. And so the same example of some people spend a hundred dollars on paid ads a day. Some people spend a hundred thousand dollars on paid ads a day.

No joke. Some people spend that much on paid ads, and it's the same thing with email. Some people only send a thousand emails per day. Some people might send a hundred fifty thousand emails per day.

It really just depends on what makes sense for the business. And if it's working, as long as they wanna scale, that's the first most natural place you should look to expand services is scale volume. If you send more volume, you can increase your tech fee, and you'll just book more calls, which you can then charge more money for. Simple.

Right? So when you scale volume, the same way you look at scaling ad spend, it just comes down to CAC, cost of acquisition. If the CAC is good, there's no reason not to scale it unless for whatever reason they are bottlenecked on how many new clients they can take on.

And cold email is one of those channels that just scales close to linearly with more volume.

And so, again, you increase the monthly tech fee to cover the added cost. So if you add let's just say you go from one bundle to five bundles. Instead of the tech fee being six hundred dollars for one bundle, it's three thousand dollars for five bundles. So you can just cover the added cost through the tech fee if you wanna increase volume and add more bundles.

And really what's in it for you since the tech fee is really just covering costs is you're booking more calls. Right? All of your upside comes from calls booked. And so if you can book five calls from one bundle, what's to say you can't book twenty five calls from five bundles?

Right? You just five x the amount that you get paid from that one client because you got them to scale volume. Right?

And then it didn't cost you anything extra because you just increased the monthly tech fee. But as you already know, to scale volume of sends, you need to scale volume of campaign angles launching every single week. The same way if you were to spend a lot more money on paid ads, you'd need a lot more creatives. Same thing with cold email. We've already went over this. And so then and only then should you start to add services. Don't expand services, meaning LinkedIn outreach and cold calling until you have success with the one core service first.

Go deep before you go wide. So LinkedIn outreach, for example, is the most natural next step because you already have LinkedIn URLs for every prospect for your clients from Listkit without paying anything extra.

And we're planning to build LinkedIn outreach into Listkit directly.

So, hopefully, by the end of this year, it'll be there for, you know, you to expand services at that point. So maybe there is a much simpler path to add LinkedIn Outreach as part of your offer stack directly in Listkit by the end of this year. We'll see. But the most natural step is first to increase volume, then add services. So LinkedIn outreach being one of those, and then cold calling. But cold calling is so high in terms of its complexity as a standalone services.

And so I don't like to add cold calling as a stand alone service. I like to keep it where it belongs, which is inside your inbox management process, period. I don't even talk about cold calling because it's just it's way too difficult for for most people If they're focused on other things and cold calling isn't the primary service. And then capitalize on your winners. Right? Once you've gotten a client result, you feel good about, go and collect assets, social proof. So go get a video recorded case study, which is the most valuable asset by far because you can show this to your prospects that are thinking about signing on to your agency.

And you can say, look. Look at what I did for this client. And he talks about it in a twenty minute video. You can get trust pilot reviews, which you could then convert the case study into a written review.

They just sign off on. Right? Two for one. So if you get them on a case study interview and then you put into, Claude, hey.

Can you turn this case study interview transcript into Trustpilot review that I can send to this client to, simply approve? You can build a trust pilot page that looks like this, where there's two hundred ninety four reviews with essentially a five star rating for client ascension. Right? This is a literally a case study of one of our students named Tyler who sold a cold email agency that he got to seventy thousand dollars a month for seven hundred thousand dollars cash. So if you go to Daniel's YouTube channel and you go to playlist and then you go to case studies, you'll see there's fifty eight case study videos, literally anywhere from ten to twenty to thirty minutes long of business owners that went through our programs and got case study worthy results that we then turn into trust pilot reviews, right, which gives us huge credibility to go out and get more clients like yourself.

And if they have something that they're happy with, they're most likely gonna tell their business owner friends about it, especially if you incentivize them by saying, hey. If you get us a referral, we'll lower your cost per call. Or if you get us a referral, we'll pay you out this one time cash prize, something along these lines.

So if you delivered and communicated the whole way through, you should feel completely confident asking for any of these things or really all of these things. So if you implemented everything we taught in the previous modules and it's going well with your client, you should feel confident asking for all these things, capitalizing on your winners.

The next thing to understand is that churn is not a bug. Like, the expected monthly churn, what I've seen is normal for the cold email agency business model is anywhere from ten to twenty percent. Obviously, ten percent is the goal. Twenty percent is probably where you're gonna start, and you just work your way down.

And here's the thing. Most of it isn't because cold email doesn't work or you're bad at your job. It's because it didn't work for their business. So you're churning businesses that cold email just doesn't work for.

Whether they have a weak offer, they don't have product market fit, they're bad at sales, or they're just too early into this.

That's who you're gonna that's who you're gonna churn. And so again, cut your losers, double down on your winners. The way to think about this is if you churn twenty percent, can you upsell the other twenty percent? Right?

If you have ten clients and you churn two, can you get at least two clients to commit to sending more volume? Because by doing that, you just canceled out churn. Like, yeah, churn sucks because you lost clients, but you just canceled it out by getting two clients to upsell, and so you didn't really lose anything. Right?

So cut your losers, double down on your winners. And a lot of people are scared of churn, but you shouldn't be scared of churn if you have a bunch of clients that you're not getting any results for, but you're still doing a lot of work for. Like, you are better off churning those clients and making room for new clients to come in that can potentially become winners you double down on. Does that make sense?

Again, upsells and referrals cancel out churn. It's the flywheel. Right? That's the actual math of this business.

Your top twenty percent of clients produce the case studies. They produce the trust pilot reviews. They give you referrals, and they upsell for more volume that attract and fund the replacement for the ones who leave. So spend your energy accordingly.

Double down on your winners. Imagine if you're running a pay per call agency, and you have one client that's getting you one call every single month, and they're a pain in the neck, and you're spending most of your time there, but then you have one client that's getting you ten calls booked per month, and you're not spending as much time as you should be there, spend your energy accordingly. Don't think of churn as just a percentage. Think of churn as a percentage of revenue.

Imagine. Let's just let's just do the math real quick.

Let's just say you have ten clients. Right? And let's say, client one is zero dollars, client two is, two hundred fifty dollars. Let's just say this is, at two fifty per call.

And then client ten is twenty five hundred. Right? So ten calls booked, eight calls booked, five calls booked, four calls booked, two calls booked, one call booked, zero calls booked. Imagine you churn four out of ten clients.

Right? So these clients. Yeah. It looks like your churn is forty percent because you've churned four out of ten clients, but you only churned seven hundred and fifty dollars in revenue churn out of if we do the math in this scenario, it's forty five hundred plus, sixty seven fifty plus seventy seven fifty plus eight eight five, I think, in total revenue.

I think that's the math. I don't know for sure. I mean, if you look at it this way, you forty percent churn in terms of clients, but less than ten percent churn in terms of actual revenue. So don't worry about clients churning, especially the ones that you're not getting results for. Because as a percentage of your actual revenue, the percentage of churn will look a lot better than the percentage in terms of your clients. So upsells and referrals will cancel out your churn. And by understanding this, you'll learn to spend your energy accordingly.

And then churn with class or churn with keeping your reputation intact. Right? So we've signed thousands and thousands of clients for our cold email services, and thousands of them, literally thousands, have churned over the years, and we still keep in touch with a lot of them. So how do we do this? Well, you have a defined cancellation path, a clear cancellation request process with proper notice typically found in your contract agreement.

You do your best work until the very last day.

So don't stop doing good work for your client just because they said they're gonna cancel. Deliver your best work until the very last day of service. Collect churn reasons. So a lot of times you wanna get on an exit interview, it's called, when someone says they're gonna churn, and you collect the reason for why they churn on the exit interview, which is actually, this next one.

It goes hand in hand with collecting churn reasons. It's just a lot easier to get churn reasons on an exit interview because you can talk to the customer and ask questions and and go a little bit deeper as to what was the main reason for churn. And I've actually seen exit interviews that have won clients back. So maybe you lose one of those clients later down in the list that we just wrote out where they were bringing in a thousand dollars for you, so it hurts a little bit more to lose that client.

Do an exit interview if you can get them to spend time with you on an exit interview, and maybe you find out why they churn and you have a solution for it and you can win them back. And, again, exactly like it says here, implement learnings back into the service. So as you learn why customers are churning, implement those learnings back into the service, and it's really just gonna reinforce a lot of the things that we taught throughout this course as to what you should be doing. Quicker wins, better inbox management, more campaign delivery, more dialed in billing ops, these sorts of things, right, is is really what's gonna, prevent people from churning.

And then the win back is real. In the seven years that I've been running a cold email business, I've watched clients start and stop, start and stop, and start and stop again. Like, it it's just this cyclical thing that businesses get into where sometimes it makes sense to do cold email, and then sometimes it doesn't. And maybe they reinvent themselves or they start a new business or launch a new offer, and then all of a sudden, they wanna try cold email again.

So, again, sometimes they cracked a new market or a new offer. Now they're finally ready to scale with cold email when before they just didn't have product market fit. So leave every relationship on a good note so that you get to be there when that happens.

I've won back so many churn customers throughout the years because I churned with class. So churn is inevitable. It's gonna happen, but don't churn without class. Don't churn without doing yourself and your reputation as solid. Because if you don't, if you leave your clients in a bad spot, if you get lazy with the work ever since the cancellation notice comes in until the end of the service, if you try to screw them over by invoicing them for something that they didn't get, if you are just hard or difficult to work with, people are not gonna wanna come back. So always leave the door open for people to come back.

And I get it. Asking for honest feedback when someone is not happy with you or left because they just are not satisfied with the service, it's scary.

You're essentially asking them to tell you things that might be very negative or discouraging for you to hear, but don't think of it that way. Instead, look at it as an opportunity to improve and lean into it anyway with the intention of using all the information, all the feedback that you can collect to make the service better for your existing and your future clients and for them if they ever were to consider returning. So this, again, is what the best agency owners in the world do, and that's what you're expected to do as well after going through this course.

Alright. So our final module is all about hiring and removing yourself from the fulfillment part of your agency. Now I'll say this as a warning. Most of you will not be ready to do this for a little while until you have ten plus clients, until you've fulfilled for those clients in a way where you've generated legitimate revenue for them consistently.

Like, this is months out for most of you guys because there's so much to put into place before this. But when you get to this point, I wanna have a video that you guys can revisit so that it's very clear on how to approach the hiring process to remove yourself from the day to day fulfillment. So as you sign more clients and upsell existing ones, you'll be ready to hire, but you should hire in the right order only. And the rule is to hire closest to the money first.

Closest to the money, meaning what actually produces the revenue. So hire for the step that actually makes your agency money, which as you guys know, outside of your own sales process, meaning you doing your own cold email, getting on sales calls to close a client in the first place.

The closest thing to the money is the inbox management because that's where positive replies are converted into booked calls that your agency gets paid for.

But before you go and hire someone to do inbox management, do the work yourself first because you can never hire for a role that you've never done yourself. At least you can't hire in a way that is gonna work successfully or you're gonna have good results from your hire if you've never done the role you're hiring for yourself successfully. So you should know inbox management through and through because you've done it for three months successfully. Then you go out and you hire.

And the way to hire an inbox manager is to basically assign one inbox manager anywhere from ten to twenty clients.

As long as they're able to follow all the best practices from module five, where they do omnichannel, they reach out to different colleagues, they follow-up thirty or forty times if necessary, they pick up the phone and cold call, they're interfacing with the clients to get valuable, follow-up assets like lead magnets. Like, the capacity is pretty much defined as how many clients can you do inbox management for while following every best practice from module five. And you'll probably be the the the guinea pig for this. Like, if you can do ten clients on your own while doing everything else in your agency, then there's no reason one full time inbox manager can't do ten to twenty clients, while following all the best practices for module five. And one thing to understand is that this is a sales role, and so hire accordingly.

In terms of what you should be looking for, it's someone who's sales minded. It's someone who thinks on their feet and adapts quickly in conversations. It's someone who is really creative in follow ups and finds new angles to reengage prospects. It's someone who's relentless and will follow-up until until there's a booked call or a firm no, and it's someone who's not afraid to pick up the phone and call.

In terms of how do you pay them, you pay them how you get paid. Because if you pay them how you get paid, they'll be all these things naturally. Naturally. Like they'll be relentless.

They'll pick up the phone. They'll get creative in their follow ups because that's how they get paid. They only get paid if they book calls. So pretty much you can do a small monthly pace if needed.

Couple hundred dollars a month depending on how many clients they're managing. But then the lion's share comes from a per book call model exactly the way your agency earns, typically anywhere from, like, five to ten percent. So if you get paid two hundred fifty dollars per call, you can pay your inbox manager twenty five dollars for all the calls that they book in for your agency's clients. Right?

So you're paying them twenty five while your client's paying you two hundred fifty dollars. There's really good profit in that to fully remove it from your responsibilities. And two things happen automatically when you do this. One, it's ROI positive by design.

Like, I just did the math for you. The world pays for itself through the revenue it generates. Similar to if you were to hire a closer, they only get paid on cash collected that they sold. And then the person that you're hiring is naturally hungry because they don't get paid unless they get results.

The same way you're naturally hungry to get results for your clients. So they will deploy every best practice because their income depends on it. It's just on you to give them those best practices and to give them access to training and resources that are gonna help them to succeed in this role.

So anyways, performance based comp before fixed pay every time. Don't don't don't. Please don't. Dear god, don't go out there and hire an inbox manager for a thousand dollars a month on a base salary.

Like, they will not perform. I promise you they'll not perform. The only way you should comp them is exactly how you get comped by your client, which is performance based pay in a small month small monthly base if needed. Meaning, if you don't have enough clients and those clients don't produce enough book call opportunities for them to earn a good living through this role.

The second hire to consider is the cold email strategist. So they own the actual fulfillment, like the target market and offer selection, such as identifying the right audience and crafting the right offer. They do the leads list building, they do the script writing, and they set it all up and manage it all. And ListKit keeping the one campaign per week cadence alive without you.

And that cadence increases as volume increases. Right? And then the third hire becomes a CSM, and they own the client relationship. They own the communication and the touch points happening in Slack.

They take care of the onboarding call. They send the weekly KPI reports. And really anything that comes up from the start of the engagement through the full life cycle of clients are complaining about something or asking questions or wanna get on a call to just get fully caught up on all the work you're doing, the CSM or the client success manager, they own the relationship with the client, and then they just communicate with the strategist and with the inbox manager so that they can keep the client informed on what's happening with their account.

And so that's really it. Like, there's three hires and you're out. You get an inbox manager first, then you go and get the cold email strategist, then you go and get the CSM to communicate with the clients. And with those three roles filled, you're fully removed from fulfillment and free to spend a hundred percent of your time on marketing and sales to sign more clients for your business, and that's the entire business.

It's really that simple. But you have to go through the fulfillment processes yourself, onboarding infrastructure, billing ops, campaign delivery, inbox management, client communication, getting them quick wins, scaling, collecting assets like social proof, and fighting and mitigating churn. Then after you've done this to a really high standard that you're happy with, you can start to hire inbox managers, cold email strategists, client success managers. And now all you're focused on is overseeing and managing the fulfillment, basically coaching your team up to success, and then spending all of your time marketing and selling to sign more clients so that you can become a case study like some of the ones I showed you in the previous videos and scale your agency to multiple thousands of dollars per month and even have the opportunity to exit for hundreds of thousands of dollars a month because we've seen cold email agencies that have gone through our program actually accomplish that for themselves, and there's no reason you can't be next.

What's up guys, Lucas here. So today I'm going to be going over the AI client onboarding agent. This is going to be useful regardless of what type of agency you run. Essentially what it's going to allow you to do is input the client details, get their information, turn it into tasks inside of your Go High Level and add your client to Slack along with a welcome email.

So as usual, let's break down what you're going to need to have set up for this and what each node does. So first of all, you're going to have to have Go High Level set up. This is about offers.

This is about positioning and we're gonna tackle some of that now. So the problem solution loop. Solving one problem always creates the next problem. This is a principle that's going to benefit us the entire way when we're talking about offers, when we're talking about marketing, when we're talking about sales.

Each solution you provide clears the path that reveals the next challenge. This is not a bug. This is a feature. This is the entire business model.

So the reason why this matters is because you're the expert. You've seen these problems before. You know the journey your clients will take before they do. You can preemptively anticipate what's going to happen to said person with what you sell when you take heed of this principle, which is ubiquitous across all types of agencies.

If a client has a six-step problem and you solve the first two steps, you already know that they're going to hit step three. It's not prediction. It's pattern recognition. So your job is to anticipate the next problem and have the solution ready before they even ask for it.

So this is how it kind of works from a sort of like first principles perspective. So step one is you solve the initial problem and that is the entry point. There's an element of like fractional COO and fractional CRO that can sometimes go into these way beyond what's necessary now. Sometimes problem one or problem A is the only problem. So with GTM systems, they get leads. Now that they have leads, they want more leads. So you sell them on leads and the core offer is more leads.

The problem solution loop is therefore either horizontal or vertical. So this is really important to understand. Horizontal is what I described above where someone has a problem at one part of the funnel. You provide a solution to now widen that part of the funnel so that there's extra throughput and the bottleneck has been alleviated.

That then shows a second problem or a new problem, which is better quality because it's further down the line. It's closer to the money. So you then provide solution two, which then fills that up and then way more goes through that part of the funnel. That's horizontal.

You do one thing, you solve this problem, that creates a problem downstream, which isn't the exact same flavor of problem. So you solve that one too because solution one and solution two come as a pair. Then vertical is problem, solution. I want more of solution.

So I get more solution. A lot of these are very much, lead generation is like the perfect example for this, which is as you can see above with the GTM systems. You only need one thing there and that one service is not just the initial service, it's also most of the, it's also the rest of the service. Content is the same.

Once you've done the chatbot, you're probably going to do an op system. Once you've done the chatbot, you probably do a sales system, something like that. So how to apply this? When you're designing your offers, thinking sequences, what's the first problem?

This becomes your intro offer or your main service entry point. What's the problem that emerges after you solve the first one? This becomes your upsell. What's the problem after that?

This becomes your next upsell or your retainer. You're not forcing solutions they don't need. Now, there's two types of offers that you're going to need and they're based on the thing that you are selling and you can turn any of the four that we recommend, ops, GTM, sales and chatbots into these two types of offers.

Number one, intro offers, low friction entry points and number two, main service offerings, which are the real money makers. The timeline for delivery is 7 to 14 days. The scope is you solving the most urgent and most painful problem that you've discovered through the discovery call process. It's not going to be the entire thing. It's going to be the aspect of the entire thing, which is the most painful element of it.

And the goal is to create immediate visible value that naturally leads to your main service. So again, in an example, in the personal injury law firm example, they're losing leads because they respond too slowly. So the intro offer is a lead response chatbot for 2K delivered in 10 days. It qualifies the leads, it asks the key questions and it books consultations instantly.

The result is response time drops from two hours to two minutes and they book three times more consultations in the first week. Our sales systems are a mess.

We're terrible with follow-ups. We're terrible with the initial lead nurture. It takes too long to get people over the line and the amount of leads that we're getting are all terrible. You could hit all five of those.

The most pressing one, which is the one that you sold, is the chatbot solution, responding too slowly. Because even of the leads that do trickle through this terrible process, the team aren't doing what they need to do in order to get them over the line. So selling that is the thing that just leads to immediate revenue. Okay, now we'll handle the rest of these.

That becomes the main service upsell. Sell system implementation for 8 to 12k plus 750 a month for continual servicing. You automate their entire follow-up process, build a CRM pipeline, ensure no leads for the food cracks. You're already using GHL for the chatbot build, so you just flesh it out with the rest of the systems.

Easy win, clear upfront value. The intro offer proved that you can deliver. The main service ends up being the natural next step that is a comprehensive solution to every stated problem. That's how main offers work.

So, critical rule for the intro offers themselves. It must solve a real urgent problem. So you don't want to sell AI strategy consulting or automation audits or anything along those lines. Those are vague and they don't lead to the same amount of value that doing something for someone will actually lead to.

You want to sell, we'll double your book to call rate by cutting your customer response time from four hours to four minutes. You're not selling the deliverable, you're selling the solution to a problem and it needs to be a real and urgent problem. It needs to be deliverable fast, seven to 14 days maximum. Speed creates momentum and if you take six weeks to deliver a $1,500 project, you've lost a sale on your main service.

You can solve the problem at an effective hourly rate above 250 bucks an hour. So this is a nice rule of thumb. You most likely won't get this out of the gate, especially if you're doing this from scratch. But if you keep this in mind and you know now that after you've sold this once or twice, it takes you X amount to do, as long as you're making effectively above 250 bucks an hour, very, very, very scalable and it leads to a really quick turnaround on a number of these.

So for example, a $1,500 build should not take you more than six hours to complete. It will always be slower the first time you do it, so don't stress about it. And even if it took 10 hours instead of six, were you getting paid 150 bucks an hour at your day job? And were those $150 hours also going to get you closer to a $400 or $500 an hour, which is from the main service?

So yeah, it must create demand for your main service. The intro offer should make the next problem obvious. If you solve lead qualification, the natural next question is how do I convert these leads faster? So that ends up being your main service.

And time to value must be immediate. Don't make them wait until everything's 100% complete for them to see results. If you're building a PM system, you want to show them the complete layout and how their work will be organized immediately, even if you're still completing the backend setup because visible progress maintains momentum. So that's less of a critical rule as far as how you structure the offer, but more so how you deliver it.

Now, main service offerings, and this is where you actually make money. So your core high value services are your main service offerings. And this is where you solve the significant problems and you generate the majority of your revenue. And there's two ways of doing this, either project or retainer.

So we talk about project, this is what goes into it. Project-based means fixed scope, fixed price. It's a one-time engagement with a clearly defined scope, specific deliverables and a set price. Pricing usually is around five to six K in the low end and 50 K on the high end.

And this is best for solving a contained problem with a clear beginning and end. For example, the AI powered sales system implementation that we described for the personal injury marketing firm. You build up their entire CRM, you automate lead nurture, you integrate with their email platform and you set up pipeline tracking. Price, 10 K, timeline, four to six weeks.

The pros, predictable for both you and the client, clear milestones and deliverables, easier to sell because it's a finite commitment and people don't like retainers or subscriptions and it's great for building case studies, especially at pace. It's great for doing it at pace because you can go from intro offer to end of this main service project in eight weeks and have a video out of it as well as 10 K and LTV. Cons, revenue stops when the project ends, you need to constantly find new clients or upsell. You want to use this when starting out, when the client is new to you or when the problem has a clear end point.

The number two is with retainers, which is ongoing service, recurring revenue. Now, retainers can be split in two ways. There's what you do after you've delivered the main project, which is like continual maintenance or continual management. And then there's the retainer, which is this is X amount a month for a set number of months.

So, retainers are what happens when clients pay a recurring monthly fee for continuous access to your services, ongoing support, optimization or strategic guidance. I would also include unlimited builds in this case. So, if you're someone who's actually really good at NAN and make and you're building stuff around sales or around ops, you can put people on retainers because they have a ton of ideas of things that they would want to want to automate. And with that, you can basically say, all right, cool, we'll just automate everything for you open-ended.

We'll commit to X amount per month and then with all of those ideas that you have, we can just stick them in a backlog and we'll just build them. And those, again, aren't productized but it's a retainer at the end of the day and if those builds aren't super hard, you can get a lot of them, you can get a lot of people to pay you a high LTV for that. So, pricing is 2 to 10k plus per month depending on the scope and the value delivered. This is best for customization, maintenance or continuous service delivery.

So, for example, after building a sales system for that marketing agency, you offer 3k a month retainers to fill their pipeline with cold email leads via their GTM systems. The pros, predictable recurring revenue, long-term client relationships, easier to upsell additional services and you get a lot of business stability. The cons, you're going to consistently deliver value every month so you start at zero every single time the month comes around. Scope creep can be deadly if not managed properly and clients can cancel if they don't see ongoing benefit.

So again, the unlimited builds, especially this part here, incredibly, incredibly important. You want to use this after a successful project for clients who need ongoing maintenance or for services that deliver continuous value like lead generation. So, pricing. Businesses will only pay you 5 to 10 times the value that they receive as a fundamental rule or principle to follow.

So if you charge 5k, they need to get 25 to 50k in benefit. If you charge 20k, they need to get 100 to 200 plus k in benefit. This applies monthly too. So a 2k a month retainer means that they're consistently getting 10 to 20k a month in value.

Now, how do you calculate value? Well, if your lead gen system brought them 10 extra clients at 3k a month each, that's 30k a month in new revenue. So a 3k retainer is a bit of a no-brainer. If your system gives the founders about 10 hours a week and with that, they can close an extra four deals valued at 5k, then you can charge 8k one time and they'll make the money back within a month because they've made an extra 20k per month.

You can charge 8k. This 20k per month, it could last forever. It could last two months. If it lasts two months, then congratulations, 8 into 40 is 5.

That is your 5x value right there. So the bigger the business, the bigger the absolute numbers. Because a 5% uplift for a 20k a month company is a grand, but for a 200k a month company, it's 10k, which is why companies doing less than 30k a month will often bulk at your prices. They literally can't afford to pay you or really anybody else what you're worth because the math doesn't work for them.

So you want to focus on bigger clients as soon as you have your first case study. Now, this is kind of a really important metaphor for what you would need to pay attention to when it comes to time to look at your offers and it's called the onion peel approach. Your first offer will not be your best. It never is.

That's fine. There will also be different things that you're going to need to add to your offer over time that you won't know until you've sold it a few times. Business growth is about iteration, not perfection. So the cycle that actually occurs is as follows.

You want to create your initial offer based on AI market research and the above offers and everything else that I've told you so far. Then you want to launch it, take it to market, start trying to sell it, talk to prospects, get on sales calls, close and fulfill. Then you want to gather feedback. What objections are you hearing?

What problems emerged during delivery? What do clients say was most valuable? What did you hate doing? What didn't actually deliver any value to the client that you spent a ton of time doing in the first place?

Then you refine. You adjust your messaging, you adjust your pricing, you adjust your scope, you adjust your deliverables and then you'd repeat. You just take refined offer back to market and then you do more and more and you deliver more and more value and generate more and more revenue. Each cycle, you're peeling back another layer and you're getting closer to the perfect offer for your niche.

So the way to gather feedback, you can do it during sales calls by listening for how they describe their problems and that language becomes your marketing language. After delivery, you can ask people what was most valuable about the service. The answers might actually surprise you and reveal to you what you should actually be emphasizing more when you sell or what you shouldn't be selling at all. When you get objections, every objection is a signal.

It's about trust, urgency, price, fit. Which one is it about? Use these to refine your positioning. And this is not a one-time exercise.

It's continuous. I'm still doing it to this day, 18 months down the line. So the best agencies are constantly refining their offers based on real market feedback and not just their own assumptions. So that's kind of everything there.

So for you, understanding the problems for the niche is the first step. Understanding how problems naturally emerge is the second step. Deciding if you're going to do a project or a retainer, I would honestly start with a intro offer, which is a project, and then a main offer, which is a bigger project after that, and then move into continual servicing for a lower retainer just for a little bit of extra trickling of LTV so you don't go down to zero after they're closed. And how much value in dollars does your solution create for the client?

And also what's included in the scope and what's considered additional work? These are all questions that you need to ask yourself. Some of these you don't have the answer to now, which is just natural, but others are things that you can 100% think about now and I recommend that you start thinking about them right now as well, especially when it comes to the problems that you're solving and that problem solution loop. If you can think about what a problem solution loop is for your op system, your sell system, your DCM system, or your chatbot right now, you know exactly what you're trying to sell and that's the entire purpose of this video and that's exactly what I wanted to get across.

So that's offers done.

The biggest lever that you can pull when it comes to making ad creative that converts is doing an audience conversion report that comes from doing deep customer research. We're looking for not only desires and pain points and benefits like most people look for, we're looking for objections as well, reasons why they might not buy your product, behaviors, moments that happen that people usually do so you can call them out on it, and also the terminology that they use. Do they say, I wake up with a hangover, or do they say, I woke up like I got hit by the train? If you use the right words, if you use the same words that they use, they're going to see the ad and go, oh my god, it's meta spying on me.

And if you do that, they're more likely to go and click on the ad because they go, okay, this is really well targeted. Or they're going to be like, oh, this really speaks to me, I'm going to go to your website, and now I'm more warmed up because this brand clearly understands me. And the way we do that is by looking at Reddit forums, reviews people leave on your products and your competitors, and lastly, looking at TikTok comments. misconceptions, objections, golden nuggets from the reviews. Research Document Creation: Part 1
BONUS: Ad Creative Masterclass

Research LLM Prompt:

You are an expert audience researcher and copy strategist. You are given audience data that includes the following fields: pain_points failed_solutions desired_outcomes objections misconceptions golden_nuggets language_notes Objective: Analyze and synthesize this data into a clean, structured format using the following exact sections: Categorized Insights  Top Pain Points Format (in tabular form): Pain Point → Short, clear title capturing the core frustration. Description → 1–2 lines summarizing the emotional reality behind it. Group similar issues where appropriate (e.g., brake issues + overheating = Recurring Mechanical Failures).  Only include pain points relevant to the brand’s ICP, product, and service. Ignore off-topic or irrelevant entries.  Failed Solutions Format (in tabular form): Attempt → What users tried. Why It Failed → Why it didn’t solve the problem. Group similar failed attempts if needed (e.g., dealership repairs, DIY fixes).  Only include attempts tied to the brand’s core offer or target problem.  Desired Outcomes Format (in tabular form): Outcome → Desired state the user wants. Explanation → Why that matters to them emotionally or practically.  Objections Format (in tabular form): Objection → User hesitation captured in simple, natural phrasing. Real Quote/Paraphrase → Write it like a Redditor would speak, using natural skepticism and casual tone.  Misconceptions Format (in tabular form): Misconception → Wrong belief the audience holds. Clarification → Correct understanding written simply.  Golden Nuggets (Quotes from Reddit) Format: Take the golden_nuggets entries. If the golden nugget already sounds like a natural Reddit comment, keep it verbatim. If the quote sounds too formal or clunky, rewrite it using the style in language_notes (DIY tone, slang, contractions, emotional phrasing). Maintain honesty — no invented quotes. Focus on quotes expressing: Frustration Skepticism Humor/sarcasm Hopelessness DIY struggle  ONLY include nuggets directly tied to the brand’s ICP, product, or service. Ignore irrelevant ones. Strategy Implications for [Brand Name] Format: Opportunity | How [Brand] Can Win ------------|-------------------- Summarize practical, marketing-relevant opportunities from the audience’s real experiences.  ICP Language Analysis Based on language_notes, summarize: Natural tone (formal vs informal) Emotional style (skeptical, stressed, proud, fed up, hopeful) Vocabulary (specific mechanical terms, warranty phrases, slang words) Copywriting Tips: How to speak exactly like the ICP. Use real examples where possible ("pads and discs", "lot-pack", "safe to drive", "I don't get it").  Key Personas Format: Persona Name ("Nickname") Age Range Quick Summary: 1–2 lines of their situation and emotional needs. Desire: Pain point: Objection: Lifestyle: How they perceive risk: What activities they do: Their opinions: Their interests: Their values: How they speak:  Important Rules: Stay 100% true to the CSV data. Use language from the raw threads and reviews to guide rewrites whenever golden nuggets need to sound more natural. Ignore and exclude any data irrelevant to the brand’s target audience, offer, or service. Group and synthesize carefully without inventing new ideas. Keep the final output clean, highly readable, and marketing-useful.

As you can see here, the questions we ask are the name of the client, the email, the niche that they're in, their channel URL, are they a returning client?

Now, the other thing you have to do is set up a Google Drive with a clients folder. You should have this anyway, but just go to Google Drive, create a folder called clients. That's all you need. You can see in here, I've got the folder name clients and I've got myself already in here along with their test client.

So that's why when it came to returning client, I set it to true. I just said, yes, they're a returning client. So that information then goes to the parser. And then there's three different sections that runs through.

This one decides that if they are a returning client, sorry, no, if they have a YouTube channel input, because not all of your clients will have a YouTube channel, but if they have a YouTube channel, it scrapes some of their most recent videos using Apefy. Then it sends that data to the merge node. The other if statement says that if they are a returning client, then it searches your client's folder for the client's name, finds their last created script and sends that to the merge node too. And then this agent looks for more information on the client, does deep research using perplexity to get a ton of information about the client and context.

You can see here, we got a big comprehensive market intelligence report on me just using perplexity. There is the prompt you can see in here what it looks for. It looks for the creator business profile analysis, their YouTube channel deep dive, content strategy, competitive landscape, all this stuff. Just goes to a full deep dive on the client.

Actually, if I go back here again, you'll see it says you're conducting a market intelligence research on me, monitoring research me, my channel, and other people, and then just more information we got from the form. So after that, all that information is taken and put together. So we have my YouTube videos, we have my client research, and we have previous videos that this AI has created that are in the client folder. This goes to a data intelligence agent.

And this basically does another structured analysis of the client researching information and looking for things like content opportunities, competitor insights, audience behavior, things like that. That thing goes to a YouTube category agent. And all this does determine what YouTube category the video should be created in. So we can see here, it says the category should be business and entrepreneurship with a confidence level 95 and explains why it thinks that.

Then we go to the audience persona agent, and this creates a detailed audience persona. So based on the information we got from all the other parts, the data intelligence agent, the client research agent, it will create a basic audience persona. Demographics are people aged 30 to 45, male, location, primarily developed English-speaking markets, education, income, all these sort of things. Basically, you're coming up with who your likely audience viewers are.

Then we create a content strategy from all of this information. This creates content pillars, content types and formats, publishing schedule, video concept, SEO strategy, all that sort of stuff there. Again, based on our previous information from the other agents. The whole time here, we're passing through the data collected by other agents.

Finally, we get to the script writer agent. This script writer will do a few things. It will obviously write the script, but using the information from previous agents, it gets the content strategy, the target audience, the market intelligence report. It also looks for our previous AI-generated YouTube script.

This is so that we don't keep making the same script each time, because if we're doing the same research, get the same information for the client over and over, it could very likely produce the same videos each time. So then it sends it the most recent YouTube script generated and says, don't make this script again, essentially. Then it gives it examples of other clients' other scripts. Again, if they don't have other scripts from YouTube for their YouTube videos, that's totally fine.

It'll just use all the other information. Then it writes the script, as you can see over here. Now, we could be done there, but we're not. So the next thing we do is we make an SEO package based on this.

So it comes up with suggestions on how to improve the script based on information we've gathered from professional YouTubers and professional script writers. Then it sends those edits to the script improver agent, which takes the original script and improves it based on the suggestions given by the previous quality reviewer agent. Then we send that over here to our final results aggregator, just sorts things properly in the right kind of string names and things. You have a copywriter, somebody who writes your emails, all the text on the emails, and then you have the designer who's putting the pretty designs, putting in the brand assets and everything there. So that's typically what we're looking at right here for how it's used. So that's like a very broad overview of the email of what an email agency is.

Now email sending platforms. So these are platforms that e-commerce brands have set up that are connected to their store. And on these platforms, you're able to create sign-up forms, hold your list, create automations, and send emails for brands. It'll house everything for you.

And so the main platforms are going to be Klaviyo, which is best option, and then OmniSend is coming up right now. Good option for brands on a budget, but most often you are going to be using Klaviyo. Again, it's just going to hold. It's where you can set up pop-up forms, set up automations where, like, if somebody abandons a cart, Klaviyo will recognize that, and then you can set up an email that'll send to those people who abandon a cart and then, like, hey, finish your order, that sort of stuff.

And then it allows you to track how much revenue your emails are making. You could send emails from Gmail, but you're not going to be able to send to that many people, and you're not going to be able to track your sales. So that's why we use these platforms. And so every brand is going to have one of these platforms that they use, and Klaviyo is the most used one.

So that's the email-sending platforms. Now the last thing I want to touch on is just the different aspects of email marketing because there are three different parts of email marketing. We have your list growth, your pop-up forms. So pretty self-explanatory, growing your list.

If you want to see a ton of examples, here's just, like, Alia. These are, like, the sort of pop-ups that brands can set up. You can do this inside of Klaviyo or in a platform like Alia where it's, like, hey, here's a discount. Give us your email, something like that.

And you can get fancy by asking a question and then asking for their email address. But this is what we are doing, and this is super important to nail your pop-up form because this is how you grow the list. And then you have your campaigns. So I like to think of this as casting a wide net.

It's an email blast just sent to people that you have their email. And so that's what a campaign is. Typically, we're sending two to four of these campaigns per week. You can see these big brands sending these campaigns, like, almost every day.

But really, until you're doing over a mil a month, until a brand is doing over a mil a month, you really don't need to be sending every day. We want to be sending usually, like, three times per week is a good sweet spot. And this is where you're sending things like back in stock, sale emails, new product releases. And then you have, like, the educational emails, which is mostly what you want to be doing.

Just, like, reminding of your brand and things like that, like this example. What to bring, Camp Kitchen Edition. We made it easy to get out the door with our packing checklist. And so stuff like this, where you don't always need to – you don't need to be sending only discounts to make sales.

You can do stuff like this and just remind of your product. So those are the campaigns. And then we have our flows, which are, for me, I think of, like, campaigns casting a wide net. And then flows is, like, super targeted.

You're targeting specific people at a certain point in their journey. So automated emails will fire when a customer does a specific action. So we're going to be going over all these core flows and whatnot and what these core flows are. But an example is, like, the welcome flow.

So we're going to send somebody a sequence of emails when they give us their email address right here. So we're going to send them an email being, like, hey, here's your discount code. Here's a little bit of information about our brand. Here's our best sellers.

So we'll set up a couple emails being, like, hey, your discount's about to expire, things like that. That's a welcome flow. And you have, like, our abandonment flows. So there are different abandonment flows.

So if somebody abandons a cart, they add an item to their cart, but then they leave. We want a couple of emails in place being, like, hey, get your cart back. Or overcoming objections, anything like that. You've abandoned checkout.

Somebody goes a step further, they go to checkout, and then they leave. We have browse abandoned. Somebody views a product. They don't add it to cart or anything.

They just click on the product page, and then they leave. We have a couple emails in place being, like, hey, did you like this? What can we do to help? Things like that.

Then you have, like, post-purchase. So right after somebody purchases, what emails do we send them? To try to get them to come back. So those are the different flows, and that's what we're setting up.

So this is literally all that we're doing for email marketing. We're setting up these pop-up forms, and then ideally optimizing, testing these. We're sending consistent campaigns, which when you're working with brands, it's going to be the bulk of it. It's sending these consistent email campaigns over time, like three times per week.

And then you're setting up these automated flows, which you set up once, and then they're going to continue to fire. And then obviously, ideally, you're optimizing these flows over time. So that is what email marketing is, and that is kind of just like a brief overview of what an email marketing agency is, why you need it, and everything there. So hopefully that was helpful.

## E-Com Email Marketing Agency / Deliverability Metrics

Lesson: https://learn.clientascension.com/products/ai-assisted-agency/categories/2158294126/posts/2190272100

Lesson ID: 2190272100

### Preserved transcript

Published video caption text; may contain transcription errors

So I wanted to briefly go over deliverability metrics and kind of where you want to be in stand as far as like all the metrics. I don't look too, too, too much into these besides open rates, which we'll talk about in a second. A lot of them, it's really hard to gauge metrics because every brand is different, every audience is different. It's really hard to say like this is the number you want to be at.

That's just not how it works. So it's very fluid. But like these are like general numbers of where you want to be open rates. We want to make sure we're above 45 percent across our flows and our campaigns.

If you're lower than 45 percent, all you can do is for the emails that you're sending in campaigns, if they're lower than 45 percent, just create a segment of people who have opened an email in the past 30 days and only send to those people. You pump your open rates just by only sending to people who open your emails. That helps a ton. If you send campaigns to those people, you'll slowly start increasing your reputation and then your flow open rates will start to rise as well.

So greater than 45 percent is where we want to be at with our open rates. Don't want to be lower than that. If you're lower, do that or there's going to be a six-week delivery recovery protocol in another module. So make sure you're doing that.

Click rates. So what's the rate at which somebody clicks your email? We want to be greater than 1 percent here ideally. Now, this is less of a deliverability thing and more of an email design and content thing, but I get asked about click rates a lot.

So ideally, we want to be at 1 percent. Big brands, sometimes you can have less. I have one brand whose average click rates are 0.6 percent, and they're eight figures.

We're sending to like a million-person list every time we're sending. And you know what? That's okay to be a little bit lower. That'll happen.

But we have perfect deliverability. Our inbox placement rate is super-duper high. And so it's like not as much of a concern. It's more of a design issue.

If you're a smaller brand, you're sending to less than 5,000 to 10,000 people, and you're under 1 percent, it's going to be a design thing. So refer to the design modules. Bounce rate, less than 1 percent. Ideally, way less than that, 0.5

percent. But bounce rate is essentially emails like that didn't get delivered for whatever reason. Either it's like a blocked email or it's a fake email that doesn't exist. Those are all bounces.

We want to make sure we have less than 1 percent on all of our emails. So you can just create an exclusion segment in your email sending, which is just like if somebody's bounced an email at least once over all time, then we're just going to remove them. So that's bounce rate. Make sure you're less than 1 percent.

Spam complaint rate. So this is tough to track because sometimes people will do it directly with Gmail and not in Klaviyo. But we want to be less than 0.01 percent.

0.05 percent is really where we want to be at. The spam complaint rate. This can harm your inbox placement.

So you want to make sure your spam is low. But it's tough to track. Really, you're going to be raising red flags if you're over like 0.1 to 2 percent.

But ideally, we want to be lower than 0.01 percent. Unsubscribe rate. This actually doesn't affect deliverability because unsubscribes are natural.

You want people to unsubscribe who don't want to receive your emails. Like that's totally fine. We want to be less than 0.5 percent though so that we can keep people on our list.

Unsubscribe rate. If you're lower, if you're higher than 0.5 percent, like 1 percent, then you probably have some issues going on with your content. You're not sending good enough emails to these people to keep them engaged in wanting to continue to be subscribed to you.

So these are the base metrics. Main one is open rates that we really want to pay attention to because that's going to have the biggest impact.

Look at revenue when you're testing your subject lines and preview text. That's all we care about. Maybe one has a slightly lower open rate, but it has more revenue. Those people who did open, they were more ready to purchase based on the subject line and preview text. And all we care about is revenue. That's what we want if we want to scale. [0:00] So let's talk about why segment. So the purpose of it. Segmentation allows you to pinpoint certain members of your list so you can gather data. That's one of the main things that I use segmentation for, gather data. And then also create targeted emails to send based on where they're at in the customer journey. So some benefits. The main benefits is you can make more sales from it if you do it the right way. You can improve your deliverability as long as you're focusing on content in targeting the right people. You can save time with automation. So putting people into segments and having automations to send emails to these people based on characteristics. And then a personalized customer experience. That's the other thing that you don't really see too much like on revenue. But having customized experience really helps like the customer makes them feel like valued. So basic use case, use cases kind of extending upon which we had before. So these are kind of like the four main use cases that you can use. So using engaged list for improved deliverability. So you can segment your general list for campaigns to only include people who have recently opened or clicked emails so that you ensure you're only sending people who want to open your emails.

[1:00] This is the biggest use of segmentation. And you should never be sending an email campaign to your whole email list. Except maybe like Black Friday or a massive announcement. Because the truth is a lot of people won't care about your brand. And a lot of people use fake email addresses. And so they're never going to open an email of yours. So by you continuing to send emails to these people who will never open your emails, they don't care about your brand, they changed email addresses, they used a fake email address. If you send to them, you're just ruining your deliverability. Because if an inbox provider sees you're sending emails to a lot of people and not a lot of people are opening them, that's going to tell Google, be like, hey, not a lot of people want to receive these emails. Not a lot of people opened it. Let's send them to spam. And so if you can just only send to people who have opened your emails before, it's a huge difference on your deliverability in the long run and make sure that you will continue to land in the inbox. And then the next one, two interested customers for more sales. So you can target people who have been like active on your site or have like added items to their cart, but haven't made a purchase and send them extra content to try to get them across the line. That's something extra that you can do. A lot of this stuff can be taken

[2:00] care of with your flows and your automations, setting up just like your abandoned cart flow, for example, to send emails, people who abandoned a cart, but you can also send campaigns on top of this, like maybe a couple of times a month, you send a special discount to people who have abandoned an item recently, but they haven't purchased. So that's something else that you can do. You can also do a targeted campaigns based on product interests. So people who show interest in certain products or categories, you can send them information. Like maybe you have a new colorway that came out for like your shoes, your, your clothing story of all sorts of different stuff, but you only want to send this like my growth campaign to people who have bought shoes before or have looked at your shoes before. You can do that and send like more targeted campaigns to them without bothering the rest of your list. That's another use case. And another one, remove unengaged profiles for improved deliverability. So kind of tied to number one, but kind of the opposite, removing the unengaged profile. So it's important to always track and suppress people who haven't been engaging with your emails since customers will just naturally churn. You can't expect someone to be with you until they're 80 years old. They're going to naturally,

[3:00] there's going to be a point where they stop opening your emails. So since they aren't opening your emails, you want to remove them from your list so that you aren't harming your deliverability, A, to not send to them. And then also to save your Klaviyo bill so that you can know to suppress these people so that you're not getting charged by your active profile.

The "D100 Machine" with Jake Mamrak
Guest Coaching Calls

The tech stack:
• Claude Code: Builds the funnels, the pages that replace Gamma docs, and the whole D100 Machine UI
• Vercel: hosts the live pages + funnels and handles the tracking
• GitHub: where each build gets pushed, then Vercel auto-deploys from it
• Anymail finder: Email lookups (optional based on deliverable)
• OpenAI: ad image generation (optional based on deliverable)

*How I'd build it again:*
1. Start with the asset you want on to create as your main deliverable (mine was a quiz funnel). 10x easier if it's already built in Claude Code.
2. Have Claude Code recreate your existing Gamma doc as a simple HTML page.
3.Have Claude code build a front-end UI with a Kanban board to track every client and their status as they move through your pipeline
4. Upload both your asset + simple HTML page to your Claude Code project and tell it create a "+New Client" feature in the UI. Upon clicking create a new client, you can tell it to collect fields for inputs of info needed to fill in the assets (business name, contact name, logo etc). Then tell it to dynamically fill in the asset + HTML based on the information inside of the new client creation. Finally, tell Claude code to push all completed deliverable to github + vercel so you can share.

This is a 30,000 foot overview on how this was built,  but DM me if you want me to go deeper on any piece
